[**Figure 4.4**](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-fig-0004) TF representation of an epileptic waveform in (a) for different time resolutions using the Hanning window of (b) 1 ms, and (c) 2 ms duration.

(4.23)![equation](images/c4-disp-0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>&#981;</mi></msub></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mi>a</mi></msqrt></mfrac><mi>W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi>&#981;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mi>a</mi></mfrac></mfenced><mfrac><mtext mathvariant="italic">dadb</mtext><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></math> 

where

(4.24)![equation](images/c4-disp-0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>&#981;</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><mfrac><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>v</mi></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>v</mi></mfenced></mrow><mi>v</mi></mfrac><mi mathvariant="italic">dv</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mn>0</mn></msubsup><mfrac><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>v</mi></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>&#981;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>v</mi></mfenced></mrow><mi>v</mi></mfrac><mi mathvariant="italic">dv</mi></math> 

Although often it is considered that *ψ*(*t*) = *ϕ*(*t*), other alternatives for *ϕ*(*t*) may enhance certain features for some specific applications [\[20\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0020). The reconstruction of *f*(*t*) is subject to having *C*[*ϕ*] defined (admissibility condition). The case *ψ*(*t*) = *ϕ*(*t*) implies ![images](images/c4-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>0</mn></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, i.e. the mean of the wavelet function is zero.

 

#### 4.5.1.2 Examples of Continuous Wavelets

Different waveforms/wavelets/kernels have been defined for the continuous WTs. The most popular ones are given below.

Morlet's wavelet is a complex waveform defined as:

(4.25)![equation](images/c4-disp-0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></math> 

This wavelet may be decomposed into its constituent real and imaginary parts as:

(4.26)![equation](images/c4-disp-0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo mathvariant="italic">cos</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> (4.27)![equation](images/c4-disp-0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo mathvariant="italic">sin</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *b*[*0*] is a constant, and it is considered that b[0] > 0 to satisfy the admissibility condition. [Figure 4.5](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0005) shows respectively the real and imaginary parts.

The Mexican hat defined by Murenzi [\[17\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0017) is:

(4.28)![equation](images/c4-disp-0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>0.5</mn><msup><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msup></math> 

which is the second derivative of a Gaussian waveform (see [Figure 4.6](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0006)).

 

#### 4.5.1.3 Discrete‐Time Wavelet Transform

In order to process digital signals a discrete approximation of the wavelet coefficients is required. The discrete wavelet transform (DWT) can be derived in accordance with the sampling theorem if we process a frequency band‐limited signal.

The continuous form of the WT may be discretized with some simple considerations on the modification of the wavelet pattern by dilation. Since generally the wavelet function ![images](images/c4-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#968;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced></math> is not band limited, it is necessary to suppress the values outside the frequency components above half the sampling frequency to avoid aliasing (overlapping in frequency) effects.

![Figure 4.5 Morlet's wavelet: real and imaginary parts shown respectively in (a) and (b).](images/c04f005.gif)

[**Figure 4.5**](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-fig-0005) Morlet's wavelet: real and imaginary parts shown respectively in (a) and (b).

![Figure 4.6 Mexican hat wavelet.](images/c04f006.gif)

[**Figure 4.6**](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-fig-0006) Mexican hat wavelet.

A Fourier space may be used to compute the transform scale‐by‐scale. The number of elements for a scale can be reduced if the frequency bandwidth is also reduced. This requires a band‐limited wavelet. The decomposition proposed by Littlewood and Paley [\[21\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0021) provides a very nice illustration of the reduction of elements scale‐by‐scale. This decomposition is based on an iterative dichotomy of the frequency band. The associated wavelet is well localized in Fourier space where it allows a reasonable analysis to be made although not in the original space. The search for a discrete transform, which is well localized in both spaces leads to multiresolution analysis.

 

#### 4.5.1.4 Multiresolution Analysis

Multiresolution analysis results from the embedded subsets generated by the interpolations (or down‐sampling and filtering) of the signal at different scales. A function *f*(*t*) is projected at each step *j* onto the subset *V*[*j*] . This projection is defined by the scalar product *c*[*j*] (*k*) of *f*(*t*) with the scaling function *φ*(*t*), which is dilated and translated:

(4.29)![equation](images/c4-disp-0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where 〈·, ·〉 denotes an inner product and *φ*(*t*) has the property:

(4.30)![equation](images/c4-disp-0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>&#966;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><mi>h</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi>&#966;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where the right side is convolution of *h* and *ϕ*. By taking the Fourier transform of both sides:

[(4.31)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0031)![equation](images/c4-disp-0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mi>&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> 

where ![images](images/c4-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> and ![images](images/c4-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> are the Fourier transforms of *h*(*t*) and *ϕ*(*t*) respectively. For a discrete frequency space (i.e. using the DFT) the above equation ([Eq. 4.31](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0031)) permits the computation of the wavelet coefficient *C*[*j* + 1](*k*) from *C*[*j*] (*k*) directly. If we start from *C* [0](*k*) we compute all *C*[*j*] (*k*), with *j* > 0, without directly computing any other scalar product:

(4.32)![equation](images/c4-disp-0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi>h</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *k* is the discrete frequency index.

At each step, the number of scalar products is divided by two and consequently the signal is smoothed. Using this procedure, the first part of a filter bank is built up. In order to restore the original data, Mallat uses the properties of orthogonal wavelets, but the theory has been generalized to a large class of filters by introducing two other filters ![images](images/c4-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#732;</mo></mover></math> and ![images](images/c4-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#732;</mo></mover></math>, also called conjugate filters. The restoration is performed with:

(4.33)![equation](images/c4-disp-0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>l</mi></msub><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>l</mi></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>l</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>l</mi></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>l</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *w*[*j* + 1](∙) are the wavelet coefficients at the scale *j +* 1 defined later in this section. For an exact restoration, two conditions have to be satisfied for the conjugate filters:

*Anti‐aliasing condition*:

[(4.34)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0034)![equation](images/c4-disp-0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> 

*Exact restoration:*

[(4.35)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0035)![equation](images/c4-disp-0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> 

In the decomposition, the input is successively convolved with the two filters *H* (low frequencies) and *G* (high frequencies). Each resulting function is decimated by suppression of one sample out of two. The high frequency signal is left, and we iterate with the low frequency signal (left side of [Figure 4.7](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0007)). In the reconstruction, we restore the sampling by inserting a zero between each sample, then we convolve with the conjugate filters ![images](images/c4-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#732;</mo></mover></math> and ![images](images/c4-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#732;</mo></mover></math>, we add the resulting outputs and we multiply the result by 2. We iterate up to the smallest scale (right side of [Figure 4.7](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0007)). Orthogonal wavelets correspond to the restricted case where:

(4.36)![equation](images/c4-disp-0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="italic">&#960;&#969;</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math>  ![Figure 4.7 The filter bank associated with the multiresolution analysis.](images/c04f007.gif)

[**Figure 4.7**](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-fig-0007) The filter bank associated with the multiresolution analysis.

(4.37)![equation](images/c4-disp-0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> (4.38)![equation](images/c4-disp-0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>G</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> 

and

(4.39)![equation](images/c4-disp-0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></math> 

We can easily see that this set satisfies the two basic [relations (4.72)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0074) and [(4.73)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0075). Among various wavelets, Daubechies wavelets are the only compact solutions to satisfy the above conditions. For bi‐orthogonal wavelets we have the relations:

(4.40)![equation](images/c4-disp-0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="italic">&#960;&#969;</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math> (4.41)![equation](images/c4-disp-0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="italic">&#960;&#969;</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math> 

and

(4.42)![equation](images/c4-disp-0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> 

The relations [(4.34)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0034) and [(4.35)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0035) have to be also satisfied. A large class of compact wavelet functions can be used. Many sets of filters were proposed, especially for coding [\[22\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0022). It was shown that the choice of these filters must be guided by the regularity of the scaling and the wavelet functions. The complexity is proportional to *N*. The algorithm provides a pyramid of *N* elements.

 

#### 4.5.1.5 Wavelet Transform Using Fourier Transform

Consider the scalar products *c* [0](*k*) = 〈*f*(*t*). *φ*(*t* − *k*)〉 for continuous wavelets. If *φ*(*t*) is band limited to half of the sampling frequency, the data are correctly sampled. The data at the resolution *j* = 1 are:

(4.43)![equation](images/c4-disp-0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>.</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>&#966;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mfrac><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

and we can compute the set *c* [1](*k*) from *c* [0](*k*) with a discrete‐time filter with frequency response ![images](images/c4-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math>:

(4.44)![equation](images/c4-disp-0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#60;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

and for ![images](images/c4-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></math> and ![images](images/c4-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8704;</mo><mspace width="0.25em"/><mtext>integer</mtext><mspace width="0.12em"/><mi>m</mi></math>

(4.45)![equation](images/c4-disp-0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> 

Therefore, an estimate of the coefficients is:

(4.46)![equation](images/c4-disp-0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

The cut‐off frequency is reduced by a factor 2 at each step, allowing a reduction of the number of samples by this factor. The wavelet coefficients at the scale *j* + 1 are:

(4.47)![equation](images/c4-disp-0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></mrow></msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></mrow></msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

and they can be computed directly from *C*[*j*] by:

(4.48)![equation](images/c4-disp-0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *G* is the following discrete‐time filter:

(4.49)![equation](images/c4-disp-0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#936;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#60;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

and for ![images](images/c4-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></math> and ![images](images/c4-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8704;</mo><mtext>integer</mtext><mspace width="0.12em"/><mi>m</mi></math>:

(4.50)![equation](images/c4-disp-0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> 

The frequency band is also reduced by a factor of two at each step. These relationships are also valid for DWT following [Section 4.5.1.4](#c04.xhtml#c4-sec-0010).

 

#### 4.5.1.6 Reconstruction

The reconstruction of the data from its wavelet coefficients can be performed step‐by‐step, starting from the lowest resolution. At each scale, we compute:

(4.51)![equation](images/c4-disp-0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> (4.52)![equation](images/c4-disp-0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> 

we look for *C*[*j*] knowing *C*[*j* + 1], *W*[*j* + 1], *h*, and *g*. Then ![images](images/c4-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> is restored by minimizing:

(4.53)![equation](images/c4-disp-0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

using a least minimum squares estimator. ![images](images/c4-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> and ![images](images/c4-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> are weight functions which permit a general solution to the restoration of ![images](images/c4-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math>. The relationship from of ![images](images/c4-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> is in the form of:

(4.54)![equation](images/c4-disp-0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mover accent="true"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>j</mi></msup><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where the conjugate filters have the expressions:

[(4.55)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0055)![equation](images/c4-disp-0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> [(4.56)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0056)![equation](images/c4-disp-0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msup><mi>G</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> 

It is straightforward to see that these filters satisfy the exact reconstruction condition given in [Eq. (4.35)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0035). In fact, [Eqs. (4.55)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0055) and [(4.56)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0056) give the general solutions to this equation. In this analysis, the Shannon sampling condition is always respected. No aliasing exists, so that the anti‐aliasing condition [(4.76)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0078) is not necessary.

The denominator is reduced if we choose:

(4.57)![equation](images/c4-disp-0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>G</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msqrt></math> 

This corresponds to the case where the wavelet is the difference between the squares of two resolutions:

(4.58)![equation](images/c4-disp-0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>&#936;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

The reconstruction algorithm then carries out the following steps:

1.  Compute the fast Fourier transform (FFT) of the signal at the low resolution.
2.  Set *j* to *n*[*p*] (number of WT resolutions); perform the following iteration steps:
3.  Compute the FFT of the wavelet coefficients at the scale *j*.
4.  Multiply the wavelet coefficients *W*[*j*] by ![images](images/c4-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover></math>.
5.  Multiply the signal coefficients at the lower resolution *C*[*j*] by ![images](images/c4-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover></math>.
6.  The inverse Fourier transform of ![images](images/c4-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mover accent="true"><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mover accent="true"><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover></math> gives the coefficients *C*[*j*‐1].
7.  *j* = *j* − 1 and return to step 3.

The use of a band‐limited scaling function allows a reduction of sampling at each scale and limits the computation complexity.

The WT has been widely used in EEG signal analysis. Its application to seizure detection, especially for neonates, modelling of the neuron potentials, and the detection of EP and ERPs will be discussed in the corresponding chapters of this book.

 

### 4.5.2 Synchro‐Squeezed Wavelet Transform

The synchro‐squeezing wavelet transform (SSWT) has been introduced as a post‐processing technique to enhance the TF spectrum obtained by applying the WT [\[23\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0023). Assuming that the input *f*(*t*) is a pure harmonic signal (*f*(*t*) = *Acos*(*ωt*)), using Plancherel's theorem, the following equations are derived from [(4.20)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0020) [\[23\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0023):

![equation](images/c4-disp-0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><msup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mover><mi>&#968;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mi>a</mi></mfrac></mfenced><mi mathvariant="italic">dt</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#949;</mi></mfenced><msup><mi>a</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mover accent="true"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="italic">a&#949;</mi></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ib&#949;</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="italic">d&#949;</mi></math> [(4.59)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0060)![equation](images/c4-disp-0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mspace width="3.3em"/><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>&#948;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>a</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mover accent="true"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="italic">a&#949;</mi></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ib&#949;</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="italic">d&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>A</mi><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><msup><mi>a</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></msup><mover accent="true"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="italic">a&#969;</mi></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ib&#969;</mi></msup></math> 

One assumption in the above equation ([Eq. 4.59](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0060)) is that the selected mother wavelet is concentrated within the positive energy range, which means ![images](images/c4-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#949;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, for *ε* < 0. If ![images](images/c4-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#968;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#949;</mi></mfenced></math> is concentrated around *ε* = *ω* [0], then, *W*(*a*, *b*) is concentrated around *a* = *ω* [0]/*ω*. This is spread out over a region of the horizontal line (e.g. *a* = *ω* [0]/*ω*). In the situation where *ω* is almost but not exactly similar to the actual instantaneous frequency (IF) of the input signal, then, *W*(*a*, *b*) has non‐zero energy. By synchro‐squeezing, the idea is to move this energy away from *ω*. The proposed method in the SSWT aims to reassign the frequency locations which are closer to the actual IF to obtain an enhanced spectrum. To do that, first, the candidate IFs are calculated. For these IFs, *W*(*a*, *b*) ≠ 0:

(4.60)![equation](images/c4-disp-0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#969;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfrac><mi>&#8706;</mi><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi>W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

Considering the selected pure harmonic signal *f*(*t*) = *Acos*(*ωt*), it is simple to observe that *ω*(*a*, *b*) = *ω*. The candidate IFs are exploited to recover the actual frequencies. Therefore, a reallocation technique has been used to map the time domain into TF domain using (*b*, *a*) ⇒ (*b*, *ω*(*a*, *b*)). Based on this, each value of *W*(*a*, *b*) (computed at discrete values of *a*[*k*] ) is re‐allocated into *T*[*f*] (*ω*[*l*] , *b*) as provided in the following equation ([Eq. 4.61](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0062)):

[(4.61)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0062)![equation](images/c4-disp-0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mo>&#8710;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8804;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8710;</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></munder><mi>W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>3</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msubsup><msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mo>&#8710;</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi>k</mi></msub></math> 

where *ω*[*l*] is the nearest frequency to the original point *ω*(*a*, *b*), ∆*ω* is the width of the frequency bins ![images](images/c4-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mtext>&#8710;</mtext><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mtext>&#8710;</mtext><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced></math>,∆*ω* = *ω*[*l*]  − *ω*[*l* − 1], and (∆*a*) [*k*] = *a*[*k*]  − *a*[*k* − 1]. *T*[*f*] (*ω*[*l*] , *b*) represents the synchro‐squeezed transform at the centres *ω*[*l*] of consecutive frequency bins. For each fixed time point *b*, the reassigned frequencies should be estimated for all scales using [Eq. (4.103)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0105). For each desired IF of *ω*[*l*] , *T*[*f*] (*ω*[*l*] , *b*) is calculated using summation of all *W*(*a*[*k*] , *b*) considering that the distance between the reassigned frequency *ω*(*a*[*k*] , *b*) and *ω*[*l*] must be within the specified frequency bin width (∆*ω*). It has been shown that the original signal can be reconstructed after the synchro‐squeezing process [\[23\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0023).

 

### 4.5.3 Ambiguity Function and the Wigner–Ville Distribution

The ambiguity function for a continuous time signal is defined as:

(4.62)![equation](images/c4-disp-0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">j&#965;t</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="italic">dt</mi></math> 

This function has its maximum value at the origin as

(4.63)![equation](images/c4-disp-0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="italic">dt</mi></math> 

As an example, if we consider a continuous time signal consisting of two modulated signals with different carrier frequencies such as

![equation](images/c4-disp-0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced></math> (4.64)![equation](images/c4-disp-0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mspace width="1.57em"/><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></math> 

The ambiguity function *A*[*x*] (*τ,ν*) will be in the form of:

(4.65)![equation](images/c4-disp-0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mtext>cross terms</mtext></math> 

This concept is very important in separation of signals using the TF domain. This will be addressed in the context of blind source separation (BSS) later in this chapter. [Figure 4.8](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0008) demonstrates this concept.

The Wigner–Ville frequency distribution of a signal *x*(*t*) is then defined as the two‐dimensional Fourier transform of the ambiguity function:

(4.66)![equation](images/c4-disp-0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mspace width="-26.5em"/><msub><mi>X</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo mathvariant="italic">d&#957;d&#964;</mtext><mspace width="6.8em"/><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo
