close=")"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">j&#965;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></msup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">j&#969;&#964;</mi></mrow></msup><mtext mathvariant="italic">d&#946;d&#957;d&#964;</mtext></math> 

which changes to the dual form of the ambiguity function as:

(4.67)![equation](images/c4-disp-0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">j&#969;&#964;</mi></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="italic">d&#964;</mi></math> 

A quadratic form for the TF representation with the Wigner–Ville distribution can also be obtained using the signal in the frequency domain as:

(4.68)![equation](images/c4-disp-0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msup><mi>X</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#957;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mi>X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>&#957;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">j&#957;t</mi></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="italic">d&#957;</mi></math> 

The Wigner–Ville distribution is real and has very good resolution in both the time‐ and frequency‐domains. Also it has time and frequency support properties, i.e. if *x*(*t*) = 0 for | *t* | > *t*[*0*] , then *X*[*WV*] (*t*, *ω*) = 0 for | *t* | > *t*[*0*] , and if *X*(*ω*) = 0 for | *ω* | > *ω* [0], then *X*[*WV*] (*t*, *ω*) = 0 for | *ω* | > *ω* [0]. It has also both time‐marginal and frequency‐marginal conditions of the form:

(4.69)![equation](images/c4-disp-0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msub><mi>X</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi mathvariant="italic">dt</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

and

(4.70)![equation](images/c4-disp-0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msub><mi>X</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi mathvariant="italic">dt</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><mi>X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

If *x*(*t*) is the sum of two signals *x* [1](*t*) and *x* [2](*t*), i.e. *x*(*t*) = *x* [1](*t*) + *x* [2](*t*), the Wigner–Ville distribution of *x*(*t*) with respect to the distributions of *x* [1](*t*) and *x* [2](*t*) will be:

(4.71)![equation](images/c4-disp-0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>X</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo mathvariant="italic">Re</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><msub><msub><mi>X</mi><mn>12</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where Re{.} denotes the real part of a complex value and

[(4.72)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0074)![equation](images/c4-disp-0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>X</mi><mrow><mn>12</mn><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">j&#969;&#964;</mi></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="italic">d&#964;</mi></math> 

It is seen that the distribution is related to the spectra of both auto‐ and cross‐correlations. A pseudo‐Wigner–Ville distribution (PWVD) is defined by applying a window function, *w*(*τ*), centred at τ = 0 to the time‐based correlations, i.e.:

[(4.73)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0075)![equation](images/c4-disp-0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>X</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mi>w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#964;</mi></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">j&#969;&#964;</mi></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="italic">d&#964;</mi></math>  ![Figure 4.8 (a) A segment of a signal consisting of two modulated components, (b) ambiguity function for x 1(t) only, and (c) the ambiguity function for x(t) = x 1(t) + x 2(t).](images/c04f008.gif)

[**Figure 4.8**](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-fig-0008) (a) A segment of a signal consisting of two modulated components, (b) ambiguity function for *x* [1](*t*) only, and (c) the ambiguity function for *x*(*t*) = *x* [1](*t*) + *x* [2](*t*).

In order to suppress the undesired cross‐terms the two‐dimensional Wigner–Ville (WV) distribution may be convolved with a TF‐domain window. The window is a two‐dimensional lowpass filter, which satisfies the time and frequency‐marginal (uncertainty) conditions, as described earlier. This can be performed as:

(4.74)![equation](images/c4-disp-0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msub><mi>X</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">WV</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></mfenced><mi>&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></mfenced><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> 

where

(4.75)![equation](images/c4-disp-0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><msubsup><mo>&#8747;</mo><mrow><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>&#8734;</mo></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">j&#957;t</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">j&#969;&#964;</mi></mrow></msup><mtext mathvariant="italic">d&#957;d&#964;</mtext></math> 

and *φ*(*τ*, *ν*) is often selected from a set of well known waveforms called *Cohen's class*. The most popular member of the Cohen's class of functions is the bell‐shaped function defined as:

[(4.76)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0078)![equation](images/c4-disp-0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#966;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>&#957;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>&#960;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> 

A graphical illustration of such a function can be seen in [Figure 4.9](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0009). In this case the distribution is referred to as a Choi–Williams distribution.

The application of a discrete‐time form of the Wigner–Ville distribution to BSS will be discussed later in this chapter and its application to seizure detection has been explained in the chapter devoted to seizure. To improve the distribution a signal‐dependent kernel may also be used [\[24\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0024).

![Figure 4.9 Illustration of images for the Choi–Williams distribution.](images/c04f009.gif)

[**Figure 4.9**](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-fig-0009) Illustration of ![images](images/c4-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#981;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=","><mi>&#964;</mi><mi>v</mi></mfenced></math> for the Choi–Williams distribution.

 

## 4.6 Empirical Mode Decomposition

Empirical mode decomposition (EMD) may be considered as a multiresolution signal decomposition technique. EMD is an adaptive time–space analysis method suitable for processing nonstationary and nonlinear time series. EMD partitions a series into ‘modes’ namely, intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) in the time domain. Like Fourier and WTs EMD does not follow any physical concept. However, the modes may provide insight into various signals contained within the data and have distinct frequency bands/components.

EMD is based on The Hilbert–Huang transform (HHT) which is a way to decompose a signal into IMFs along with a trend and obtain IF data. Its difference from other common transforms like the Fourier transform, is that the HHT is more like an algorithm (an empirical approach) that can be applied to a data set, rather than a theoretical tool.

IMF represents a simple oscillatory mode as a counterpart to the simple harmonic function, but instead of constant amplitude and frequency in a simple harmonic component, an IMF can have variable amplitude and frequency along the time axis.

The procedure of extracting an IMF is called sifting. The sifting process is as follows \[[25](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0025), [26](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0026)\]:

1.  Identify all the local extrema in the test data.
2.  Connect all the local maxima by a cubic spline line as the upper envelope.
3.  Repeat the procedure for the local minima to produce the lower envelope.

The upper and lower envelopes should cover all the data between them. Their mean is *m* [1]. The difference between the data and *m* [1] is the first component *d* [1]:

(4.77)![equation](images/c4-disp-0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> 

Ideally, *d* [1] should satisfy the definition of an IMF, since the construction of *d* [1] described above should have made it symmetric and having all maxima positive and all minima negative. After the first round of sifting, a crest may become a local maximum. New extrema generated in this way actually reveal the proper modes lost in the initial examination. In the subsequent sifting process, *d* [1] can only be treated as a proto‐IMF. In the next step, *d* [1] is treated as data:

(4.78)![equation](images/c4-disp-0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>11</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>11</mn></msub></math> 

After repeated sifting up to *k* times, *d* [1] becomes an IMF, i.e.:

(4.79)![equation](images/c4-disp-0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> 

*C* [1] = *d* [1*k*] is considered as the first IMF of the signal *x*(*t*).

The iteration above can be stopped in different ways such as when the power (standard deviation) of the difference (between current and previous iteration) signal becomes less than a predefined threshold, or when the number of iterations reaches a reasonable number [\[27\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0027).

For calculation of the other IMFs:

(4.80)![equation](images/c4-disp-0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> 

The residue *r* [1] is then treated as the new signal and the same processing is applied to that. Therefore

(4.81)![equation](images/c4-disp-0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> 

The sifting process finally stops when the residue, *r*[*n*] , becomes a monotonic function from which no more IMFs can be extracted. From the above equations, it is induced that:

(4.82)![equation](images/c4-disp-0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">t</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">j</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></msub></math> 

This results in decomposition of the data into n‐empirical modes \[[25](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0025), [26](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0026)\].

Ensemble EMD (EEMD) is a noise assisted data analysis method. EEMD consists of ‘sifting’ an ensemble of white noise‐added signal. EEMD can separate scales naturally without any a priori subjective criterion selection as in the intermittence test for the original EMD algorithm. Complete ensemble EMD with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN) is a variation of the EEMD algorithm that provides an exact reconstruction of the original signal and a better spectral separation of the IMFs.

 

## 4.7 Coherency, Multivariate Autoregressive Modelling, and Directed Transfer Function

In some applications such as in detection and classification of finger movement, it is very useful to find out how the associated movement signals propagate within the neural network of the brain. As will be shown in [Chapter 16](#c16.xhtml), there is a consistent movement of the source signals from the occipital to temporal regions. It is also clear that during the mental tasks different regions within the brain communicate with each other. The interaction and cross‐talk among the EEG channels may be the only clue to understanding this process. This requires recognition of the transient periods of synchrony between various regions in the brain. These phenomena are not easy to observe by visual inspection of the EEGs. Therefore, some signal processing techniques have to be used in order to infer such causal relationships. One time series is said to be causal to another if the information contained in that time series enables the prediction of the other time series.

The spatial statistics of scalp EEG are usually presented as coherence in individual frequency bands, these coherences result both from correlations among neocortical sources and volume conduction through the tissues of the head, i.e. brain, cerebrospinal fluid, skull, and scalp. Therefore, spectral coherence [\[28\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0028) is a common method for determining the synchrony in EEG activity. Coherency is given as:

(4.83)![equation](images/c4-disp-0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">Co</mi><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}"><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ii</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">jj</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfrac></math> ![Figure 4.10 Cross‐spectral coherence for a set of three electrode EEGs, one second before the right‐finger movement. Each block refers to one electrode. By careful inspection of the figure, it is observed that the same waveform is transferred from Cz to C3.](images/c04f010.gif)

[**Figure 4.10**](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-fig-0010) Cross‐spectral coherence for a set of three electrode EEGs, one second before the right‐finger movement. Each block refers to one electrode. By careful inspection of the figure, it is observed that the same waveform is transferred from C[z] to C[3].

where ![images](images/c4-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msubsup><mi>X</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> is the Fourier transform of the cross‐correlation coefficients between channel *i* and channel *j* of the EEGs. [Figure 4.10](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0010) shows an example of the cross‐spectral coherence around one second prior to finger movement. A measure of this coherency, such as an average over a frequency band, is capable of detecting zero time‐lag synchronization and fixed time non‐zero time‐lag synchronization, which may occur when there is a significant delay between the two neuronal population sites [\[29\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0029). However, it does not provide any information on the directionality of the coupling between the two recording sites.

Granger causality (also called as Wiener–Granger causality) [\[30\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0030) is another measure, which attempts to extract and quantify the directionality from EEGs. Granger causality is based on bivariate AR estimates of the data. In a multichannel environment this causality is calculated from pair‐wise combinations of electrodes. This method has been used to evaluate the directionality of the source movement from the local field potential in the visual system of cats [\[31\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0031).

For multivariate data in a multichannel recording, however, application of the Granger causality is not computationally efficient \[[31](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0031), [32](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0032)\]. The directed transfer function (DTF) [\[33\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0033), as an extension of Granger causality, is obtained from multichannel data and can be used to detect and quantify the coupling directions. The advantage of the DTF over spectral coherence is that it can determine the directionality in the coupling when the frequency spectra of the two brain regions have overlapping spectra. The DTF has been adopted by some researchers for determining the directionality in the coupling \[[34](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0034), [35](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0035)\] since it has been demonstrated that [\[36\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0036) there is a directed flow of information or cross‐talk between the sensors around the sensory motor area before finger movement. The DTF is based on fitting the EEGs to an MVAR model. Assuming that **x**(*n*) is an *M*‐channel EEG signal, it can be modelled in vector form as:

[(4.84)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0086)![equation](images/c4-disp-0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where *n* is the discrete‐time index, *p* is the prediction order, **v**(*n*) is zero‐mean noise, and **L** [***k***] is generally an *M* × *p* matrix of prediction coefficients. A similar method to the Durbin algorithm for single‐channel signals, namely the Levinson–Wiggins–Robinson (LWR) algorithm is used to calculate the MVAR coefficients [\[14\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0014). The Akaike information criterion (AIC) [\[37\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0037) is also used for the estimation of prediction order *p*. By multiplying both sides of the above equation ([Eq. 4.84](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0086)) by **x**^(*T*) (*n* − *k*) and performing the statistical expectation the A set of Yule–Walker equation is obtained as [\[38\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0038):

(4.85)![equation](images/c4-disp-0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>;</mo><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> 

where **R**(*q*) = *E*\[**x**(*n*)**x**^(*T*) (*n* + *q*)\] is the covariance matrix of **x**(*n*), and the cross‐correlations of the signal and noise are zero since they are assumed uncorrelated. Similarly, the noise autocorrelation is zero for non‐zero shift since the noise samples are uncorrelated. The data segment is considered short enough for the signal to remain statistically stationary within that interval and long enough to enable accurate measurement of the prediction coefficients. Given the MVAR model coefficients, a multivariate spectrum can be achieved. Here it is assumed that the residual signal, **v**(*n*), is white noise. Therefore,

(4.86)![equation](images/c4-disp-0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> 

where

[(4.87)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0089)![equation](images/c4-disp-0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>p</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">j&#969;m</mi></mrow></msup></math> 

and **L**(0) = **I**. Rearranging the above equation ([Eq. 4.87](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0089)) and replacing noise by σ[v] ²**I** yields

(4.88)![equation](images/c4-disp-0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#215;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> 

which represents the model spectrum of the signals or the transfer matrix of the MVAR system. The DTF or causal relationship between channel *i* and channel *j* can be defined directly from the transform coefficients [\[32\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0032) given by:

(4.89)![equation](images/c4-disp-0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>&#920;</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

Electrode *i* is causal to *j* at frequency *f* if:

(4.90)![equation](images/c4-disp-0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>&#920;</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> 

A time‐varying DTF can also be generated (mainly to track the source signals) by calculating the DTF over short windows to achieve the short‐time DTF (SDTF) [\[32\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0032).

As an important feature in classification of left and right‐finger movements, or tracking the mental task related sources, SDTF plays an important role. Some results of using SDTF for detection and classification of finger movement have been given in the context of BCI.

 

## 4.8 Filtering and Denoising

The EEG signals are subject to noise and artefacts. Electrocardiograms (ECGs), electro‐oculograms (EOG) or eye blinks affect the EEG signals. Any multimodal recording such as EEG–functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) significantly disturbs the EEG signals because of both magnetic fields and the change in the blood oxygen level and sensitivity of oxygen molecule to the magnetic field (balisto‐cardiogram). Artefact removal from the EEGs will be explained in the related chapters. The noise in the EEGs, however, may be estimated and mitigated using adaptive and non‐adaptive filtering techniques.

The EEG signals contain neuronal information below 100 Hz (in many applications the information lies below 30 Hz). Any frequency component above these frequencies can be simply removed by using lowpass filters. In the cases where the EEG data acquisition system is unable to cancel out the 50 Hz line frequency (due to a fault in grounding or imperfect balancing of the inputs to the differential amplifiers associated with the EEG system) a notch filter is used to remove it.

The nonlinearities in the recording system related to the frequency response of the amplifiers, if known, are compensated by using equalizing filters. However, the characteristics of the internal and external noises affecting the EEG signals are often unknown. The noise may be characterized if the signal and noise subspaces can be accurately separated. Using principal component analysis (PCA) or independent component analysis (ICA) we are able to decompose the multichannel EEG observations to their constituent components such as the neural activities and noise. Combining these two together, the estimated noise components can be extracted, characterized, and separated from the actual EEGs. These concepts are explained in the following sections and their applications to the artefact and noise removal will be brought in the later chapters.

Adaptive noise cancellers used in communications, signal processing, and biomedical signal analysis can also be used for removing noise and artefacts from the EEG signals. An effective adaptive noise canceller however requires a reference signal. [Figure 4.11](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0011) shows a general block diagram of an adaptive filter for noise cancellation. The reference signal carries significant information about the noise or artefact and its statistical properties. For example, in the removal of eye‐blinking artefacts (discussed in [Chapter 16](#c16.xhtml)) a signature of the eye‐blink signal can be captured from the FP1 and FP2 EEG electrodes. In detection of the ERP signals, as another example, the reference signal can be obtained by averaging a number of ERP segments. There are many other examples such as ECG cancellation from EEGs and the removal of fMRI scanner artefacts from EEG‐fMRI simultaneous recordings where the reference signals can be provided.

![Figure 4.11 An adaptive noise canceller.](images/c04f011.gif)

[**Figure 4.11**](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-fig-0011) An adaptive noise canceller.

Adaptive Wiener filters are probably the most fundamental type of adaptive filters. In [Figure 4.11](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0011) the optimal weights for the filter, **w**(*n*), are calculated such that ![images](images/c4-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> is the best estimate of the actual signal **s**(*n*) in the mean square sense. The Wiener filter minimizes the mean square value of the error defined as:

(4.91)![equation](images/c4-disp-0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>e</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where **w** is the Wiener filter coefficient vector. Using the orthogonality principle [\[39\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0039) the final form of the mean squared error will be:

(4.92)![equation](images/c4-disp-0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi>e</mi><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi>x</mi><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">Rw</mi></math> 

where *E*(.) represents statistical expectation:

(4.93)![equation](images/c4-disp-0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></math> 

and

(4.94)![equation](images/c4-disp-0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></math> 

By taking the gradient with respect to **w** and equating it to zero we have:

(4.95)![equation](images/c4-disp-0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi></math> 

As **R** and **p** are usually unknown the above minimization is performed iteratively by substituting time averages for statistical averages. The adaptive filter in this case, decorrelates the output signals. The general update equation is in the form of:

(4.96)![equation](images/c4-disp-0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where *n* is the iteration number which typically corresponds to discrete‐time index. Δ ***w*** (*n*) has to be computed such that *E*\[**e**(*n*)\]² reaches to a reasonable minimum. The simplest and most common way of calculating Δ**w**(*n*) is by using gradient descent or steepest descent algorithm [\[39\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0039). In both cases, a criterion is defined as a function of the squared error (often called a performance index) such as *η* (*e*(*n*)²), such that it monotonically decreases after each iteration and converges to a global minimum. This requires:

(4.97)![equation](images/c4-disp-0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced></math> 

Assuming ΔW is very small, it is concluded that:

[(4.98)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0100)![equation](images/c4-disp-0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced></math> 

where, ∇[**w**] (.)represents gradient with respect to **w**. This means that the above equation ([Eq. 4.98](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0100)) is satisfied by setting Δ**w** =  − *μ*∇[**w**] (.), where *μ* is the learning rate or convergence parameter. Hence, the general update equation takes the form:

(4.99)![equation](images/c4-disp-0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#951;</mi><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

Using the least mean square (LMS) approach, ∇[**w**] (*η*(**w**)) is replaced by an instantaneous gradient of the squared error signal, i.e.:

(4.100)![equation](images/c4-disp-0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8773;</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>e</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

Therefore, the LMS‐based update equation is

(4.101)![equation](images/c4-disp-0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="italic">&#956;e</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

Also, the convergence parameter, *μ*, must be positive and should satisfy the following:

(4.102)![equation](images/c4-disp-0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">max</mi></msub></mfrac></math> 

where *λ* [max] represents the maximum eigenvalue of the autocorrelation matrix ***R*** . The LMS algorithm is the most simple and computationally efficient algorithm. However, the speed of convergence can be slow especially for correlated signals. The recursive least‐squares (RLS) algorithm attempts to provide a high speed stable filter, but it is numerically unstable for real‐time applications \[[40](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0040), [41](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0041)\]. Defining the performance index as:

[(4.103)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0105)![equation](images/c4-disp-0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>&#947;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msup><msup><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></math> 

Then, by taking the derivative with respect to **w** we obtain

[(4.104)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0106)![equation](images/c4-disp-0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></msub><mi>&#951;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>&#947;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msup><mi>e</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></math> 

where 0 < *γ* ≤ 1 is the forgetting factor \[[40](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0040), [41](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0041)\]. Replacing for *e*(*n*) in the above equation ([Eq. 4.104](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0106)) and writing it in vector form gives:

(4.105)![equation](images/c4-disp-0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where

(4.106)![equation](images/c4-disp-0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></math> 

and

(4.107)![equation](images/c4-disp-0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>&#955;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msup><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></math> 

From this equation:

(4.108)![equation](images/c4-disp-0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

The RLS algorithm performs the above operation recursively such that **P** and **R** are estimated at the current time *n* as:

(4.109)![equation](images/c4-disp-0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> (4.110)![equation](images/c4-disp-0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

In this case

(4.111)![equation](images/c4-disp-0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mi>r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mi>r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mspace width="1em"/><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mspace width="1em"/><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mi>r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mfenced></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

where *M* represents the finite impulse response (FIR) filter order. Conversely:

(4.112)![equation](images/c4-disp-0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> 

which can be simplified using the matrix inversion lemma [\[42\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0042):

(4.113)![equation](images/c4-disp-0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>&#955;</mi></mfrac><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math> 

and finally, the update equation can be written as:

(4.114)![equation](images/c4-disp-0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where

[(4.115)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0116)![equation](images/c4-disp-0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

and the error *e*(*n*) after each iteration is recalculated as:

(4.116)![equation](images/c4-disp-0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>e</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

The second term in the right‐hand side of the above equation is ![images](images/c4-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math>. Presence of **R** ^(−1)(*n*) in [Eq. (4.115)](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0116) is the major difference between RLS and LMS, but the RLS approach increases computation complexity by an order of magnitude.

 

## 4.9 Principal Component Analysis

All suboptimal transforms such as the DFT and DCT decompose the signals into a set of coefficients, which do not necessarily represent the constituent components of the signals. Moreover, the transform kernel is independent of the data hence they are not efficient in terms of both decorrelation of the samples and energy compaction. Therefore, separation of the signal and noise components is generally not achievable using these suboptimal transforms.

Expansion of the data into a set of orthogonal components certainly achieves maximum decorrelation of the signals. This enables separation of the data into the signal and noise subspaces.

![Figure 4.12 The general application of PCA.](images/c04f012.gif)

[**Figure 4.12**](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-fig-0012) The general application of PCA.

For a single‐channel EEG the Karhunen–Loéve transform is used to decompose the *i*th channel signal into a set of weighted orthogonal basis functions:

(4.117)![equation](images/c4-disp-0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>&#981;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>or</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> 

where **Φ** = {*ϕ*[*k*] } is the set of orthogonal basis functions. The weights *w*[*i*, *k*] are then calculated as:

(4.118)![equation](images/c4-disp-0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>or</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mi>&#981;</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

Often noise is added to the signal, i.e. *x*[*i*] (*n*) = *s*[*i*] (*n*) + *v*[*i*] (*n*), where *v*[*i*] (*n*) is additive noise. This degrades the decorrelation process. The weights are then estimated in order to minimize a function of the error between the signal and its expansion by the orthogonal basis, i.e. ***e*** [*i*] = **x**[*i*]  − **Φw**[*i*] . Minimization of the error in this case is generally carried out by solving the least‐squares problem. In a typical application of PCA as depicted in [Figure 4.12](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0012), the signal and noise subspaces are separated by means of some classification procedure.

 

### 4.9.1 Singular Value Decomposition

Singular value decomposition (SVD) is often used for solving the least‐squares (LS) problem. This is performed by decomposition of the *M × M* square autocorrelation matrix **R** into its eigenvalue matrix **Λ** = *diag*(λ[1], λ[2], … λ [*M*] ) and an *M* × *M* orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors **V**, i.e. **R = VΛV**^(*H*) , where (.) ^(*H*) denotes Hermitian (conjugate transpose) operation. Moreover, if **A** is an *M* × *M* data matrix such that **R** = **A**^(*H*) **A** then there exist an *M × M* orthogonal matrix **U**, an *M* × *M* orthogonal matrix **V**, and an *M* × *M* diagonal matrix **∑** with diagonal elements equal to ![images](images/c4-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="italic">&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, such that:

(4.119)![equation](images/c4-disp-0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U&#8721;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi>H</mi></msup></math> 

Hence **∑** ^(**2**) = **Λ.** The columns of **U** are called left singular vectors and the rows of **V**^(*H*) are called right singular vectors. If **A** is rectangular *N* × *M* matrix of rank *k* then **U** will be *N* × *N* and **∑** will be:

(4.120)![equation](images/c4-disp-0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#8721;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

where **S** = *diag*(σ[1], σ[2], … σ [*k*] ), where σ [*i*] = ![images](images/c4-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>. For such a matrix the Moore–Penrose pseudo‐inverse is defined as an *M* × *N* matrix A^† defined as:

(4.121)![equation](images/c4-disp-0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#8721;</mi><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi>H</mi></msup></math> 

where **∑** ^† is an *M* × *N* matrix defined as:

(4.122)![equation](images/c4-disp-0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#8721;</mi><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mspace width="0.2em"/><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1.4em"/><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

**A** ^† has a major role in the solutions of least‐squares problems, and **S** ^(−1) is a *k* × *k* diagonal matrix with elements equal to the reciprocals of the singular values of **A**, i.e.

(4.123)![equation](images/c4-disp-0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">diag</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math> 

In order to see the application of the SVD in solving the LS problem consider the error vector **e** defined as:

[(4.124)](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-disp-0126)![equation](images/c4-disp-0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mo>&#8211;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Ah</mi></math> 

where **d** is the desired signal vector and **Ah** is the estimate ![images](images/c4-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></math>. To find **h** we replace **A** with its SVD in the above equation ([Eq. 4.124](#c04.xhtml#c4-disp-0126)) and find **h,** which thereby minimizes the squared Euclidean norm of the error vector, ‖**e** ²‖. By using the SVD we obtain:

(4.125)![equation](images/c4-disp-0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mo>&#8721;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></math> 

or equivalently

(4.126)![equation](images/c4-disp-0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8721;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></math> 

Since **U** is a unitary matrix, ‖**e** ²‖ = ‖**U**^(*H*) **e** ‖². Hence, the vector **h** that minimizes ‖**e** ²‖ also minimizes ‖**U**^(*H*) **e** ‖². Finally, the unique solution as an optimum **h** (coefficient vector) may be expressed as [\[43\]](#c04.xhtml#c4-bib-0043):

(4.127)![equation](images/c4-disp-0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>H</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">d</mi></mrow><msub><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfrac><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> 

where *k* is the rank of **A**. Alternatively, as the optimum least‐squares coefficient vector:

(4.128)![equation](images/c4-disp-0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi></math> 

Performing PCA is equivalent to performing an SVD on the covariance matrix. PCA uses the same concept as SVD and orthogonalization to decompose the data into its constituent uncorrelated orthogonal components such that the autocorrelation matrix is diagonalized. Each eigenvector represents a principal component and the individual eigenvalues are numerically related to the variance they capture in the direction of the principal components. In this case the mean squared error (MSE) is simply the sum of the *N‐K* eigenvalues, i.e.:

(4.129)![equation](images/c4-disp-0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">MSE</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>&#981;</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#981;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>&#981;</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#981;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> 

PCA is widely used in data decomposition, classification, filtering, and whitening. In filtering applications, the signal and noise subspaces are separated and the data are reconstructed from only the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the actual signals. PCA is also used for BSS of correlated mixtures if the original sources can be considered statistically uncorrelated.

![Figure 4.13 Adaptive estimation of the weight vector w(n).](images/c04f013.gif)

[**Figure 4.13**](#c04.xhtml#R_c4-fig-0013) Adaptive estimation of the weight vector **w**(*n*).

The PCA problem is then summarized as how to find the weights **w** in order to minimize the error given the observations only. The LMS algorithm is used here to iteratively minimize the MSE as:

(4.130)![equation](images/c4-disp-0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mfenced></math> 

The update rule for the weights is then:

(4.131)![equation](images/c4-disp-0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where the error signal **e**(*n*) = **x**(*n*) − **Φ**^(*T*) (*n*)**w**(*n*), **x**(*n*) is the noisy input and *n* is the iteration index. The step size μ may be selected empirically or adaptively. These weights are then used to reconstruct the sources from the set of orthogonal basis functions. [Figure 4.13](#c04.xhtml#c4-fig-0013) shows the overall system for adaptive estimation of the weight vector **w** using the LMS algorithm.

 

## 4.10 Summary

In this chapter some basic signal processing tools and algorithms applicable to EEG signals have been reviewed. These fundamental techniques can be applied to reveal the inherent structure and the major characteristics of the signals based on which the state of the brain can be determined. TF‐domain analysis is indeed a good EEG descriptive for both normal and abnormal cases. The change in entropy Conversely, may describe the transitions between preictal to ictal states for epileptic patients. These concepts will be exploited in the following chapters of this book.

# 5  
EEG Signal Decomposition

 

## 5.1 Introduction

Electroencephalography (EEG) signals record the combination of many signals originated from inside the brain. These sources can be cortical, deep sources, or artefacts. Since there is not any considerable differences between the time lags from the source to sensors, the combinations are considered as linear mixtures.

Although in the majority of cases EEG signals are processed as multichannel data there are cases where only a single EEG channel is available. Examples include some nonintrusive brain–computer interfacing (BCI) applications, monitoring driver fatigue, or human machine interfacing mainly for computer games. This makes single‐channel EEG processing, and in some cases decomposition, an agenda for research.

Single‐channel source decomposition is not always effective and not very accurate. Nevertheless, it is useful for analysis of many single‐channel biological signals including simple and nonintrusive EEG recordings as stated above.

Another limitation in decomposition of multichannel EEGs is the relationship between the number of channels and the number of possible sources. In such cases, regularization methods such as sparse component analysis (SCA) may be applied.

In the following sections of this chapter, we start with single‐channel source separation, then move to multichannel cases which can be performed by independent component analysis (ICA), matrix factorization, or tensor factorization. Then we will focus on SCA for two important scenarios: first when only one source is active at each time sample, and second when the number of active sources can be up to one less than the number of electrodes at each time sample or signal segment.

 

## 5.2 Singular Spectrum Analysis

One of the single‐channel source decomposition methods is singular spectrum analysis (SSA).

The basic SSA method consists of two complementary stages: decomposition and reconstruction [\[148\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0148); each stage includes two separate steps. In the first step the time series is decomposed and in the second stage the original time series is reconstructed and used for further analysis. The main concept in studying the properties of SSA is *separability*, which characterizes how well different components can be separated from each other. The absence of approximate separability is often observed in series with complex structure. For these time series and time series with special structure, there are different ways of modifying SSA leading to different versions such as SSA with single and double centring, Toeplitz SSA, and sequential SSA [\[148\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0148).

SSA is becoming an effective and powerful tool for time series analysis in meteorology, hydrology, geophysics, climatology, economics, biology, physics, medicine and other sciences where short and long, one‐dimensional and multidimensional, stationary and nonstationary, almost deterministic and noisy time series are to be analyzed [\[149\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0149). A brief description of the SSA (decomposition and reconstruction) stages is given in the following subsections.

 

### 5.2.1 Decomposition

This stage includes an embedding operation followed by singular value decomposition (SVD). The embedding operation maps a one‐dimensional time series **f** into a *l* × *k* matrix as [\[148\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0148):

where *r* = *k + l* − 1 is the window length (1 ≤ *l* ≤ *r*), and superscript *T* denotes the transpose of a vector. Vectors **x**[*i*] are called *l‐lagged vectors* (or, simply, *lagged vectors*). The window length *l* should be sufficiently large. Note that the trajectory matrix **X** is a Hankel matrix, which means that all the elements along the diagonal *i* + *j* = *const*. are equal.

In the SVD stage the SVD of the trajectory matrix is computed and represented as sum of rank one bi‐orthogonal elementary matrices. Consider the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix **C** [x] = **XX**^(*T*) are denoted by λ[1],…, λ [*l*] in decreasing order of magnitude (λ[1] ≥*…* ≥ λ [*l*]  ≥ 0) and the corresponding orthogonal eigenvectors by **u** [**1**] , **u** [2], …, **u**[*l*] . Set *d* = max(*i*; such that λ [*i*] *\>* 0) = *rank*(**X)**: If we denote ![images](images/c5-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msqrt></math>, then the SVD of the trajectory matrix can be written as:

(5.2)![equation](images/c5-disp-0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msqrt><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msqrt><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math> 

The constituting components are separated through a constrained procedure of configuring **X** and the SVD operation. Since the desired signal might have different energy levels, in general there is no assumption about the relationship between the order of the eigenvalues and the physiologically dominant component (note that if λ[1] *\>>* λ[2], the information energy will be mostly concentrated in the most dominant matrix ![images](images/c5-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msqrt><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math> associated with the first singular values).

In general, ICA can be used instead of SVD. This changes the subspace decomposition problem into the ICA problem which can be solved by employing a suitable ICA technique. ICA is discussed later in this chapter.

 

### 5.2.2 Reconstruction

During reconstruction the elementary matrices are first split into several groups (depending on the number of components in the time series – in this application electromyogram (EMG) and electrocardiograms (ECG) signals, and the matrices within each group are added together). The size of the group or in other words, the length of each subspace may be specified based on some a priori information. In the case of ECG removal from recorded EMGs this feature and the desired component are jointly (and automatically) identified based on a constraint on the statistical properties of the signal to be extracted. Let *I* = {*i* [1],…, *i*[*p*] } be the indices corresponding to the *p* eigenvalues of the desired component. Then the matrix ![images](images/c5-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>I</mi></msub></math> corresponding to the group *I* is defined as ![images](images/c5-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>. In splitting the set of indices *J* = {1, …, *d*} into disjoint subsets *I* [1] to *I*[*m*] we always have:

[(5.3)](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-disp-0004)![equation](images/c5-disp-0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></msubsup><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub></math> 

The procedure of choosing the sets *I* [1], … *I*[*m*] is called eigentriple grouping. For a given group *I* the contribution of the component **X**[*I*] in expansion [(5.3)](#c05.xhtml#c5-disp-0004) is measured by the contribution of the corresponding eigenvalues: ![images](images/c5-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. In the next step the obtained matrix is transformed to the form of a Hankel matrix which can be subsequently converted to a time series. If *z*[*ij*] stands for an element of a matrix **Z**, then the *k*‐th term of the resulting series is obtained by averaging *z*[*ij*] over all *i,j* such that *i* + *j* = *k* + 1. This procedure is called diagonal averaging or Hankelization of matrix **Z**. The Hankelized *m* × *n* matrix **X**[*h*] is defined as:

where

where *num* abbreviates number.

A recursive SSA algorithm has been developed recently [\[150\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0150). Such a method is advantageous for real‐time processing of the data. The main problems in solving SSA problem are selection of appropriate embedding dimension (i.e. the window lengths) and establishing an effective criterion for selection of the desired subspace of eigentriples.
