## 5.3 Multichannel EEG Decomposition

EEG signals are inherently multichannel in their normal recording formats. However, the number of channels can be as low as 16 or as high as 256 in conventional clinical EEG systems.

 

### 5.3.1 Independent Component Analysis

In order to effectively separate the underlying sources from the electrode signals we should have more electrodes than source signals over any segment of time.

As a very popular approach for decomposition of multichannel EEGs, the concept of ICA lies in the fact that the constituent brain sources are independent from each other. In places where the combined source signals can be assumed independent from each other this concept plays a crucial role in separation and denoising the signals.

A measure of independency may be easily described to evaluate the independence of the decomposed components. Generally, considering the multichannel signal as **y**(n) and the constituent signal components as *y*[*i*] (*n*), the *y*[*i*] (*n*) are independent if:

(5.6)![equation](images/c5-disp-0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8719;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>n</mi></math> ![Figure 5.2 BSS concept; mixing and blind separation of the EEG signals.](images/c05f002.gif)

[**Figure 5.2**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0002) BSS concept; mixing and blind separation of the EEG signals.

where *p*(**Y**) is the joint probability distribution, *p*[*y*] (*y*[*i*] (*n*)) are the marginal distributions and *m* is the number of independent components.

An important application of ICA is in blind source separation (BSS). BSS is an approach to estimate and recover the independent source signals using only the information of their mixtures observed at the recording channels. Due to its variety of applications BSS has attracted much attention recently. BSS of acoustic signals is often referred to as the Cocktail Party Problem [\[104\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0104), which means separation of individual sounds from a number of recordings in an uncontrolled environment such as a cocktail party. [Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0002) illustrates the BSS concept. As expected, ICA can be useful if the original sources are independent, i.e. ![images](images/c5-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8719;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">m</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math>.

A perfect separation of the signals requires taking into account the structure of the mixing process. In a real‐life application, however, this process is unknown, but some assumptions may be made about the source statistics.

Generally, the BSS algorithms do not make realistic assumptions about the environment in order to make the problem more tractable. There are typically three assumptions about the mixing medium. The simplest but very popular and applicable BSS type is the instantaneous case, where the source signals arrive at the sensors at the same time. This has been considered for separation of biological signals such as the EEG where the signals have narrow bandwidths and the sampling frequency is normally low. The BSS model in this case can be easily formulated as:

(5.7)![equation](images/c5-disp-0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Hs</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where *m* × *1***s**(*n*), *n*[*e*]  × *1* ***x*** (*n*), and *n*[*e*]  × *1* ***v*** (*n*) denote respectively the vector of source signals, observed signals, and noise at discrete time *n*. **H** is the mixing matrix of size *n*[*e*]  × *m*. The separation is performed by means of a separating *m* × *n*[*e*] matrix, **W**, which uses only the information about **x**(*n*) to reconstruct the original source signals (or the independent components) as:

(5.8)![equation](images/c5-disp-0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Wx</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

In the context of EEG signal processing *n*[*e*] denotes the number of electrodes. The early approaches in instantaneous BSS started from the work by Herault and Jutten [\[6\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0006) in 1986. In their approach, they considered non‐Gaussian sources with similar number of independent sources and mixtures. They proposed a solution based on a recurrent artificial neural network (ANN) for separation of the sources.

In acoustic applications, however, there are usually time lags between the arrival of the signals at the sensors. The signals also may arrive through multiple paths. This type of mixing model is called a convolutive model. One example is in places where the acoustic properties of the environment vary, such as a room environment surrounded by walls. Based on these assumptions the convolutive mixing model can be classified into two more types: anechoic and echoic. In both cases the vector representations of mixing and separating processes are changed to **x**(*n*) = **H**(*n*) \* **s**(*n*) + **v**(*n*) and **y**(*n*) = **W**(*n*) \* **x**(*n*) respectively, where \* denotes the convolution operation.

In an anechoic model, however, the expansion of the mixing process may be given as:

(5.9)![equation](images/c5-disp-0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>h</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></math> 

where the attenuation, *h*[*ij*] , and delay, *δ*[*ij*] , of source *j* to sensor *i* would be determined by the physical position of the source relative to the sensors. Then the unmixing process will be given as:

(5.10)![equation](images/c5-disp-0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>m</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ji</mi></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ji</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></math> 

where the *w*[*ji*] s are the elements of W. In an echoic mixing environment it is expected that the signals from the same sources reach to the sensors through multiple paths. The reverberation time changes and can continue infinitely. However, in practical acoustic models, the number of paths in a multipath scenario as well as the overall reverberation time are considered limited. Therefore, the expansion of the mixing and separating models will be changed to:

(5.11)![equation](images/c5-disp-0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#948;</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></math> 

where *K* denotes the number of paths and *v*[*i*] (*n*) is the accumulated noise at sensor *i*. The unmixing process will be formulated similarly to the anechoic one. Obviously, for a known number of sources an accurate result may be expected if the number of paths is known.

The aim of BSS using ICA is to estimate an unmixing matrix **W** such that **Y = WX** best approximates the independent sources S, where **Y** and **X** are respectively matrices with columns ***y*** (*n*) = \[*y* [1](*n*), *y* [2](*n*), ⋯*y*[*m*] (*n*)\] ^(*T*) and ***x*** (*n*) = \[*x* [1](*n*), *x* [2](*n*), ⋯*x*[*ne*] (*n*)\] ^(*T*) .

In any case, the unmixing matrix for the instantaneous case is expected to be equal to the inverse of the mixing matrix, i.e. **W** = **H** ^(−1). However, since in all ICA algorithms are based upon restoring independence, the separation is subject to permutation and scaling ambiguities in the output independent components, i.e. **W** = **PDH** ^(−1), where **P** and **D** are respectively the permutation and scaling matrices.

There are three major approaches in using ICA for BSS:

1.  Factorizing the joint pdf of the reconstructed signals into its marginal pdfs. Under the assumption that the source signals are stationary and non‐Gaussian, the independence of the reconstructed signals can be measured by a statistical distance between the joint distribution and the product of its marginal pdfs. Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence (distance) is an example. For nonstationary cases and for the short‐length data, there will be poor estimation of the pdfs. Therefore, in such cases, this approach may not lead to good results. Conversely, such methods are not robust for noisy data since in this situation the pdf of the signal will be distorted.
2.  Decorrelating the reconstructed signals through time, that is, diagonalizing the covariance matrices at every time instant. If the signals are mutually independent, the off‐diagonal elements of the covariance matrix vanish. Although the reverse of this statement is not always true. If the signals are nonstationary, we can utilize the time‐varying covariance structure to estimate the unmixing matrix. An advantage of this method is that it only uses second‐order statistics (SOS), which implies that it is likely to perform better in noisy and short data length conditions than higher‐order statistics (HOS).
3.  Eliminating the temporal cross‐correlation functions of the reconstructed signals as much as possible. In order to perform this, the correlation matrix of observations can be diagonalized at different time lags simultaneously. Here, SOS are also normally used. As another advantage, it can be applied in the presence of white noise since such noise can be avoided by using the cross‐correlation only for τ ≠ 0. Such a method is appropriate for stationary and weakly stationary sources (i.e. when the stationarity condition holds within a short segment of data).

It has been shown [\[64\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0064) that mutual information (MI) is a measure of independence and that maximizing the non‐Gaussianity of the source signals is equivalent to minimizing the MI between them.

In the majority of cases the number of sources is known. This assumption avoids any ambiguity caused by false estimation of the number of sources. In exactly‐determined cases the number of sources is equal to the number of mixtures. In over‐determined situations however, the number of mixtures is more than the number of sources.

There have been many attempts to apply BSS to EEG signals \[[72](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0072)–[82](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0082)\] for separation of normal brain rhythms, event‐related signals, or mental or physical movement‐related sources.

If the number of sources is unknown, a criterion has to be established to estimate the number of sources beforehand. This process is a difficult task especially when noise is involved.

In those cases where the number of sources is more than the number of mixtures (known as underdetermined systems), the above BSS schemes can not be applied simply because the unmixing matrix will not be invertible, and generally the original sources cannot be extracted. However, when the signals are sparse other methods based on clustering may be utilized.

A signal is said to be sparse when it has many zero or at least approximately zero samples. Separation of the mixtures of such signals is potentially possible in the situation where at each sample instant the number of non‐zero sources is not more than the number of sensors. The mixtures of sparse signals can also be instantaneous or convolutive. However, as we will briefly describe later, the solution for only simple case of a small number of idealized sources has been given in the literature.

In the context of EEG analysis, although the number of signals mixed at the electrodes seems to be limited, the number of sources corresponding to the neurons firing at a time can be enormous. However, if the objective is to study a certain rhythm in the brain the problem can be transformed to the time–frequency (TF) domain or even to the space–time–frequency (STF) domain. In such domains the sources may be considered disjoint and generally sparse. Also it is said that in the brain neurons encode data in a sparse way if their firing pattern is characterized by a long period of inactivity \[[65](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0065), [66](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0066)\].

 

### 5.3.2 Instantaneous BSS

This is the most commonly used scheme for processing of the EEGs. The early work by Herault and Jutten led to a simple but fundamental adaptive algorithm [\[67\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0067). Linsker [\[68\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0068) proposed unsupervised learning rules based on information theory that maximize the average MI between the inputs and outputs of an ANN. Comon [\[64\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0064) performed minimization of MI to make the outputs independent. The Infomax algorithm [\[69\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0069) in spirit is similar to the Linsker method. It uses an elegant stochastic gradient learning rule previously proposed by Amari et al. [\[70\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0070). Non‐Gaussianity of the sources was first exploited by Hyvarinen and Oja [\[71\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0071) in developing their fast ICA (fICA) algorithm. fICA is actually a blind source extraction algorithm, which extracts the sources one by one based on their kurtosis; the signals with transient peaks have high kurtosis. Later it was demonstrated that the Infomax algorithm and maximum likelihood estimation are in fact equivalent \[[1](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0001), [28](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0028)\].

Based on the Infomax algorithm [\[69\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0069) for signals with positive kurtosis such as simultaneous EEG‐fMRI and speech signals, minimizing the MI between the source estimates and maximizing the entropy of the source estimates are equivalent. Therefore, a stochastic gradient ascent algorithm can be used to iteratively find the unmixing matrix by maximization of the entropy. The Infomax finds a **w** which minimizes the following cost function:

(5.12)![equation](images/c5-disp-0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *H*(**z**) is the entropy of the output, *H*(**z|x**) is the entropy of the output subject to a known input, and **z** = *f*(**y**) is a nonlinear activation function applied element‐wise to **y**, the estimated sources. *I*(**z,x**) is the MI between the input and output of the constructed ANN. *H*(**z|x**) is independent of **W**, therefore, the gradient of *J* is only proportional to the gradient of *H*(**z**). Correspondingly, the natural gradient [\[70\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0070) of *J* devoted as ∇[**W**] *J* will be:

(5.13)![equation](images/c5-disp-0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></msub><mi>J</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">I</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></math> 

in which the time index *n* is dropped for convenience of presentation. Then, the sequential adaptation rule for the unmixing matrix **W** becomes:

(5.14)![equation](images/c5-disp-0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mo>+</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where *f*( ***y*** (*n*)) = (1 +  *exp* (− ***y*** (*n*)))^(−1), assuming the outputs are super‐Gaussian, and μ is the learning rate, which is either a small constant or gradually changes following the speed of convergence.

Joint diagonalization of eigen matrices (JADE) is another well known BSS algorithm [\[2\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0002) based on HOS. The JADE algorithm effectively diagonalizes the fourth‐order cumulant of the estimated sources. This procedure uses certain matrices Q [*z*] (M) formed by the inner product of the fourth‐order cumulant tensor of the outputs with an arbitrary matrix **M**, i.e.:

[(5.15)](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-disp-0016)![equation](images/c5-disp-0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msubsup><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msubsup><mi mathvariant="italic">Cum</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mi>l</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">lk</mi></msub></math> 

where the (*l,k*)th component of the matrix *M* is written as *m*[*lk*] , **Z = CY**, and \* denotes complex conjugate. The matrix **Q**[*z*] (**M**) has the important property that it is diagonalized by the correct rotation matrix **U**, i.e. ***U*** ^(*H*) ***QU*** = ***Λ*** [*M*] , and **Λ**[*M*] is a diagonal matrix whose diagonal elements depend on the particular matrix *M* as well as **Z**. By using [Eq. (5.15)](#c05.xhtml#c5-disp-0016), for a set of different matrices **M**, a set of cumulant matrices **Q**[*z*] (**M**) can be calculated. The desired rotation matrix **U** then, jointly diagonalizes these matrices. In practise, only approximate joint diagonalization is possible [\[2\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0002), i.e. the problem can be stated as minimization of ![images](images/c5-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msubsup><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msubsup><mi mathvariant="italic">off</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> where:

(5.16)![equation](images/c5-disp-0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">off</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mfenced open="|" close="|"><msub><mi>m</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi></msub></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

EEG signals are however nonstationary. Nonstationarity of the signals has been exploited in developing an effective BSS algorithm based on SOS called (second‐order blind identification) [\[102\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0102). In this algorithm separation is performed at a number of discrete time lags simultaneously. At each lag the algorithm unitarily diagonalizes the whitened data covariance matrix. It also mitigates the effect of noise on the observation by using a whitening matrix calculation, which can improve robustness to noise. Unitary diagonalization can be explained as follows: If **V** is a whitening matrix and **X** is the observation matrix, the covariance matrix of the whitened observation is **C** [**X**] = E\[**VXX**^(*H*) **V**^(*H*) \] = **VR** [x]**V**^(*H*) = **VHR** [s]**H**^(*H*) **V**^(*H*) = **I**, where **R** [x] and **R** [s] denote respectively the covariance matrices of the observed data and the original sources. It is assumed that **R** [s] = **I**, i.e. the sources have unit variance and they are uncorrelated, so **VH** is a unitary matrix. Therefore, **H** can be factored as **H** = **V** ^(−1)**U**, where **U** = **VH**. The joint approximate diagonalization for a number of time lags can be obtained efficiently using a generalization of the Jacobi technique for the exact diagonalization of a single Hermitian matrix. The SOBI algorithm is implemented through the following steps as given in [\[102\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0102):

1.  The sample covariance matrix ![images](images/c5-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>0</mn></mfenced></math> is estimated from *T* data samples. The *m* largest eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors of ![images](images/c5-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>0</mn></mfenced></math> are denoted as λ[1], λ[2], *…*, λ [*m*] and **h** [1], **h** [2], *…*, **h**[*m*] respectively.
2.  Under the white noise assumption, an estimate ![images](images/c5-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup></math> of the noise variance is the average of the *n*[*e*] *‐m* smallest eigenvalues of ![images](images/c5-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>0</mn></mfenced></math>. The whitened signals are **z**(*n*) = \[*z* [1](*n*), *z* [2](*n*), …, *z*[*ne*] (*n*)\] ^(*T*) , computed by ![images](images/c5-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>H</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> for 1 ≤ *i* ≤ *n*[*e*] . This is equivalent to forming a whitening matrix as ![images](images/c5-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>W</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mfenced><mi>H</mi></msup></math>.
3.  Form sample estimates ![images](images/c5-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><munder accentunder="false"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mtext>\_</mtext></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#964;</mi></mfenced></math> by computing the sample covariance matrices of **z**(*t*) for a fixed set of time lags *τ* ∈ {*τ*[*j*]  ∣ *j* = 1, …, *K*}.
4.  A unitary matrix ![images](images/c5-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></math> is then obtained as a joint diagonalizer of the set ![images](images/c5-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><munder accentunder="false"><mover accent="true"><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mtext>\_</mtext></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>&#964;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mfenced></math>.
5.  The source signals are estimated as ![images](images/c5-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced></math> or the mixing matrix **A** is estimated as ![images](images/c5-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>#</mo></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></math>, where superscript ^# denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudo‐inverse.

The Fast Intelligent Crawling Algorithm (FICA) [\[71\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0071) is another very popular BSS technique, which extracts the signals one by one based on their kurtosis. In fact, the algorithm uses an independence criterion that exploits non‐Gaussianity of the estimated sources. In some places where the objective is to remove the spiky artefacts, such as the removal of the fMRI artefact from the simultaneous EEG‐fMRI recordings, application of an iterative fICA followed by deflation of the artefact component gives excellent results [\[83\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0083). A typical signal of this type is given in [Figure 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0003).

Practically, fICA maximizes the negentropy, which represents the distance between a distribution and a Gaussian distribution having the same mean and variance, i.e.:

(5.17)![equation](images/c5-disp-0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">Neg</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>y</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8733;</mo><msup><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>y</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext mathvariant="italic">Gaussian</mtext></msub></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

where, *f* is a score function [\[3\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0003) and *Neg* stands for negentropy. This, as mentioned previously is equivalent to maximizing the kurtosis. Therefore, the cost function can be simply defined as:

(5.18)![equation](images/c5-disp-0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#946;</mi><mn>4</mn></mfrac><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mfenced></math> ![Figure 5.3 A sample of an EEG signal simultaneously recorded with fMRI.](images/c05f003.gif)

[Figure 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0004) shows the results after application of fICA to remove the scanner artefact from the EEGs.

In a TF approach which assume the sources are approximately cyclostationary and nonstationary, the auto‐terms and cross‐terms of the covariance matrix of the mixtures are first separated and BSS is applied to both terms \[[103](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0103), [105](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0105)\]. In this approach, the spatial time–frequency distribution (STFD) of the mixed signals is defined as

![Figure 5.4 The EEG signals after removal of the scanner artefact.](images/c05f004.gif)

[**Figure 5.4**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0004) The EEG signals after removal of the scanner artefact.

[(5.24)](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-disp-0025)![equation](images/c5-disp-0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">xx</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mfrac><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">i&#969;&#964;</mi></mrow></msup><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#964;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ϕ(.) is the discretized kernel function defining a distribution from Cohen's class of TF distributions [\[4\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0004) and **x**(.) is an *N* sample observation of the signals, which is normally contaminated by noise. Assuming **x**(*t*) = **As**(*t*) + **v**(*t*), using the above equation we find

(5.25)![equation](images/c5-disp-0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">xx</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ss</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></math>

From this equation it is clear that both **D** [***xx***] and **D** [***ss***] exhibit the same eigen‐structure. The covariance matrix of the source signals is then replaced by the source STFD matrix composed of auto‐source and cross‐source time–frequency distributions (TFDs) respectively, on the diagonal and off‐diagonal entries.

Defining a whitening matrix **W** such that **U** = **WA** is unitary, a whitened and noise compensated STFD matrix is defined as:

(5.26)![equation](images/c5-disp-0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">xx</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">xx</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>H</mi></msup></math> ![equation](images/c5-disp-0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ss</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>H</mi></msup></math>

(5.24)](#c05.xhtml#c5-disp-0025) it is known that the mixture STFD matrix exhibits the same eigen‐structure as the data covariance matrix commonly used for cyclic data [\[105\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0105). The covariance matrix of the source signals is replaced by a source STFD matrix composed of the auto‐ and cross‐source TFDs on the diagonal and off‐diagonal entries respectively. The peaks occur in mutually exclusive locations on the TF plane. The kernel function can be defined in such a way as to maximize disjointedness of the points in the TF plane. By estimation of the STFD in [(5.24)](#c05.xhtml#c5-disp-0025) at appropriate TFD points, one may recover the source signals by estimating a unitary transformation ![images](images/c5-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></math>, via optimization of a joint diagonal and off‐diagonal criterion, to have:

(5.27)![equation](images/c5-disp-0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">Wx</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></math> 

In order to define and extract the peaks of the **D** [***xx***] a suitable clustering approach has to be followed. This algorithm has potential application for estimating the EEG sources since in the most normal cases the sources are cyclic or quasi‐cyclic.

 

### 5.3.3 Convolutive BSS

In many practical situations the signals reach the sensors with different time delays. The corresponding delay between source *j* and sensor *i*, in terms of number of samples, is directly proportional to the sampling frequency and conversely to the speed of sound, i.e. *δ*[*ij*]  ∝ *d*[*ij*]  × *f*[*s*] /*c*, where *d*[*ij*] , *f*[*s*] , and *c* are respectively, the distance between source *j* and sensor *i*, the sampling frequency, and the speed of sound. For speech and music in the air as an example we may have *d*[*ij*] in terms of metres, *f*[*s*] between 8 and 44 KHz, and *c*\=330 m/s. Also, in an acoustic environment the sound signals can reach the sensors through multipaths after reflections by obstacles (such as walls). The above cases have been addressed respectively, as anechoic and echoic BSS models and formulated at the beginning of this section. The solution to echoic cases is obviously more difficult and it normally involves some approximations to the actual system. As an example, in the previously mentioned Cocktail Party Problem the source signals propagate through a dynamic medium with many parasitic effects such as multiple echoes and reverberation. So, the received signals are a weighted sum of mixed and delayed components. In other words, the received signals at each microphone are the convolutive mixtures of speech signals.

In the case of spatial ICA, convolutive BSS should be applied where the source locations change within a segment. A good example is separation of video signals. Spatial ICA can also be applied to EEGs in order to separate the movement‐related cortical sources when distributed sources are considered.

Unfortunately, most of the proposed BSS approaches to instantaneous mixtures fail or are limited in separation of convolutive mixtures mainly because either there are delays involved for propagation of the sources or a number of copies of the sources, delayed and weighted differently, reach to the sensors.

 

#### 5.3.3.1 General Applications

Convolutive BSS has been a focus of research in the acoustic signal processing community. Two major approaches have been followed for both anechoic and echoic cases; the first approach is to solve the problem in the time domain. In such methods in order to have accurate results both the weights of the unmixing matrix and the delays have to be estimated. However, in the second approach, the problem is transformed into the frequency domain as ![images](images/c5-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#42;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mover><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>F</mi></mover><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#183;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> and instantaneous BSS applied to each frequency bin mixed signal. The separated signals at different frequency bins are then combined and transformed to the time domain to reconstruct the estimated sources. The short‐term Fourier transform is often used for this purpose. However, the inherent permutation problem of BSS severely deteriorates the results since the order of the separated sources in different frequency bins can vary.

An early work in convolutive BSS by Platt and Faggin [\[5\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0005) who applied the adaptive noise cancellation network to the BSS model of Herault and Jutten [\[6\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0006), which has delays in the feedback path was based on the minimum output power principle. This scheme exploits the fact that the signal corrupted by noise has more power than the clean signal. The feedback path cancels out the interferences as the result of delayed versions of the other sources. This circuit was also used later to extend the Infomax BSS to convolutive cases [\[7\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0007). The combined network maximizes the entropy at the output of the network with respect to the weights and delays. Torkkola [\[8\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0008) extended this algorithm to the echoic cases too. In order to achieve a reasonable convergence, some prior knowledge of the recording situation is necessary.

In another work an extension of SOBI has been used for anechoic BSS [\[9\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0009); the problem has been transformed to the frequency domain and joint diagonalization of spectral matrices has been utilized to estimate the mixing coefficients as well as the delays [\[10\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0010). In attempts by Parra et al. [\[11\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0011), Ikram and Morgan [\[12\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0012), and Cherkani and Deville [\[13\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0013) SOS have been used to ensure that the estimated sources, **Y**(*ω,m*), are uncorrelated at each frequency bin. **W**(*ω*) is estimated in such a way that it diagonalizes the covariance matrices **R** [Y](*ω*, *k*) simultaneously for all time blocks *k; k =* 0, 1, *…*, *K‐*1, i.e.:

![equation](images/c5-disp-0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">Y</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">X</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> ![equation](images/c5-disp-0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></math> (5.28)![equation](images/c5-disp-0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ***Λ*** [*S*] (*ω*, *k*) is the covariance matrix of the source signals, which changes with *k*, ***Λ*** [*c*] (*ω*, *k*) is an arbitrary diagonal matrix, and ***R*** [*X*] (*ω*, *k*) is the covariance matrix of **X**(*ω*).

The unmixing filter **W**(*ω*) for each frequency bin *ω* that simultaneously satisfies the *K* decorrelation equations can be obtained using an over‐determined least‐squares solution. Since the output covariance matrix **R** [Y](*ω*, *k*) has to be diagonalized the update equation for estimation of the unmixing matrix **W** can be found by minimizing the off‐diagonal elements of **R** [Y](*ω*, *k*), which leads to:

(5.29)![equation](images/c5-disp-0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>&#183;</mo><mfrac><mi>&#8706;</mi><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>H</mi></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mfenced open="{" close="}"><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mfenced></math> 

where *ρ* is the iteration index ‖∙‖² is the squared Frobenius norm:

(5.30)![equation](images/c5-disp-0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#956;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> 

and

(5.31)![equation](images/c5-disp-0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">diag</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi>X</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *α* is a constant which is set empirically.

In these methods a number of solutions for mitigating the permutation ambiguity have been suggested. Smaragdis [\[14\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0014) reformulated the Infomax algorithm for the complex domain and used it to solve BSS in the frequency domain. Murata et al. [\[15\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0015) also formulated the problem of BSS in each frequency bin using a simultaneous diagonalization method similar to the SOBI method. To mitigate the permutation problem a method based on the temporal structure of signals, which exploits the nonstationarity of speech was introduced. The method exploits the correlations between the frequency bins of the spectrum of the signals. Detecting and exploiting the silence periods to either localize the speakers individually or to detect the source statistics such as pitch period for each speaker, are other options to alleviate the permutation problem.

 

#### 5.3.3.2 Application of Convolutive BSS to EEG

For the EEG mixing model the *f*[*s*] is normally low (since the bandwidth <100 Hz) and the propagation velocity is equivalent to that of electromagnetic waves (300 000 km s^(−1)). Therefore, the delay is almost zero and we can always consider the mixing model for temporal BSS as instantaneous. For EEGs the signal sources are considered stationary (fixed in position). This important assumption which in many cases, such as separation of normal brain rhythms of eye‐blink artefact, is acceptable, enables effective application of linear BSS. However, in some other cases such as prolonged physical movements, the sources are considered as the current source, i.e. the location can change. To extract such sources the linear BSS solution is no longer valid. Spatial BSS of EEGs, where the mixed signals are in sample per channel (i.e. alternating samples in the electrode space), therefore, this can be considered convolutive. Spatial shift, analogous to time delay, is mainly due to source movement within one spatial signal segment. This idea has been developed in [\[100\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0100) in a spatiotemporal analysis of EEG using maximum likelihood convolutive ICA.

The main drawbacks for the application of BSS to separation of EEG signals is due to the:

*   unknown physiological and measurement noise statistics
*   unknown and varying number of sources
*   nonstationarity of the sources mainly due to evoked and movement‐related brain responses
*   existence of distributed moving sources related to synaptic currents.

Although many attempts have been made to solve the above problems more efforts are required to provide robust solutions for different applications.

 

## 5.4 Sparse Component Analysis

Solution to underdetermined system problems where the number of sources are more than the number of mixtures, is often very challenging and cannot be carried out using the conventional BSS systems. This means in such cases more a priori information is required to be integrated within the decomposition algorithm. In nature, there are many events and sources with sparse nature. Some examples include interictal discharges within the hippocampus, QRS signals within ECGs, eye blinks within EEG, and mutations within genomic sequence. In places where the sources are sparse, i.e. at each time instant only one of the sources has significant non‐zero value, the columns of the mixing matrix may be calculated individually, which makes the solution to the underdetermined case possible. The problem can be stated as a clustering problem since the lines in the scatter plot can be separated based on their directionalities by means of clustering \[[16](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0016), [17](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0017)\]. The same idea has been followed more comprehensively by Li et al. [\[18\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0018). In his method, however, the separation has been performed in two different stages. First, the unknown mixing matrix is estimated using the *k‐*means clustering method. Then, the source matrix is estimated using a standard linear programming algorithm. The line orientation of a data set may be thought of as the direction of its greatest variance. One way is to perform eigenvector decomposition on the covariance matrix of the data, the resultant principal eigenvector, i.e. the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue, indicates the direction of the data. There are many cases for which the sources are disjoint in other domains rather than the time domain. In these cases the SCA can be performed in those domains more efficiently. One such approach called degenerate unmixing estimation technique (DUET) [\[19\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0019) transforms the anechoic convolutive observations into the time–frequency domain using a short‐time Fourier transform and the relative attenuation and delay values between the two observations are calculated from the ratio of corresponding TF points. The regions of significant amplitudes (atoms) are then considered to be the source components in the TF domain.

For instantaneous cases, in separation of sparse sources the common approach used by most researchers is to attempt to maximize the sparsity of the extracted signals in the output of the separator. The columns of the mixing matrix A assign each observed data point to only one source based on some measure of proximity to those columns [\[20\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0020), i.e. at each instant only one source is considered active. Therefore, the mixing system can be presented as:

(5.32)![equation](images/c5-disp-0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">M</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">ji</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mfenced><mspace width="1em"/><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">N</mi></math> 

where in an ideal case *a*[*ji*] *\= 0* for *i ≠ j*. Minimization of the ***l*** [**0**] ‐norm (i.e. the number of non‐zero samples), which in most of the cases is approximated by the ***l*** [**1**] ‐norm (sum of the absolute values of the non‐zero samples), is one of the most logical methods for estimation of the sources. ***l*** [**1**] ‐norm minimization is a piecewise linear operation that partially assigns the energy of **x**(*n*) to the *M* columns of **A** that form a cone around **x**(*n*) in ℜ^M space. The remaining *N‐M* columns are assigned zero coefficients. Therefore, the ***l*** [**1**] ‐norm minimization can be manifested as:

[(5.33)](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-disp-0037)![equation](images/c5-disp-0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mo mathvariant="bold">min</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi></munder><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext mathvariant="bold">subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">As</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mfenced></math> 

A detailed discussion of signal recovery using *l* [1]‐norm minimization is presented by Takigawa et al. [\[21\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0021).

A number of methods such as basis pursuit, smoothed *l* [0] [\[161\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0161), focal underdetermined system solver (FOCUSS), and orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) are used to approximate the solution to ![images](images/c5-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><munder><mo mathvariant="bold">min</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi></munder><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext mathvariant="bold">subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">As</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi></mfenced></math>. In the following subsection a brief explanation of the most popular methods is provided.

 

### 5.4.1 Standard Algorithms for Sparse Source Recovery

Among the popular approaches are family of the greedy methods which focus on the support, and then, the non‐zero values of **s** are obtained using a simple least‐squares method. The greedy algorithms are mostly discrete due to the discrete nature of the support. In contrast, a different family of the algorithm, namely the relaxation family, attempts to approximate the sparse signal with a continuous one, and adopts a continuous optimization procedure.

 

#### 5.4.1.1 Greedy‐Based Solution

Mallat and Zhang [\[159\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0159) introduced a greedy method for sparse decomposition called matching pursuit (MP). They showed that when the dictionary (mixing matrix) is orthogonal and the observed signal is composed of *k* << *n* atoms, the algorithm recovers the sources exactly after *n* steps [\[163\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0163). In fact, MP is based on a suboptimal forward search through the mixing matrix. Succeeding greedy algorithms such as OMP [\[164\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0164) and compressive sampling matching pursuit (CoSaMP) [\[165\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0165) is based on the MP concept. The OMP method chooses the column of maximal correlation with residue, in fact, it is also the one having the steepest decline in the residue, which implies that OMP is greedy.

Recalling **x** = **As**, where **s** is a *k*‐sparse signal. Since the number of non‐zero coefficients of a *k*‐sparse signal is equal to *k*, if the locations of these coefficients are determined, the non‐zero values could be found by inverting or pseudo‐inverting the corresponding *m* × *k* sub‐matrices in **A**. This is the most complicated part of the algorithm. In the OMP algorithm, the non‐zero places are found one by one. First, the highest degree of belonging (relating) a row of **x** to a column of **A** provides the most likelihood of that column of **A** is the support. To find the other members of the support, the recovered signal (and the related column) is deflated. This process is repeated until the other members of the support are estimated.

 

#### 5.4.1.2 Relaxation‐Based Solution

The relaxation methods smooth the *l* [0]‐norm by approximating that with other functions or norms.

Given ρ [*α*] (*s*) ≈ ‖*s*‖[0], then, as examples, ρ [*α*] (*s*) can be ![images](images/c5-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#961;</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>s</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo>exp</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>&#945;</mi></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math>, ![images](images/c5-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#961;</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>s</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> or ρ [*α*] (*s*) = |*s*| ^(*α*) . By *α* approaching zero, these functions get closer to the *l* [0]‐norm. It is worth mentioning that, these functions are applied to the source vector elements and the final norm is calculated according to the following equation ([Eq. 5.34](#c05.xhtml#c5-disp-0038)):

[(5.34)](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-disp-0038)![equation](images/c5-disp-0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#961;</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mfenced></math> 

where *s*[*q*] and *f*(**s**) refer to the *q*th element and smoothed norm of **s**, respectively. A popular algorithm of this family is the FOCUSS [\[171\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0171). FOCUSS employs an optimization method called iterative recursive least squares (IRLS). Based on this concept the smoothed *l* [0]‐norm (ρ [*α*] (*s*)) is posed as a weighted *l* [2]‐norm as:

(5.35)![equation](images/c5-disp-0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#961;</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>&#8594;</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#961;</mi><mi>&#945;</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mfrac><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> 

IRLS iterates between a solution of the *l* [2]‐norm and update of the weights **w**. Similar approaches have been followed by many other researchers. The *l* [1]‐norm, i.e. ||**s||** [**1**] is the one more commonly used in the literature. The *l* [1]**‐**norm is presented by an absolute value of **s**, leading to an *l* [1]‐norm penalty as presented in [Eq. (5.33)](#c05.xhtml#c5-disp-0037). This convex relaxation technique is called basis pursuit \[[160](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0160), [161](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0161)\] and is solved via linear programming.

 

### 5.4.2 k‐Sparse Mixtures

Most SCA‐based methods for source separation and underdetermined blind identification (UBI) problems \[[18](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0018),[152](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0152)–[156](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0156)\] use the information about the signal intervals which include only one dominant source active in particular instants. These methods fail when there are not enough intervals including one single dominant source to enable estimation of all columns of **A**.

Some more recent approaches have extended the SCA to the cases where more than one source, say *k*[*a*] , where *k*[*a*] < *N*[*x*] , are active in an instant or interval. Their methods are able to use the information about these intervals to estimate the columns of mixing matrix **A** \[[22](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0022)–[24](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0024)\]. These methods are called *k*‐SCA methods [\[25\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0025) and under some mild conditions (i.e. i. having enough time samples to have enough planes/subspaces to cover all columns of **A** and ii. having *k*[*a*] < *N*[*x*] ) \[[25](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0025), [154](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0154)\], are able to estimate **A** and the sources using some clustering methods.

In [\[22\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0022) it is assumed that at each instant of time there are on average *k*[*a*] < *N*[*x*] /2 sources active (non‐zero). The main idea in this paper is to convert the problem of multiple dominant sources to a series of single dominant source problems, which may be solved by the well known methods. Each column of **A** is then separately estimated by solving these single dominant problems. In this approach the number of sources has to be known. This latter problem has been addressed in [\[23\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0023) and a solution has been proposed. The adaptivity to changing environment and the robustness against noise and outliers (i.e. the intervals which do not satisfy sparseness conditions) have been improved by the algorithm proposed in [\[24\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0024). Conversely, in this method *k*[*a*] satisfies *N*[*x*] − 1 > *k*[*a*] > *N*[*x*] /2. SCA has been applied for EEG source estimation for ERP detection and source localization \[[157](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0157), [158](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0158)\].

The separation performance of current underdetermined source recovery (USR) solutions, including the relaxation and greedy families, reduces with decreasing the mixing system dimension and increasing the sparsity level *k*. Hence, in [\[151\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0151) the authors consider the applications where the sources are densely sparse, i.e. the number of active sources is high and very close to the number of sensors. In their work they developed a *k*‐SCA‐based algorithm that is suitable for USR in low‐dimensional mixing systems. Assuming the sources are at most (*m* − 1) sparse where *m* is the number of mixtures. Their method is capable of recovering the sources after estimating the mixing matrix using a subspace detection approach.

The *k*‐SCA algorithms for solving the underdetermined blind source separation (UBSS) problem often focus on identifying the mixing matrix through UBI such as in [\[162\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0162) and utilize conventional source recovery algorithms, i.e. greedy methods, such as OMP [\[159\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0159), relaxation methods, e.g. basis pursuit [\[160\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0160) or the smoothed *l*[*0*] algorithm [\[161\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0161).

It has been proved that [\[153\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0153), as long as *k* ≤ *m* − 1, where *k* is the number of active sources at each column of **S**, **A** can be identified and **S** estimated. One recent approach for solving this problem is based on the above proof and the definitions of disjoint subspaces [\[151\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0151). These definitions state that if there is no common mixing vector between the subspaces, then they are called disjoint subspaces and if there is *f* common mixing vector between the subspaces, then they are called *f* ‐nondisjoint subspaces. In that case, the number of *f* ‐nondisjoint subspaces is ![images](images/c5-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> where *f* = 1, 2, *… m* − 1.

Then, in order to find the closest subspace to each observed vector, we first find the set of all subsets of {1,…, *n*} containing *k* ≤ *m* − 1 elements called I. I [*i*] is the *i*th member of I representing the indices of *k* columns of **A** where ![images](images/c5-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>:</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup></math>. Next, we should identify an orthogonal complement space which is orthogonal to the observed data point and *k* columns of **A**. Then, the observed data point lies in that subspace spanned by those *k* columns of **A**, i.e. the observed data point will be the linear combination of those *k* vectors. This requires identification of the subspaces of each data point.

For this, the columns of the mixing matrix are normalized with respect to their *l* [2]‐norms. Then, for a given data point **x**[*t*] and all members of I, the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, are calculated; set **F**^(*i*) = \[**x**[*t*] **A**(:, I [*i*] )\] and then calculate ![images](images/c5-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><msup><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></msup></mrow></mfenced></math>, which is called the augmented mixing matrix (AMM). Then, the eigenvector corresponding to the minimum eigenvalue which is most orthogonal to **F**[*i*] is calculated. For *k = m* – 1 the number of disjoint subspaces is 1. The smaller *k < m* – 1 becomes the higher number of disjoint subspaces become available in which a sample **x**[*i*] can be assigned. This means ![images](images/c5-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>1</mn> <ce:anchor id="pp:132 np:133" role="page-break"/></math>. Then, the *k* basis vectors that have the maximum redundancy between *n*[*k*] members of I are estimated. These indices are inserted in a new vector **h**. These *k* basis vectors span the subspace where **x**[*t*] is assigned to. In this way the generating mixing vectors of each data point, i.e. the columns of **W** are found. Finally, each source point is recovered by pseudo‐inverse minimum mean squared error (MMSE) [\[151\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0151):

(5.36)![equation](images/c5-disp-0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></msup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></msup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> 

where *t* = 1, *… T*, the number of data points, **W**^(*t*) = **A**(:, **h**^(*t*) ), ![images](images/c5-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mi>t</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfenced></math>, **I**[*m*] is an *m × m* identity matrix and ![images](images/c5-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>N</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> is the noise variance estimated iteratively. To find **h**[*t*] , for each time instant we can have ![images](images/c5-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8592;</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup></math> the indices from I corresponding to the first lower eigenvalues of the AMM.

It has been shown that [\[151\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0151) this method outperforms the state‐of‐the‐art USR algorithms such as basis pursuit, minimizing *l* [1] – norm based constrained system, smoothed *l* [0] [\[161\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0161), FOCUSS, and OMP.

 

## 5.5 Nonlinear BSS

Consider the cases where the parameters of the mixing system change because of the changes in the mixing environment or the changes in the source statistics. For example, if the images of both sides of a semi‐transparent paper are photocopied the results will be two mixtures of the original sources. However, since the minimum observable grey level is black (or zero) and the maximum is white (say 1), the sum of the grey levels cannot go beyond these limits. This represents a nonlinear mixing system. As another example, think of the joint sounds heard from surface electrodes from over the skin. The mixing medium involves acoustic parameters of the body tissues. Since the tissues are not rigid, in such cases if the tissues vibrate due to the sound energy then the mixing system will be a nonlinear. The mixing and unmixing can be generally modelled respectively as:

(5.37)![equation](images/c5-disp-0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">As</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">n</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> (5.38)![equation](images/c5-disp-0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>g</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Wx</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *f*(∙) and *g*(∙) represent respectively the nonlinearities in the mixing and unmixing processes. There have been some attempts in solving nonlinear BSS problems especially for separation of image mixtures \[[94](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0094), [95](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0095)\]. In the attempt in [\[95\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0095) the mixing system has been modelled as a radial basis function (RBF) neural network. The parameters of this network are then computed iteratively. However, in these methods often an assumption about the mixing model is made \[101\].

An interesting example of a nonlinear mixing system is combination of heart and lung sounds mixing environment. Both heart and lung vary in shape during both heart beating and inhaling and exhaling processes. In order to solve the BSS for such a system, both heart and lung acoustics should be accurately modelled. Such a model has not been revealed so far and unfortunately, none of the nonlinear methods currently give satisfactory results.

  

## 5.6 Constrained BSS

The optimization problem underlying the solution to BSS problem may be subject to fulfilment of a number of conditions. These may be based on a priori knowledge of the sources or the mixing system. Any constraint on the estimated sources or the mixing system (or unmixing system) can lead to a more accurate estimation of the sources. Statistical [\[1\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0001) as well as geometrical constraints [\[2\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0002) have been very recently used in developing new BSS algorithms. In most of the cases the constrained problem is converted to an unconstrained one by means of a regularization parameter such as a Lagrange multiplier or more generally a nonlinear penalty function as used in [\[1\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0001).

Incorporating nonlinear penalty functions [\[13\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0013) into a joint diagonalization problem not only exploits nonstationarity of the signals but also ensures fast convergence of the update equation. A general formulation for the cost function of such a system can be in the form of:

(5.39)![equation](images/c5-disp-0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">&#954;&#981;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *J*[*m*] (**W**) and *J*[*c*] (**W**) are respectively the main and the constraint cost functions, *ϕ*(·) is the nonlinear penalty function, and *κ* is the penalty parameter.

Constrained BSS has a very high potential in incorporating clinical and physiological information into the main optimization formulation.

As a new application of constrained BSS, an effective algorithm has been developed for removing the eye‐blinking artefacts from EEGs. A similar method to the joint diagonalization of correlation matrices by using gradient methods [\[26\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0026) has been developed [\[27\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0027), which exploits the temporal structure of the underlying EEG sources. The algorithm is an extension of SOBI with the aim of iteratively performing the joint diagonalization of multiple time lagged covariance matrices of the estimated sources and exploiting the statistical structure of the eye‐blink signal as a constraint. The estimated source covariance matrix is given by

(5.40)![equation](images/c5-disp-0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></math> 

where ***R*** [***X***] (*k*) = *E*{ ***x*** (*n*) ***x*** ^(*T*) (*n* − *k*)} is the covariance matrix of the electrode signal. Following the same procedure as in [\[28\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0028), the least‐squares (LS) estimate of W is found from:
