(5.41)![equation](images/c5-disp-0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">arg</mo><munder><mo>min</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></munder><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></msubsup><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> 

where ![images](images/c5-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mo>.</mo></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> is the squared Frobenius norm and *E*(*k*) is the error to be minimized between the covariances of the source signals, **R** [**s**] (*k*) and the estimated sources, **R** [**Y**] (*k*). The corresponding cost function has been defined based on minimizing the off‐diagonal elements for each time block, that is:

(5.42)![equation](images/c5-disp-0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>J</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mfenced></math> 

where

(5.43)![equation](images/c5-disp-0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></msubsup><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo form="postfix">&#8722;</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">diag</mo><mo stretchy="true" form="prefix">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> 

and

(5.44)![equation](images/c5-disp-0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#958;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">g</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

is a second‐order constraint term. *ξ*(∙) is a nonlinear function approximating the cumulative density function (CDF) of the data and **Λ** = {λ[ij]} (*i =* 1, …, *N*) is the weighted factor which is governed by the correlation (matrix) between the EOG and EEG signals (**R** [GY]), defined as Λ = *κ*diag(R[GY]), where *κ* is an adjustable constant. Then a gradient approach [\[4\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0004) is followed to minimize the cost function. The incremental update equation is:

(5.45)![equation](images/c5-disp-0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi>J</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8706;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> 

which concludes the algorithm.

BSS has been widely used for processing of EEG signals some referred or presented in this book for different applications. Although, the main assumptions about the source signals such as uncorrelatedness or independency of such signals have not been verified yet, the empirical results illustrate the effectiveness of such methods. EEG signals are noisy and nonstationary and are normally affected by one or more types of internal artefacts. The most efficient approaches are those which consider all different domain statistics of the signals and take the nature of the artefacts into account. In addition, a major challenge is in how to incorporate and exploit the physiological properties of the signals and characteristics of the actual sources into the BSS algorithm. Some examples have been given here; some more will be presented in the other chapters of this book.

In the case of brain signals the independency or uncorrelatedness conditions for the sources may not be satisfied. This however may be acceptable for abnormal sources, movement‐related sources, or ERP signals. Transforming the problem into a domain such as STF‐domain, where the sources can be considered disjoint, may be a good solution.

 

## 5.7 Application of Constrained BSS; Example

In practise, natural signals such as EEG source signals are not always independent. A topographic ICA proposed in [\[29\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0029) incorporates the dependency among the nearby sources in not only grouping the independent components related to nearby sources but also separating the sources originating from different regions of the brain. In this ICA model it is proposed that the residual dependency structure of the independent components (ICs), defined as dependencies that cannot be cancelled by ICA, could be used to establish a topographic order between the components. Based on this model, if the topography is defined by a lattice or grid, the dependency of the components is a function of the distance of the components on that grid. Therefore, the generative model that implies correlation of energies for components that are close in the topographic grid is defined. The main assumption is then, the nearby sources are correlated and those far from each other are independent.

To develop such an algorithm a neighbourhood relation is initially defined as:

(5.46)![equation](images/c5-disp-0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>m</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>otherwise</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

where the constant *m* specifies the width of the neighbourhood. Such a function is therefore, a matrix of hyperparameters. This function can be incorporated into the main cost function of BSS. The update rule is then given as [\[29\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0029):

(5.47)![equation](images/c5-disp-0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8733;</mo><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></mfenced><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mspace width="0.2em"/></math> 

where **z**[*i*] is the whitened mixed signals and

(5.48)![equation](images/c5-disp-0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mi>h</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi>g</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mi>h</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced></math> 

The function *g* is the derivative of a nonlinear function such as those defined in [\[29\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0029). It is seen that the vectors **w**[*i*] are constrained to some topographic boundary defined by *h*(*i*, *j*). Finally, the orthogonalization and normalization can be accomplished, for example, by the classical method involving matrix square roots:

(5.49)![equation](images/c5-disp-0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mo>&#8592;</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></math> 

where **W** is the matrix of the vectors **w**[*i*] , i.e. **W** = \[**w** [1], **w** [2], *…*, **w**[*n*] \] ^(*T*) . The original mixing matrix **A** can be computed by inverting the whitening process as **A** = (**WV**)^(−1), where **V** is the whitening matrix.

This algorithm has been modified for separation of seizure signals, by (*i*) iteratively finding the best neighbourhood *m*, and (*ii*) constraining the desired estimated source to be within a specific frequency band originating from certain brain zones (confirmed clinically). [Figure 5.5](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0005) illustrates the independent components of a set of EEG signals from an epileptic patient, using the above constrained topographic ICA method. In [Figure 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0006) the corresponding topographic maps for all independent components (i.e. backprojection of each IC to the scalp using the inverse of the estimated unmixing matrix,) are shown. From these figures the sixth IC from the top clearly shows the seizure component. Consequently, the corresponding topograph shows the location of a seizure over the left temporal electrodes. The high quality of the results is due to two important facts: first, the sources including those elicited from the brain and noise are independent and second, the mixtures are linear combination of the sources. The two properties are the main requirement for a linear ICA system.

 

## 5.8 Multiway EEG Decompositions

The multichannel methods based on ICA exploit the time–space (channel) diversity in the source decomposition. In these cases, despite independency of the sources they are considered stationary (within the segments being processed).

As emphasized at the beginning of this chapter, most of physiological signals have nonstationary behaviour, the existing artefacts are nonstationary or the mixing system may be nonlinear. Conversely, the additive noise may not be Gaussian. As an example, consider the state of the brain when transferring from relax to attention, from preictal to ictal for epileptic patients, or from before to after hand movement (when motor area is engaged). In these and many other cases the nonstationarity stems from the changes in the signal trends or  statistics. These shortcomings have been taken into consideration and in some cases nicely exploited in development of a new class of BSS systems called nonstationary BSS. Such algorithms not only exploit the mutual statistical behaviour of the source signals but also exploit the variations in the statistical properties of those sources across smaller signal segments.

![Figure 5.5 Estimated independent components of a set of EEG signals, acquired from 16 electrodes, using constrained topographic ICA.](images/c05f005.gif)

[**Figure 5.5**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0005) Estimated independent components of a set of EEG signals, acquired from 16 electrodes, using constrained topographic ICA.

![Figure 5.6 Topographic maps, each illustrating an IC. It is clear that the sources are geometrically localized.](images/c05f006.gif)

[**Figure 5.6**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0006) Topographic maps, each illustrating an IC. It is clear that the sources are geometrically localized.

In addition, often the components of interest are not sufficiently distinct in the time–space domain. Therefore, algorithms which can extend the analysis into other domains such as frequency, segment (to exploit nonstationarity), trials and subjects become very favourable.

To accommodate this, a new mathematical representation of the signals and systems and their corresponding mixing model are needed to best exploit these variations as new dimensions for the data. The multiway approaches mainly based on tensor factorization is a solution to these problems.

Therefore, in the following subsections a number of these approaches are discussed. Before we move forward a new concept which has been recently used in source separation, channel identification, and source localization called tensor factorization, is described.

 

### 5.8.1 Tensor Factorization for BSS

With no doubt it is favourable to represent the data in a domain where the variation of such data in all aspects can be assessed and tracked. The so‐called *multiway* signal processing is an effective step in this direction. The multiway technique incorporates the concept of tensors and tensor factorization to achieve that. Tensor decompositions were first introduced by Hitchcock in 1927 \[[30](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0030), [31](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0031)\], and the idea of a multiway model is attributed to Cattell in 1944 \[[32](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0032), [33](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0033)\]. These concepts received scant attention until the work of Tucker in the 1960s \[[34](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0034)–[36](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0036)\] and Carroll and Chang [\[37\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0037) and Harshman [\[38\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0038) in 1970, all of which appeared in psychometrics. Appellof and Davidson [\[39\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0039) are generally credited as being the first to use tensor decompositions (in 1981) in chemometrics, and tensors have since become extremely popular in that field [\[40\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0040).

A tensor is a multidimensional array. More formally, an N‐way or Nth‐order tensor is an element of the tensor product of N vector spaces, each of which has its own coordinate system. A first‐order tensor is a vector, a second‐order tensor is a matrix, and a third‐order tensor has three indices. Tensors of order three or higher are called higher‐order tensors. The order of a tensor is the number of dimensions also known as way or mode. A tensor decomposition has been widely used in signal processing such as in \[[41](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0041)–[50](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0050)\] and neuroscience such as in \[[51](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0051)–[60](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0060), [96](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0060)\]. [Figure 5.7](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0007) illustrates the concept.

Decomposition of higher‐order tensors has applications in chemometrics, signal processing, communications, linear algebra, computer vision, data mining, neuroscience, and graph analysis. For detection, separation, localization, noise removal, and tracking. Traditionally, two particular tensor decompositions can be considered to be higher‐order extensions of the matrix SVD, namely Canonical decomposition (CANDECOMP)/PARAFAC (CP) tensor decomposition.

From a mathematical viewpoint, there are two general tensor factorization approaches. The first one is the Tucker model which tries to factorize a three‐way tensor to a smaller tensor (core tensor) and three other factors/matrices. This model is not unique since there are various ways the core tensor can be organized. The second one is the PARAFAC tensor model with a superdiagonal core tensor. Since there is no other variation of such a core tensor the PARAFAC factorization is unique which means for orthogonal or independent sources, the mixtures can be decomposed into their constituent sources without any ambiguity. [Figure 5.8](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0008) represents the above models. Also, PARAFAC decomposes a tensor into the sum of rank one tensors and the Tucker decomposition is a higher‐order form of principal component analysis (PCA).

There are many other tensor decompositions, including INDSCAL, PARAFAC2, CANDELINC, DEDICOM, and PARATUCK2 as well as nonnegative variants of all of them [\[61\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0061). The N‐way Toolbox, Tensor Toolbox, and Multilinear Engine are examples of software packages for working with tensors.

![Figure 5.7 Tensor and its various modes.](images/c05f007.gif)

[**Figure 5.7**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0007) Tensor and its various modes.

![Figure 5.8 Tensor factorization using: (a) Tucker and (b) PARAFAC models.](images/c05f008.gif)

[**Figure 5.8**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0008) Tensor factorization using: (a) Tucker and (b) PARAFAC models.

Recently, tensor factorization has been widely used for BSS of both instantaneous and convolutive mixtures. To be able to benefit from tensor modelling, we need to build up a tensor from our two‐dimensional multichannel measurements. As an example, a time–space‐frequency tensor can be built by initially transforming the data into the TF domain and then incorporating the space (geometrical locations of the sensors) dimension. For analysis of EEG or magnetoencephalography (MEG) this can be illustrated as in [Figure 5.9](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0009).

In general, any other dimension in which the data variation is significant and desired can be selected. For example, to exploit the nonstationarity, one of the dimensions can be represented by the signal segment number. This allows the changes in statistics of the data to be tracked effectively within the tensor model.

![Figure 5.9 A tensor representation of a set of multichannel EEG signals. (a) Time‐domain representation. (b) Time–frequency representation of each electrode signal. (c) The constructed tensor.](images/c05f009a.gif)

[**Figure 5.9**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0009) A tensor representation of a set of multichannel EEG signals. (a) Time‐domain representation. (b) Time–frequency representation of each electrode signal. (c) The constructed tensor.

In [\[60\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0060) an approach for the removal of eye‐blink artefacts from EEG signals based on a novel STF model of EEGs and the robust minimum variance beamformer (RMVB) has been proposed. In this method, in order to remove the artefact, the RMVB has been provided with a priori information, namely, an estimation of the steering vector corresponding to the point source of the eye blink. The artefact‐removed EEGs are subsequently reconstructed by deflation. The a priori knowledge, the vector corresponding to the spatial distribution of the eye‐blink factor, is identified using the STF model of EEGs, provided by the PARAFAC method. In order to reduce the computational complexity present in the estimation of the STF model using the three‐way PARAFAC, the time domain is sub‐divided into a number of segments and a four‐way array is then set to estimate the space–time–frequency‐time/segment (STF‐TS) model of the data using the four‐way PARAFAC. The correct number of the factors of the STF model has been effectively estimated by using a novel core consistency diagnostic (CORCONDIA)‐based measure.

Subsequently, the STF‐TS model is shown to approximate closely the classic STF model, with significantly lower computational cost. The results demonstrate that such an algorithm effectively identifies and removes the eye‐blink (EB) artefact from raw EEG measurements. Using this approach, [Figure 5.10](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0010) shows the space, time, and frequency signatures of an eye blink as the result of applying PARAFAC. [Figure 5.11](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0011) shows the restored EEGs after applying the STF‐TS method. In this method the nonstationarity of the data is also exploited through segmentation as discussed in [Section 5.8.2](#c05.xhtml#c5-sec-0021).

The above approach shows that PARAFAC can be combined with another modality mainly to intelligently select and extract the atom (source) of interest.

More applications of PARAFAC such as in [\[59\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0059) related to BCI are explained in other chapters of this book.

![Figure 5.10 The extracted factors using STF–TS modelling. (a) and (b) illustrate respectively the spectral and temporal signatures of the extracted factors. (c) and (d) represents the spatial distributions of those extracted factors \[60\].](images/c05f010.gif)

[**Figure 5.10**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0010) The extracted factors using STF–TS modelling. (a) and (b) illustrate respectively the spectral and temporal signatures of the extracted factors. (c) and (d) represents the spatial distributions of those extracted factors [\[60\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0060).

  

### 5.8.2 Solving BSS of Nonstationary Sources Using Tensor Factorization

Using a simple PARAFAC model may provide some insightful information about various components in the signal mixtures. As an example, [Figure 5.12](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0012) demonstrates the results of PARAFAC operation for detecting two components (atoms) of an EEG segment recording during left finger movement. The main component in [Figure 5.12](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0012)b is in the right‐hand side (contralateral) and the second component in [Figure 5.12](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0012)a is in the same side (ipsilateral) of the brain motor cortex.

In this approach, in order to localize seizure signals (within the scalp through an analysis of EEG), a tensor with three modes, i.e. time samples, scales, and electrodes, has been constructed through wavelet analysis of multichannel EEG. Next, they demonstrate that PARAFAC provides promising results in modelling the complex structure of epileptic seizure, localizing a seizure origin and extracting the artefacts.

 ![Figure 5.11 Restoration of the EEG signals in (a) from multiple eye blinks after applying the STF–TS method \[60\]; the results are shown in (b).](images/c05f011a.gif)

[**Figure 5.11**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0011) Restoration of the EEG signals in (a) from multiple eye blinks after applying the STF–TS method [\[60\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0060); the results are shown in (b).

The fundamental expression of the PARAFAC model, which is used to describe decomposition of trilinear data sets, is given as:

(5.50)![equation](images/c5-disp-0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ijk</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>R</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>a</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ir</mi></msub><msub><mi>b</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">jr</mi></msub><msub><mi>c</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">kr</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ijk</mi></msub></math> 

In matrix form this can be described as:

(5.51)![equation](images/c5-disp-0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math> 

where **X**[*k*] represents the *k*th frontal slice of tensor ![images](images/c5-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mtext>\_</mtext></munder></math> built from multichannel data **X,** and **A** and **B** are the component matrices in the first and second modes, respectively. **D**[*k*] is a diagonal matrix, whose diagonal elements correspond to the *k*th row of the third component matrix **C** denoted as **D**[*k*] = *diag*(**C**[*k,*:]). Finally, **E**[*k*] contains the error terms corresponding to the entries in the *k*th frontal slice.

In order to estimate the factors an alternating least‐squares (ALS) approach is applied. Ignoring the noise term, this leads to performing the following alternating operations until convergence:

(5.52)![equation](images/c5-disp-0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>1</mn></mfenced></msub><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mo>&#8728;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup></mfenced><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup></math> (5.53)![equation](images/c5-disp-0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>2</mn></mfenced></msub><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mo>&#8728;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup></mfenced><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup></math> (5.54)![equation](images/c5-disp-0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>3</mn></mfenced></msub><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>&#8728;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup></mfenced><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup></math> 

where (.)^† denotes the pseudo‐inverse operation, **X** [(*i*)] represents the unfolded version of tensor **X** in the *i*th dimension and ° denotes the Khatri–Rao product.

The results of PARAFAC decomposition is unique if *k* [A] + *k* [B] + *k* [C] ≥ 2*R* + 2, where *k* [**A**] refers to the Kruskal rank of **A.** For an *N* rank tensor, this however has been modified to [\[62\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0062):

(5.55)![equation](images/c5-disp-0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>R</mi><mo>+</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></math> 

Although most of the properties of the sources can be evaluated using these so‐called ‘signatures’ of the data [\[63\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0063) and they are useful for diagnostic applications but unfortunately, the original sources (in the time domain) cannot be recovered. Also, it is seen that the representing signatures do not vary for different time segments. Hence, in this model the signals are considered stationary. Therefore, such a model cannot be utilized for BSS. So, the main question here is that how tensor factorization can be used for source separation. Moreover, how this can be extended to separation of nonstationary data.

As an extension to PARAFAC, PARAFAC2 supports variation in one mode of the tensor. Mathematically, PARAFAC can be expressed in the following form:

(5.56)![equation](images/c5-disp-0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> ![Figure 5.12 Representation of the first two components (a, b) in the time–space–frequency domain for a segment of EEG signal during left finger movement.](images/c05f012.gif)

[**Figure 5.12**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0012) Representation of the first two components (a, b) in the time–space–frequency domain for a segment of EEG signal during left finger movement.

Compared with PARAFAC, PARAFAC2 is designed to deal with non‐trilinear data sets, while keeping uniqueness of the solutions as for PARAFAC. To do so, PARAFAC2 allows some freedom in the shape of the *k* slabs (**X**[*k*] ) in the variable mode. To maintain the uniqueness of the solutions ![images](images/c5-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math> are forced to have the same structure for all *k*, i.e. ![images](images/c5-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></math>. In this case the above equation is subject to ![images](images/c5-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi></math>. Consequently, **A**[*k*] can be modelled as **A**[*k*] = **P**[*k*] **A**, where ![images](images/c5-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></math>. Therefore, the *direct* form for PARAFAC2 can be in the following form:

(5.57)![equation](images/c5-disp-0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></math> 

ALS optimization is proposed to estimate the direct model parameters. Unlike for indirect PARAFAC2 [\[84\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0084), for the direct PARAFAC it is possible to apply a priori conditions, impose constraints, and generalize it to n‐way models. The steps in estimating the factors are as follows [\[85\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0085):

Considering **X**[*k*] as an *R × J × K* three‐way array with frontal planes ![images](images/c5-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>, *k* = 1,…, *K*.

*   **Step 0**. If *J* < *n*[*k*] , where *n*[*k*] is the number of columns in the *k*th data matrix, replace **X**[*k*] by **H**[*k*] , e.g. from the Cholesky decomposition ![images](images/c5-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math>.
*   **Step 1**. Initialize **B** as the loading matrix by applying PCA to ![images](images/c5-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math> and initialize **A** and **D** [1], ⋯, **D**[*k*] as **I**[*R*] .
*   **Step 1a**. Compute the SVD ![images](images/c5-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math>and update **P**[*k*] as ![images](images/c5-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math>, *k* = 1,…,*K*.
*   **Step 1b**. Update **A**, **B** and **D** [1],…, **D**[*K*] by one cycle of a PARAFAC algorithm applied to the *R × J× K* three‐way array with frontal planes ![images](images/c5-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math>, *k* = 1,…, *K*.
*   **Step 1c**. Evaluate ![images](images/c5-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. If *σ*[*old*]  − *σ*[*new*]  > *εσ*[*old*] for some small value *ε*, repeat Step 1; else go to Step 2.
*   **Step 2.** Given that **X**[*k*] has been replaced by **H**[*k*] in Step 0, now replace **H**[*k*] by **X**[*k*] again and compute **P**[*k*] according to Step 1a, *k* = 1,…, *K*.

As all the factors are estimated through the above steps, the sources can be easily estimated as **S**[*k*] = **P**[*k*] **HD**[*k*] .

In the case of nonstationary sources it is logical to have *k* as the number of segments. This allows to track and exploit the variation in signal statistics across the segments and therefore, the nonstationarities can be tolerated.

Some nonstationary BSS approaches by using tensor factorization have been developed recently. SOBI [\[3\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0003) was probably the first BSS approach tried to solve the problem of nonstationarity in BSS by applying diagonalization of covariance matrices in multiple lags. Although for nonstationary signal sources the performance of the SOBI algorithm is better than those of many other BSS approaches, for highly nonstationary cases not only the performance is not acceptable but also the statistical fluctuation within the source signals is ignored. The fundamental approach followed by the researchers recently involves dividing the input into small segments and converting the entire input signal matrices into tensors which can be processed using the corresponding mathematical techniques as described above. A number of approaches have been followed recently such as those in \[[86](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0086)–[88](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0088)\].

In the work by Hyvarinen [\[86\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0086) inspired by Matsukas et al.'s research [\[89\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0089), the nonstationarity is interpreted by smooth variation in variance and it is shown that the cross‐cumulants for nonstationary sources are positive. Consequently, a method similar to the one for maximizing the kurtosis for BSS has been developed to maximize the cumulants which measure the nonstationarity of the separated source. Since the defined positive cross‐cumulants do not require the marginal distribution of the source signals to be Gaussian, it can be used for nonstationary Gaussian sources too.

In another attempt [\[87\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0087) the algorithm utilizes the principle of maximum likelihood and minimum MI. In both cases the optimization amounts to approximate joint diagonalization of a set of *L* matrices. Intuitively, nonstationarity allows blind identification in the Gaussian case. This is because a single covariance matrix does not provide enough constraints to uniquely determine **A**. A collection of several covariance matrices estimated over different time periods does determine **A**, provided the source distributions change enough over the whole observation period. In his algorithm it is considered that the profile of changing variance of each estimated source is simply a smoothed version of the square of that source. Therefore, the variances are calculated over smaller segments of the data.

A similar concept has also been exploited in [\[88\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0088). Similarly, this method can be used for both Gaussian and non‐Gaussian sources. Also, in this approach it is assumed that the additive noise signals are temporally uncorrelated and mutually uncorrelated with the source signals. Unlike general BSS methods using SOS or HOS concepts, a first‐order blind source separation (FOBSS) has been proposed by defining a first‐order model for the mixtures. This system was then applied to separation of seizure components of a set of EEG signals. Using the FOBSS method is based on the following assumptions:

*   A1: The columns of all **S**[*k*] are mutually uncorrelated, particularly, **S**[*k*] matrices are all orthogonal.
*   A2: The source columns of all **S**[*k*] can be temporally correlated/uncorrelated.
*   A3: The source envelopes (as in [\[88\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0088)) change independently, i.e. each source has varying variance over its segments *k* and the variation for different sources is independent.
*   A4: The mixing channel A is full rank and remains unchanged for all time segments *k*.
*   A5: The additive noise signals are temporally uncorrelated and mutually uncorrelated with the sources.

Based on A1 all the source covariance matrices, i.e. ![images](images/c5-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math>, are diagonal with nonnegative diagonal values for all *k* = 1,…, *K*. So, the basic model after temporal segmentation is simply stated as:

(5.58)![equation](images/c5-disp-0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math> 

where ![images](images/c5-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> is a diagonal matrix. **A** is fixed across the segments. Each **S**[*k*] is decomposed into one row‐wise orthonormal matrix **P**[*k*] and one diagonal matrix **D**[*k*] which absorbs the norm of different columns of **S**[*k*] at each segment *k* as **S**[*k*] = **P**[*k*] **D**[*k*] . This satisfies orthogonality of the segmented sources, i.e. ![images](images/c5-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math>. Similar to the previous model, this can change the above model to:

(5.59)![equation](images/c5-disp-0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">E</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></math> 

The parameters (factors) of the above model using the FOBSS approach in [\[89\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0089) can be estimated by going through the following steps:

*   **Step 1**: Initialize all the model parameters randomly.
*   **Step 2**: Estimation of **P**[*k*] using ![images](images/c5-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math> for all k = 1, …, *K*, where **U**[*k*] and **V**[*k*] are the eigenvectors.
*   **Step 3** : **A** is estimated using ![images](images/c5-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>.</mo></math>
*   **Step 4**: To calculate **D**[*k*] the following relations (as the result of solving the above constrained optimization problem) are used: (5.60)![equation](images/c5-disp-0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi></math> 

where **Λ** is a diagonal matrix defined as **Λ** = *Ddiag*(**A**^(*T*) **A**) which sets all the non‐diagonal elements of **A**^(*T*) **A** to zero. Then, for all *k* we use:

(5.61)![equation](images/c5-disp-0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">km</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi></math> 

where ![images](images/c5-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">km</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext mathvariant="italic">Ddiag</mtext><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> are diagonal matrices for *k,m* = 1, *…*, *K*. Finally, for *r*th source using **G**[*r*] **d**[*r*] = λ[r]**d**[*r*] , where **d**[*r*] is the result of stacking all the *r*th diagonal elements of all **D**[*k*] . Solving the above problem is equal to finding the nearest eigenvalue of **G**[*r*] to ![images](images/c5-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> where **a**[*r*] is the *r*th column of mixing matrix **A**, and respectively its corresponding eigenvectors **d**[*r*] .

*   **Step 5**: If ‖**X**[*k*]  − **P**[*k*] **D**[*k*] **A**^(*T*) ‖ ≥ *σ* ², where *σ* ² is the expected noise variance, go to **Step 2**, otherwise, stop.

[Figure 5.13](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0013) shows the results of the FOBSS algorithm in separation of seizure component from the scalp EEG. The data are just the last segment of a long data recorded from the scalp of an epileptic patient in the Clinical Neuroscience Department, King's College London simultaneously with a set of intracranial signals using electrodes implanted within the brain. In [Figure 5.14](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0014) the signals from three intracranial source signals have been illustrated. From [Figure 5.14](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0014) the instant of ictal onset is very clear.

 

## 5.9 Tensor Factorization for Underdetermined Source Separation

The SCA methods in [Section 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c5-sec-0011) exploit the sparsity of the constituent sources in grouping and separation of the signals. Moreover, the main assumption in these methods is the fact that only one signal has non‐zero amplitude at each instant of time. Although in some applications with sparse sources identification of the mixing channels is achieved successfully, in many cases reconstruction of the original source signals are either difficult or less accurate.

In tensor factorization approaches recently developed for underdetermined or sparse source separation, such as in \[[41](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0041)[90](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0090)–[93](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0093)\], two main concepts have been exploited. The first property is sparsity of the sources as for the SCA approaches, and the second one, which represents one of the main advantages of tensor factorization to other separation methods, is the fact that tensors can have the ranks higher than those of related matrices. Therefore, it is expected that the maximum number of separable sources increases with increase in the rank of the tensor. Moreover, in some applications such as in [\[91\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0091) the idea of sparse events has been presented. This means that at each period of time up to a certain number of sources can be active. Such an approach can also be considered as generalization of the SCA methods described in Section to the situation where we can have more than one sources active and also, the duration of activity of a source can be more than a sample period.

Therefore, tensor factorization techniques, especially PARAFAC \[[44](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0044), [92](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0092)\], have been used to solve the UBI problem even when the sources are non‐sparse or fully active (e.g. *k*[*a*]  ≤ *N*[*s*] ) [\[88\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0088). Later, second and HOS based methods have been developed to solve the UBI problem using joint/simultaneous diagonalization of a series of symmetric square matrices such as second‐order blind identification of underdetermined mixtures (SOBIUM) [\[90\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0090) and fourth‐order cumulant‐based blind identification of underdetermined mixtures  (so‐called FOOBI) [\[41\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0041). The SOBIUM method deals with the covariance matrices of different segments and tries to convert the UBI problem to a PARAFAC problem, with two identical factors called INdividuals Differences in SCALing (INDSCAL) [\[43\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0043), to joint block diagonalization of some exact‐determined Hermitian matrices. [Table 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c5-tbl-0001) shows the upper bounds for SOBIUM and FOOBI in terms of maximum number of separable sources.

![Figure 5.13 The results of application of the FOBSS algorithm to a set of scalp EEGs in (a), (b) the separated sources, and (c) the corresponding topographs respectively.](images/c05f013a.gif)

[**Figure 5.13**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0013) The results of application of the FOBSS algorithm to a set of scalp EEGs in (a), (b) the separated sources, and (c) the corresponding topographs respectively.

![Figure 5.14 The intracranial records from three electrodes. These signals were simultaneously recorded together with the scalp EEGs in Figure 5.13a.](images/c05f014.gif)

[**Figure 5.14**](#c05.xhtml#R_c5-fig-0014) The intracranial records from three electrodes. These signals were simultaneously recorded together with the scalp EEGs in [Figure 5.13](#c05.xhtml#c5-fig-0013)a.

In [\[91\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0091) a tensor factorization based approach to *k*[*a*] ‐SCA (called *k*‐SCA in [\[28\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0028)) has been developed to solve UBSS and especially UBI problems. *k*[*a*] sources have been considered active in each signal segment. Similar to *k*[*a*] ‐SCA methods, introduced in Section, *k*[*a*] must satisfy *k*[*a*] ≤ *N*[*x*] – 1. However, in this approach instead of sparse signals (with limited signals active in each instant) sparse events (for which limited sources are active within some signal segments of particular duration) have been introduced and considered. Therefore, initially, the number of active sources in each signal segment has been estimated. A necessary condition for such a method to work is to have sufficient number of segments to have each source active in some of the segments. The UBI is then performed using the segments of sparsely active sources.

This approach improves the general upper bound in terms of maximum possible number of sources that can be achieved by the SOBIUM method [\[90\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0090). Using some synthetically mixed signals it has been shown that the separation error is less for the above UOM‐BSS method compared to those of both the SOBIUM and FOOBI methods.

 

## 5.10 Tensor Factorization for Separation of Convolutive Mixtures in the Time Domain

Due to flexibility in definition of multiway systems, convolutive BSS in the time domain can be modelled using tensors. In \[[48](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0048), [49](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0049), [97](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0097), [98](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0098)\] the anechoic convolutive BSS problem has been formulated as a tensor factorization problem. In a noiseless environment the problem has been stated as:

(5.62)![equation](images/c5-disp-0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#926;</mi><mi>&#964;</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>&#964;</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></msub></math> 

where **Ξ**[*τ*] accounts for the delays and **A**[*τ*] accommodates all the weights for the delayed terms. An effective method for estimation of the parameters/factors has been proposed particularly for estimation of **A**[*τ*] [\[98\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0098).

In this approach it has been demonstrated that the impulse response of the channels can be more accurately estimated if the locations of the sources and the sensors are known. This geometrical information can be nicely fused into the separation process.

 

## 5.11 Separation of Correlated Sources via Tensor Factorization

Unfortunately, many physiological and biological signal sources are somehow correlated mainly because of having the same origin or cause for their generation. Consider for example the actual components of a QRS signal within an ECG signal. Such components cannot be separated using conventional BSS which relies on independency of the sources. Another example is separation of P3a and P3b, subcomponents of a P300 signal, from EEGs. These components are related to the same event or stimulus and partially overlap in time and space (and albeit in frequency).

In [\[99\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0099) this problem has been addressed using tensor factorization. Promising outcomes have been obtained using synthetically mixed components. However, assessment of the application of this method to real signals is still a subject of research.

Exploitation of matrix and tensor factorization together with new optimization techniques have become central to EEG signal processing. An application of such methods to joint scalp‐intracranial EEGs namely, group component analysis for separation of common and individual components [\[166\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0166) aiming at detection of interictal epileptiform discharges (IED) [\[167\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0167) is explored in [Chapter 11](#c11.xhtml) of this book.

 

## 5.12 Common Component Analysis

Common component analysis can be posed as a tensor decomposition problem, unlike PCA, standard approaches to tensor decomposition have two drawbacks: (i) they are generally iterative and rely on the initialization. A bad initialization may lead to poor local optima and (ii) for a given level of approximation error, selection of suitable low dimensionality is not always possible.

Common component analysis can be formulated as follows. Assume a set of high‐dimensional covariance matrices **X**[*t*]  ∈ ℜ ^(*n* × *n*) , 1 ≤ *t* ≤ *T*. The key hypothesis driving the common component analysis concept is that the high‐dimensional covariance matrices are indeed a linearly transformed version of a set of low‐dimensional covariance matrices **Y**[*t*]  ∈ ℜ ^(*r* × *r*) , 1 ≤ *t* ≤ *T*, i.e.:

(5.63)![equation](images/c5-disp-0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">E</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></math> 

where **U** ∈ ℜ ^(*n* × *r*) and **E**[*t*] is the residual matrix. In the above equation both **U** and **Y**[*t*] are unknown given that **U** is orthonormal. In order to estimate them, the following optimization is carried out:

(5.64)![equation](images/c5-disp-0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mo>min</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></munder><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></math> 

This is called common component analysis because **U** determines a common subspace for all the covariance matrices. If there is only one covariance matrix **X** [1], then the model reduces to standard PCA. For more than one covariance matrices, the problem can be solved using tensor decompositions approaches.

 

## 5.13 Canonical Correlation Analysis

Another popular method for EEG analysis is called canonical correlation analysis (CCA). CCA is used to identify and measure the associations among two sets of variables. CCA determines a set of canonical variates, orthogonal linear combinations of the variables within each set that best explain the variability both within and between sets. In this decorrelation process, very similar to common spatial patterns (CSP) the sources are estimated from their mixtures in such a way that they are temporally maximally correlated and mutually uncorrelated. The main purposes for CCA are: (i) Data reduction: this explains the covariation between two sets of variables using small number of linear combinations and (ii) Data interpretation: this is to find features (i.e. canonical variates) that are important for explaining covariation between sets of variables.

Let **X** = (**x** [1], **x** [2], …, **x**[*p*] )^′ and **Y** = (**y** [1], **y** [2], …, **y**[*q*] )^′ with covariance matrices ∑ [*x*] and ∑ [*y*] respectively and cross‐covariance of ∑ [*xy*] . Considering **U** = **W**[*x*] **X** and **V** = **W**[*y*] **Y**, the objective is to find the optimum **W**[*x*] and **W**[*y*] to maximize the correlation between **U** and **V** denoted as ρ(**U**, **V**):

(5.65)![equation](images/c5-disp-0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#961;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8721;</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">xy</mi></msub><msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8721;</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></msqrt><msqrt><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8721;</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></msqrt></mrow></mfrac></math> 

CCA is used for feature detection [\[168\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0168) or source separation [\[169\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0169). There have been many applications of CCA to analysis of EEG signals such as in [\[170\]](#c05.xhtml#c5-bib-0170) for separation of muscle artefacts from EEG signals.

 

## 5.14 Summary

During the past two decades a large number of BSS methods have been proposed. A BSS problem becomes more difficult to solve when the signals are convolutively mixed, the number of sources is more than the number of sensors, the signals are nonstationary, or the system is nonlinear. In this chapter the BSS problem for different scenarios have been explained. Recently introduced tensor factorization approaches can highly alleviate these problems by relying on their three fundamental properties: first, they can map the signals into a multidimensional space where the sources can become disjoint; second, their ranks are often higher than any of the corresponding two‐dimensional representations of the data; and third, any related constraint can be easily incorporated to ensure the desired unique solution. The concepts in this chapter can be a good foundation for understanding many other approaches in BSS. The new techniques in underdetermined source separation allow k‐sparsity for which the number of active sources at each time can be very close to the number of mixtures. Representation of multichannel data, which vary from segment to segment and from subject to subject, in tensor form, efficiently exploits the data diversity for separation and classification purposes.
