where **w**[*n*, *j*] and **v**[*n*, *j*] are respectively the *M* × 1 and *L* × 1 vectors of state and observation noises, **C** is the *L* × *MF* forward matrix of source to electrode mapping, and **Λ** is an *MF* × *M* block diagonal matrix with *F* × 1 vectors **λ**^(*m*) on the diagonal representing any unknown parameters describing the spatial activity of the *m*th region [\[54\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0054). Although such a presentation is not unique, the non‐uniqueness problem does not affect the model parameter estimations [\[57\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0057). An ML approach including expectation–maximization can then be employed to estimate the model [(8.38)](#c08.xhtml#c8-disp-0038) parameters including **A** which represent the connectivity parameters.

A similar state‐space method has been applied to a radial basis function (RBF)‐based connectivity model. An MVAR of order *P* for representing the cortical signals **x**[*n*, *j*] can be described as in [\[58\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0058). This model is important since it complies with the invariance property required to evaluate Granger causality. Also, the universal approximation theorem [\[59\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0059) states that an RBF network is capable of approximating any smooth function to an arbitrary degree of accuracy [\[54\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0054). Therefore, RBF is able to model nonlinear dynamics of cortical signals. RBF has been used to estimate nonlinear Granger causality for intracranial EEG signal analysis [\[58\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0058). To use RBF for estimation of the cortical connectivity between *M* cortical regions we have [\[54\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0054):

(8.39)![equation](images/c8-disp-0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#936;&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Z</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> 

where **Ψ** is an *M* × *MI* matrix of RBF weights, and ![images](images/c8-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msubsup></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>M</mi></msup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>M</mi></msubsup></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup></math> is an *MI* × 1 vector of nonlinear functions of P variables, where ![images](images/c8-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>I</mi><mi>m</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> is an *I* × 1 vector of RBF kernels [\[54\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0054). The elements of **Ψ** reflect the coupling between brain cortical regions which can be estimated from the cortical signals by solving a system of linear equations.

In all the above methods there is no link between the brain connectivity and the task performed by the brain. Therefore, there is a need for modelling the pathways between the connectivity estimates and the performed task by the brain leading to a mental or physical action. In the following section, we see how the connectivity measures are incorporated into the design of an adaptive filter which models such pathways.

 

## 8.9 Application of Cooperative Adaptive Filters

None of the approaches mentioned above (including all previously used for brain connectivity estimation) takes into account any model of such processes, where the brain attempts to achieve certain objectives, in a concise manner, considering evolutions in both time and (electrode) space, particularly, when one brain sets the goals and the other brain follows.

Distributed sources assumption of movement‐related cortical sources and the dynamics of synaptic currents motivates a new solution for investigation of brain connectivity. Recent evidences from a finger movement experiment show that the neurons in both contralateral and ipsilateral brain lobes are engaged in the movement [\[60\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0060). However, there is no further investigation about dynamics of the movement in this literature. In this section a different and novel approach based on cooperative adaptive filtering theory, incorporating *diffusion adaptation* \[[61](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0061)–[63](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0063)\], is introduced. The fundamental aim of this research is to model the brain dynamics (i.e. varying connectivity in both time and space) for each particular body movement. There are enormous applications for this design such as brain behaviour during prolonged movement for healthy and Parkinson subjects and EEG hyper‐scanning.

In the original work in diffusion adaptation \[[64](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0064)–[66](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0066)\] a simple strategy in sharing information was introduced. In this interesting work both time and space evolutions have been exploited in the design of an adaptive filter. Therefore, a response from a node in a network corresponds to not only the input (or stimulus) of the network but also the network model, including cooperation of nearby nodes, which evolves in time.

Adaptive networks in mobile communications consist of collection of nodes with learning and motion abilities that interact with each other locally in order to solve distributed processing and distributed inference problems in real‐time. The objective of such a network is to estimate some filter coefficients in a fully distributed manner and in real‐time, where each node is allowed to interact only with its neighbours.

In [\[61\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0061) a similar adaptation algorithm inspired by bacteria mobility, has been developed for adaptation over networks with mobile nodes. The nodes have limited functionalities and are allowed to cooperate with their neighbours to optimize a common objective function. In this elegant approach the nodes do not know the form of the cost function beforehand. They can only sense variations in values of the objective function as they diffuse through the space. A good nature inspired application example is in sensing the variation in the concentration of nutrients in the environment. In this model however, sharing the information has been limited to binary choices between run and tumble for the movement of mobile nodes.

Following the above work, a diffusion adaptation algorithm that exhibited self‐organization properties was developed and applied to the model of cooperative hunting (of prey fish) among predators (sharks) while the fish herd and move towards a nutrition point [\[63\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0063). In this new application the nodes of the network wish to track the location of food source and the location of the predator. The modelling equations are therefore applied to both targets.

To better estimate the parameters such as weights of the links between nodes, other previously described methods such as SEM can be used to initialize the nodes and their mutual connectivity (presented by the link weights) levels. Time evolution of the changes in these levels can be estimated while undertaking cooperative or competitive tasks (such as hand movement in a synchronized dance). Then, a constrained diffusion adaptation algorithm is developed to model the brain responses to these tasks performed by two or more human brains to achieve or avoid a particular objective (stimulus).

This approach requires definition of a number of bio‐inspired and physiological constraints for each type of brain activity and also definition of regions of connectivity and the spatial connectivity likelihoods within each region. Eventually, depending on the brain responses, which regions of the brain are involved, the synchronization of the brains, and how they follow (or avoid) each other, the diffusion adaptation algorithm can be designed. Here, each measurement point (electrode) will be considered as a node and the expected time–space response of the brain to each stimulus becomes the target. Hence, from an algorithmic perspective a relatively complex constrained optimization problem is solved for which the optimum filter parameters are subject to decisions by the other cooperating or competing parties.

Subject to accurate definition of the constraints and pre‐determination of time–space parameters, such a filter is able to more accurately model the time‐varying interactions between two or more phenomena.

  

### 8.9.1 Use of Cooperative Kalman Filter

Most techniques in connectivity evaluation consider the signals to be stationary. They also consider the sources separately. Application of adaptive filtering in time and space in the so‐called diffusion adaptation approach tracks a time–space varying process which results in a particular function. This involves sources from a number of neurons which communicate to each other through space and evolve in time. An important initial conclusion from this approach is that the signals are considered stationary, but often the system can cope with nonstationary data.

In \[[7](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0007), [67](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0067)\] a diffusion Kalman filtering approach to cooperative multi‐agent sensor networking has been introduced. In most of these applications (excluding decentralized network) it is assumed that the correlation between estimates of two neighbouring agents is known to both agents. In addition, communication between the agents is required to be fast enough such that consensus can be reached between two consecutive Kalman filter updates. In [\[68\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0068) the filtering is based on covariance intersection (CI) method [\[69\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0069). This approach fuses multiple consistent estimates with unknown correlations with a convex combination of the estimates and chooses the corresponding combination weights by minimizing the trace or determinant of an upper bound of the error covariance matrix [\[68\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0068).

In diffusion Kalman filtering approach it is assumed that *N*[*k,i*] nodes spatially distributed over a region, centred (so‐called current node) at *k* at time *i*, communicate with each other (within limited range).

Being at state **x**[*i*] the measurement at node *k* and time *i* is denoted by **y**[*k*, *i*] , the corresponding state‐space model is of the form:

![equation](images/c8-disp-0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> (8.40)![equation](images/c8-disp-0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> 

where **w**[*i*] and **v**[*k*, *i*] are the state and measurement noises at time *i* and node *k* respectively. **F**[*i*] and **H**[*k*, *i*] are generally time‐varying (but bounded) matrices and the noises are zero‐mean, white and have [\[68\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0068):

(8.41)![equation](images/c8-disp-0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi></msub><mspace width="4em"/><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mspace width="2em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="2em"/><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>&#948;</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">kl</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="italic">&#948;ij</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

where *δ*[*ij*] is the Kronecker delta, *Q*[*i*] and *R*[*k,i*] are assumed to be positive definite and bounded.

The diffusion Kalman filtering approach in [\[67\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0067), schematically presented as in [Figure 8.4](#c08.xhtml#c8-fig-0004), aims at estimating stable state **x**[*i*] , while sharing data with its neighbours only. In this algorithm at every time instant *i*, node *k* transmits the quantities ![images](images/c8-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![images](images/c8-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> to its neighbours in updating each intermediate estimate *ψ*[*k*, *i*] . Information from the neighbouring nodes are combined using a *p* × *p* diffusion matrix *C*[*k*, *l*, *i*] subject to:

(8.42)![equation](images/c8-disp-0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></munder><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>for</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8713;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/></math> 

where **I**[*p*] is a *p* × *p* identity matrix. The combination coefficients *C*[*kl*] combine the information from the neighbouring nodes. Hence, their identification or estimation based on physical or physiological constraints, or an adaptive method such as [\[68\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0068), enhances the accuracy of overall diffusion filtering.

![Figure 8.4 Representation of node k and its neighbouring nodes for diffusion Kalman filtering algorithm.](images/c08f004.gif)

[**Figure 8.4**](#c08.xhtml#R_c8-fig-0004) Representation of node *k* and its neighbouring nodes for diffusion Kalman filtering algorithm.

As mentioned earlier connectivity estimation methods such as SEM or MVAR may be used to define the link weights. This is currently under research. CI estimation, conversely, assumes that node *k* is to fuse the estimates ![images](images/c8-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> using its neighbours and through the estimates of their error covariance matrices *P*[*l*, *i* ∣ *i* − 1] > 0. Based on the CI algorithm by Julier and Uhlman as reported in [\[68\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0068):

(8.43)![equation](images/c8-disp-0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/></math> 

where

(8.44)![equation](images/c8-disp-0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfrac linethickness="0pt"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> 

0 ≤ *β*[*k*, *l*, *i*]  ≤ 1 where ![images](images/c8-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> is computed such that the trace or determinant of Λ [*k,i*] is minimized. The above optimization is often nonlinear. Therefore, some CI algorithms such as one presented in [\[68\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0068) have been proposed to estimate these parameters.

 

### 8.9.2 Task‐Related Adaptive Connectivity

From the above connectivity estimation methods, it may be concluded that particular connectivity patterns are related to particular mental, cognitive, or movement activity. Such patterns are those which vary in both time and space (i.e. the engaged electrodes or actual brain source locations) and originate from distributed synaptic current sources. Modelling of such connectivity patterns can be of great importance in places where the neural activity corresponding to a movement or mental task such as in brain–computer interfacing (BCI), is to be learned.

Extension of adaptive filters, often used for single‐channel applications, to cooperative adaptive filters where the input is a combination of information received from its neighbours can be a solution to application of adaptive filters for multichannel (usually correlated) data. This approach has become popular in communication networks. Incremental, where the information is transferred sequentially from node to node, or consensus and diffusion where the input is an aggregate of the information received from the neighbouring nodes, have become popular solutions to cooperative networks. Diffusion adaptation filters are similar to conventional adaptive filters where the inputs are sum of the contributions (or cooperation) between the input nodes (sources). The cooperation pattern between the nodes, itself, varies in time.

As a motivation for this study, recently, a study of brain connectivity and measurement of fingertip movement between two participants, while recording their EEG simultaneously, has been carried out [\[44\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0044). In particular, the aim was evaluation of body movement synchrony during implicit social interactions between two or more participants, assessing the underlying dynamics and the effective connectivity between and within their brain, mainly cortical regions. Concurrent activity in multiple brains of a group of people may be estimated in order to indicate the causal connections between regions of different brains (hyper‐connectivity).

Among the three approaches in cooperative adaptive filtering, i.e. incremental, consensus, and diffusion, the latter is more general and guarantees stability of the networks. Diffusion adaptation can be a very good candidate to model the evolution of neuronal network connectivity during a task performance. This method is more attractive when one subject performs a task as a model target and others follow. Unlike the network of agents, where usually the combination weights are unknown and therefore the weights considered equal (traditionally as an average of the link weights within the immediate neighbourhood, in the case of brain application, the brain connectivity values can be used for this purpose. Therefore, at each stage of adaptation, the connectivity coefficients, such as DTF, can be used to adjust the instantaneous cooperation weights among the nodes E electrodes or brain sources). To understand the concept the method is briefly reviewed here.

 

### 8.9.3 Diffusion Adaptation

In diffusion adaptation, the main goal is to estimate an *M* × 1 unknown vector **w** from measurements collected at *N* nodes spread over a network. Each node *k* has access to time realizations {d [*k*] (*i*), u [*k,i*] } of the data {**d**[*k*] , **u**[*k*] } where **d**[*k*] is a vector of scalar measurements and **u**[*k*] is a 1 × *M* row regression vector [\[62\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0062). Considering these vectors from all the nodes, the data forms two global matrices **U** and **D** respectively. The objective is to estimate vector **w** that solves the minimization problem:

(8.45)![equation](images/c8-disp-0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mo>min</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></munder><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Uw</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

Assuming that by applying **w** the signal from node *k*, at time instance *i*, generates a signal ![images](images/c8-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>k</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></msubsup></math>. Each node combines the information from its neighbouring nodes to produce a new input to the filter as:

(8.46)![equation](images/c8-disp-0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>k</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>l</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></msubsup><mo>;</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *f*[*k*] is a combining function and *N*[*k*] is the number of nodes included in the neighbourhood of node *k* at time instance *i*. An option for selection of the above function is to consider it as a fixed linear averaging process. Another alternative is to consider it as a linear sum of weighted inputs from neighbouring nodes which can be adapted through time to minimize the global error [\[30\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0030). In both cases adaptation can be presented in the following set of alternating equations:

[(8.47a)](#c08.xhtml#R_c8-disp-0048)![equation](images/c8-disp-0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>k</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></msubsup><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></munder><msub><mi>C</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">kl</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>l</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></msubsup></math> [(8.47b)](#c08.xhtml#R_c8-disp-0049)![equation](images/c8-disp-0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>k</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>k</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>k</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></msubsup></math> 

In [Eq. (8.47a)](#c08.xhtml#c8-disp-0048) the new input to the model is estimated using received signals from the neighbouring nodes. In [(8.47b)](#c08.xhtml#c8-disp-0049) the output of the filter is updated for iteration/time sample *i*. By implementing the above equations using alternating adaptation we can track the signal component in both space, using *k* and time, using *i*. Alternatively, by replacing ![images](images/c8-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>k</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></msubsup></math> by *w*[*k*, *i*] Eq. (8.47) can also be written as:

(8.48a)![equation](images/c8-disp-0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>k</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> (8.48b)![equation](images/c8-disp-0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></munder><msub><mi>C</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">kl</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>&#968;</mi><mi>l</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></msubsup><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>where</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></munder><msub><mi>C</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">kl</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>  

### 8.9.4 Brain Connectivity for Cooperative Adaptation

In application of cooperative adaptive algorithms to EEG signals the block diagram in [Figure 8.5](#c08.xhtml#c8-fig-0005) can be followed.

Some examples of the above method have been reported for classification of EEG signals during clockwise and counter‐clockwise hand drawings \[[40](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0040), [41](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0041)\]. In [\[41\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0041) the authors examine the flow of information among electrodes attached to the brain and use diffusion adaptation strategies to assess the brain cortical connectivity. The method uses the DTF technique to estimate the combination coefficients to drive the adaptation and learning process. The diffusion strategy is then applied to the problem of recognizing left‐hand and right‐hand movements and its superior performance is demonstrated relative to solutions that rely on stand‐alone electrodes and do not exploit coordination among multiple electrodes. A connectivity pattern between the electrodes in the central region of the brain, as depicted in [Figure 8.6](#c08.xhtml#c8-fig-0006) has been used in the above approach. In [\[40\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0040) S‐coherency has been used instead of DTF and the diffusion adaptation algorithm has been designed to discriminate between clockwise and counter‐clockwise hand movements during drawing a circle.

![Figure 8.5 The use of brain connectivity for diffusion adaptation filtering.](images/c08f005.gif)

[**Figure 8.5**](#c08.xhtml#R_c8-fig-0005) The use of brain connectivity for diffusion adaptation filtering.

![Figure 8.6 An illustration of brain connectivity pattern. EEG signals collected at the marked electrodes are used to train a cooperative network to estimate a model for left‐hand and right‐hand movements.](images/c08f006.gif)

[**Figure 8.6**](#c08.xhtml#R_c8-fig-0006) An illustration of brain connectivity pattern. EEG signals collected at the marked electrodes are used to train a cooperative network to estimate a model for left‐hand and right‐hand movements.

In an application to detection of body (hand) tremor from the EEG signals, the time intervals with the onset of hand tremor have been detected [\[42\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0042). In this approach an adaptive multitask diffusion strategy has been introduced to estimate the underlying model between the gait information and the EEG signals. The method incorporates an S‐transform‐based connectivity measure that performs well even on a single‐trial basis. The estimated connectivity values are then combined with the combination weights of the multitask diffusion strategy to model the relation between tremor and the brain signals. The outcome is an enhanced brain connectivity measure representing its time–space relation to the tremor.

Using the S‐transform, a more robust estimation of brain connectivity can be achieved. [Figure 8.7](#c08.xhtml#c8-fig-0007) represents the variation of combination weights (brain connectivity parameters) measured by the S‐transform.

 

### 8.9.5 Other Applications of Cooperative Learning and Brain Connectivity Estimation

As explored in [Chapter 9](#c09.xhtml), related to brain event‐related potentials (ERPs), tracking of P300 waveforms and their subcomponents P3a and P3b in time can be more accurate when the cooperation between the channels is also taken into account [\[70\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0070). This exploits the spatial and temporal properties of the EEG waveforms in monitoring mental fatigue for healthy and dementia subjects more effectively. Hence, the symmetricity property of the brain left and right lobes in terms of generation of ERPs are used in the design of a collaborative adaptive particle filter. This system uses the link between C3, C4, P3, and P4 electrodes to better (compared to the non‐collaborative method [\[71\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0071) developed for mental fatigue) estimate and track the amplitude and latency of P3a and P3b waveforms.

![Figure 8.7 Variation of combination weights (brain connectivity parameters) measured by the S‐transform. This is to show that the relative changes in the weights remain fairly consistent over a short time duration.](images/c08f007.gif)

[**Figure 8.7**](#c08.xhtml#R_c8-fig-0007) Variation of combination weights (brain connectivity parameters) measured by the S‐transform. This is to show that the relative changes in the weights remain fairly consistent over a short time duration.

  

## 8.10 Graph Representation of Brain Connectivity

Graph theory studies the properties of mathematical structures, or graphs, designed to model the connections between a group of nodes which can be active sources. Graph theory was first applied by Leonhard Euler in 1736, who prefigured the idea of topology through the negative resolution for his famous Seven Bridges of Konigsberg problem. His assessment that there was no feasible way to walk through the city of Konigsberg by crossing each of the seven bridges only once, has helped him develop rigorous approaches to the field of graph theory (Euler 1741). Since then graph theory has been applied to many different areas including social sciences – used to understand the web of social relations, computer science, and currently, natural sciences with particular interest in the study of complex biological systems (Sporns 2011).

The theoretical network models have vastly contributed to the emerging field of brain connectomics, a field of analysis that combines some of the most advanced areas of study in medicine, neuroscience, and engineering to characterize and quantify the brain in terms of its structural and functional connections.

Topological changes in the brain's networks may be analyzed using graph theory, which represents the brain's connections as a set of nodes and edges.

A graph G consists of a set *N*[*G*] of *N* nodes, and a set ℑ of edges such that if nodes *m* and *n* are linked, then (*m, n*)∈ ℑ. For undirected graphs, these node pairs are unordered. At the node level, a recorded signal **y** = \[*y* [1], …,., *y*[*N*] \] ^(*T*) , assumed to be real valued, where *y*[*n*] is the sample of signal **y** at node *n*. Also, the adjacency matrix **A** \[[72](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0072), [73](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0073)\], is defined as an *N* × *N* matrix whose entries *a*[*n,m*] are zero if (*m,n*) ∉ ℑ and one otherwise. The adjacency matrix describes the interactions between entities and, by extension, can be considered as a tool for representing relationships between the data channels (vertices). In general, any one of the methods previously described in this chapter can be used to characterize or define a graph. For the particular case of brain connectivity estimation, the proposed method has the advantage of adaptability given the data are available [\[74\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0074). In this application, the graph topology is considered unknown beforehand and has been estimated from the data.

Moreover, some graphs can be dynamic, such as brain activity supported by neurons or brain regions. A network structure is then proposed to capture online the nonlinear dependencies among streaming graph signals in the form of a possibly directed, adjacency matrix. By projecting the data into a higher‐ or infinite‐dimension space, the nonlinear relationships between the electrode recordings (agents) are estimated. Kernel dictionaries are used to mitigate the increasing number of data points.

Consider that an *N*‐node graph with adjacency matrix **A**, as defined above, models a system such as the brain network. In this setting, the brain activity in each brain zone, ![images](images/c8-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="sans-serif-bold-italic">y</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="sans-serif-italic">i</mi></mfenced></math> can be measured at time instant *i*. For the case of brain connectivity, the existing nonlinearity in the connections motivates modelling the brain dynamics. Consider the following data model [\[74\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0074):

(8.49)![equation](images/c8-disp-0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></math> 

Matrix **A** models how entries of ![images](images/c8-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8796;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">col</mi><msubsup><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></msubsup></math>, where ![images](images/c8-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8476;</mi><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8476;</mi></math>, affect every node. ***v*** (*i*) accounts for additive noise. The least‐mean‐squares solution to this problem is:

(8.50)![equation](images/c8-disp-0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><munder><mtext>argmin</mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi></munder><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>E</mi><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi></mfenced><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>a</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">nm</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where Ψ(**A**) is a regularization term to account for some prior knowledge of **A** such as symmetry or sparsity. The solution to this nonlinear problem is hard to achieve in its general form. However, by selecting *f*[*m*] from the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) the graph parameters can be estimated as [\[74\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0074):

(8.51)![equation](images/c8-disp-0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#956;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover></mrow></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#951;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#915;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ![images](images/c8-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover></mrow></msub><mo>&#8776;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></math>, ![images](images/c8-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></math> is the selected RKHS nonlinearity function for ***f*** (*i*), and the entries of Γ [*n*] , i.e. Γ [*nm*] are:

(8.52)![equation](images/c8-disp-0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#915;</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">nm</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd><mfrac><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="italic">nm</mi></msub><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="italic">mn</mi></msub></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="italic">mn</mi></msub></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mspace width="1.5em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="italic">mn</mi></msub></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

In an example [\[74\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0074), seizure ECoG recordings from 76 cortical electrodes have been used. It has been found that the graph topology in terms both adjacency matrix and the connection weights differ for preictal and ictal periods.

 

## 8.11 Tensor Factorization Approach

Another interesting approach in analysis of connectivity is *link prediction*, which not only provides a measure of connectivity but also tracks the changes of the links between the nodes of a network. The problem of link prediction arises for groups of objects connected by multiple relation types. The solution should not only allow identification of the correlations (among the linked patterns) but also reveals the impact of various relations on prediction performance.

In [\[75\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0075) following the work in [\[76\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0076), it is assumed that the objects tend to form links with others having similar characteristics and related objects share the similar behaviour pattern. To formulate the link pattern prediction consider a set of *N* objects *X* = {*x* [1], *x* [2], …, *x*[*N*] } and assume there are *T* different types of relations among object pairs defined by a set of *T* trajectory matrices [\[75\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0075). An *N* × *N* × *T* tensor **Y** is then defined with entry *y*[*i*, *j*, *t*] representing the type *t* relation value between object pair *x*[*i*] and *x*[*j*] as [\[75\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0075):

For ∀*i,j* ∈ \[1,… *N*\]² and ∀*t* ∈ \[1, …, *T*\]

(8.53)![equation](images/c8-disp-0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>1</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>links to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi>by</mi><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>relation type</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi>t</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>otherwise</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

Based on this **Y** [(*i,j*,:)] is defined as the *link pattern* involving *T* different types of relations between each pair of objects *x*[*i*] and *x*[*j*] . The problem to solve here is: given some observed link patterns information for a subset of related objects in the multi‐relational network, how the unobserved link patterns for the remaining object pairs can be found? In [Figure 8.8](#c08.xhtml#c8-fig-0008) an example of the problem and its tensor model [\[77\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0077).

To mathematically express the problem consider a nonnegative *N* × *N* matrix **W** such that its entries *w*[*i,j*] for ∀*i,j*∈\[1,…, *N*\]² are defined as [\[75\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0075):

[(8.54)](#c08.xhtml#R_c8-disp-0057)![equation](images/c8-disp-0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>1</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if link pattern between</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>is known</mtext></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if link pattern between</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>is missing</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

For the decomposition the following loss function is defined:

[(8.55)](#c08.xhtml#R_c8-disp-0058)![equation](images/c8-disp-0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>L</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>:</mo></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>:</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mspace width="0.2em"/></math> ![Figure 8.8 Example of modelling the multirelational social network as a tensor for predicting the unobserved link patterns in the network. To the right is the tensor representation of the network where each slice matrix represents one relation type and each tube fibre represents the link pattern between two nodes. Unknown link patterns are represented as ‘?’ fibres.](images/c08f008.gif)

[**Figure 8.8**](#c08.xhtml#R_c8-fig-0008) Example of modelling the multirelational social network as a tensor for predicting the unobserved link patterns in the network. To the right is the tensor representation of the network where each slice matrix represents one relation type and each tube fibre represents the link pattern between two nodes. Unknown link patterns are represented as ‘?’ fibres.

where ||. || denotes Frobenius norm for a tensor. Following Canonical decomposition (CANDECOMP)/PARAFAC (CP) tensor decomposition and [(8.55)](#c08.xhtml#c8-disp-0058) we can solve the following optimization problem [\[75\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0075) using the conjugate gradient approach:

(8.56)![equation](images/c8-disp-0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo mathvariant="italic">arg</mo><munder><mo mathvariant="italic">min</mo><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder></munder><mi>L</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder></mfenced><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover><msub><mi>u</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> 

where *K* is rank of the tensor, and **U**, **V**, and **R** are the latent factor matrices for CP tensor decomposition. A popular approach to solve the problem is by alternating least‐squares (ALS) as in [\[75\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0075). This however requires estimation of a large number of parameters and consequently, needs high cost of computation and may result in over‐fitting. To overcome these problems the above constrained problem can be changed to an unconstrained problem using regularization parameters (penalty functions), which leads to the following cost function:

(8.57)![equation](images/c8-disp-0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo mathvariant="italic">arg</mo><munder><mo>min</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></munder><mi>L</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mfenced></math> 

where γ[0] and γ[T] are the regularization parameters. The above approach has a high potential in brain connectivity estimation and estimating the unknown links between different brain regions.

In the linked multiway blind source separation (BSS), an approximate decomposition of a set of data tensors ![images](images/c8-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mtext>\_</mtext></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>s</mi></mfenced></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow></msup></math> (*s* = 1, 2, …, *S*) representing multiple subjects and/or multiple tasks (see [Figure 8.9](#c08.xhtml#c8-fig-0009)) is performed. The objective is to find a set of constrained factor matrices ![images](images/c8-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mfenced></msup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>C</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>I</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mfenced></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="fraktur">R</mi><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msup></math>, *n* = 1, 2, 3) and core tensors ![images](images/c8-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">G</mi><mtext>\_</mtext></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>s</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="fraktur">R</mi><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>J</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>J</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></msup></math>, which are partially linked or maximally correlated, i.e. they have the same common components or highly correlated components. In the case of EEG signals a 4‐dimensional tensor ![images](images/c8-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><munder accentunder="false"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow><mtext>\_</mtext></munder></math> can be defined in terms of its three‐dimensional components as:

(8.58)![equation](images/c8-disp-0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>s</mi></mfenced></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">G</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>s</mi></mfenced></msup><msub><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mfenced></msup><mo>.</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><msub><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>N</mi></msub><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mfenced></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">E</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>s</mi></mfenced></msup></math> 

where × [*k*] denotes tensor multiplication along slab (dimension) *k*. Each factor **U** ^((*n*, *s*)) consists of two parts: one, ![images](images/c8-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>C</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mfenced></msubsup></math>, which are common bases for all subjects in the group and correspond to the same or maximally correlated components and another one, ![images](images/c8-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>I</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mfenced></msubsup></math>, which corresponds to stimuli/tasks independent individual characteristics. ![images](images/c8-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><munder accentunder="false"><mrow><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow><mtext>\_</mtext></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>s</mi></mfenced></msup></math> represents space (channel)–time–frequency data for the *s*th subject.

The factors are usually estimated using an alternating optimization method which minimizes the distance between the terms in the left and right of [Eq. (8.54)](#c08.xhtml#c8-disp-0057). In order to achieve unique solutions for all the factors some constraints are required. For the EEG signals such constraints can be the approximate source locations, sparsity in space or frequency domain, or a known structure of the core matrix, e.g. for independent factors the core matrix is diagonal.

![Figure 8.9 Conceptual model of tensors decomposition for linked multiway BSS. The objective is to find a set of constrained factor matrices images, n = 1, 2, 3) and core tensors images, which are partially linked or maximally correlated, i.e. they have the same common components or highly correlated components \[77\].](images/c08f009.gif)

## 8.12 Summary

Estimation of the connectivity of the brain regions using EEG or MEG signals has its root in the works carried out approximately three decades ago. Although various methods such as MVAR and DTF, SEM, PDC, and dDTF have been popular for connectivity estimation, the new approaches such as by using the S‐transform, diffusion adaptation, tensor factorization, and graph‐based signal processing have opened new fronts in both modelling and estimation of the connectivity. Application of these recent methods to EEG signals is in its early stages and therefore, more research needs to be carried out to enable robust procedures for EEG or MEG connectivity measures. A major problem with most of these methods is that all the sources are considered cortical and thus, no attempt has been made to check the connectivity for deep sources. This requires localization of multiple deep sources which is another challenging problem. In a work by Thatcher et al. [\[78\]](#c08.xhtml#c8-bib-0078) low‐resolution electromagnetic tomography algorithm (LORETA) source localization algorithm has been applied to determine the existing current sources within a large number of ROIs in the brain. Temporal and spatial correlations are later computed as the measure of connectivity. It also makes sense to restore the signals from noise and irrelevant information before estimation of connectivity and better deal with non‐cortical sources. Certainly, the correlated sources cannot be separated using conventional BSS approaches. Moreover, application of connectivity estimation is not only useful for neurological diseases such as dementia, AD, and mild cognitive impairment (MCI), but also can assist in tracking the movement‐related potentials within the brain. These concepts are discussed in future chapters of this book.
