# 9  
Event‐Related Brain Responses

 

## 9.1 Introduction

The brain responses to sensory stimuli can be noninvasively recorded and clearly seen using averaging techniques first employed by Dawson in 1947 [\[1\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0001). Peak amplitudes and latencies (in ms) are usually measured to quantify the evoked responses. These data provide quantitative extensions to the neurological examination. The clinical utility of evoked potentials (EPs) is based on their ability to: (i) demonstrate abnormal sensory system conduction, when the history and/or neurological examination is equivocal, (ii) reveal subclinical involvement of a sensory system (‘silent’ lesions), particularly when demyelination is suggested by symptoms and/or signs in another area of the central nervous system (CNS), (iii) help define the anatomic distribution and give some insight into the pathophysiology of a disease process, and (d) monitor the changes in a patient's neurological status [\[2\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0002). Longer latency responses that are related to higher ‘cognitive’ functions such as event‐related potentials (ERPs) which are a more general type of EPs. ERP is a measure of brain response that is the direct result of a specific sensory, cognitive, or motor event, or any stereotyped electrophysiological response to a stimulus. ERPs were first explained in 1964 \[[3](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0003), [4](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0004)\] and have remained as a useful diagnostic indicator in many applications in psychiatry and neurology as well as for brain–computer interfacing (BCI).

 

## 9.2 ERP Generation and Types

The brain generates different types of signals: (i) normal brain rhythms which constantly represent the state of the brain, (ii) ERPs, which are the brain responses to auditory, visual, or tactile stimulation, and (iii) movement‐related potentials (MRPs) which appear due to intentional physical or imagery movements.

An ERP consists of a sequence of labelled positive and negative amplitude components. These components reflect various sensory, cognitive (e.g. stimulus evaluation) and motor processes that are classified on the basis of their scalp distribution and response to experimental stimulus. Therefore, ERPs (which can be detected from EEG or magnetoencephalogram (MEG) signals) directly measure the electrical response of the cortex to sensory, affective, or cognitive events. They are voltage fluctuations in the EEG induced within the brain, as a sum of a large number of action potentials (APs) that are time locked to sensory, motor, or cognitive events. They are typically generated in response to peripheral or external stimulations, and appear as somatosensory, visual, and auditory brain potentials, or as slowly evolving brain activity observed before voluntary movements or during anticipation of conditional stimulation.

Compared with the background EEG activity ERPs are quite small (1–30 μV). Therefore, traditionally they often need the use of a signal‐averaging procedure for their elucidation. In addition, although evaluation of the ERP peaks may not be considered as a reliable diagnostic procedure, the application of ERP in psychiatry has been very common and widely followed.

An ERP waveform can be quantitatively characterized across three main dimensions, amplitude, latency, and scalp distribution [\[5\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0005). In addition, an ERP signal may also be analyzed with respect to the relative latencies between its subcomponents. The amplitude provides an index of the extent of neural activity (and how it responds functionally to experimental variables), the latency (i.e. the time point at which peak amplitude occurs) reveals the timing of this activation, and the scalp distribution provides the pattern of the voltage gradient of a component over the scalp at any time instant.

ERP signals are either positive, represented by letter P, such as P300, or negative, represented by letter N, such as N100 and N400. The digits indicate the time in terms of milliseconds after the stimuli (audio, visual, or somatosensory). The amplitude and latency of the components occurring within 100 ms after stimulus onset are labelled oxogenous, and are influenced by physical attributes of stimuli such as intensity, modality, and presentation rate. Conversely, endogenous components such as P300 are nonobligatory responses to stimuli, and vary in amplitude, latency, and scalp distribution with strategies, expectancies, and other mental activities triggered by the event eliciting the ERP. These components are not influenced by the physical attributes of the stimuli.

Analysis of ERPs, such as visual evoked potentials (VEP), within the EEG signals is important in the clinical diagnosis of many psychiatric diseases such as dementia. Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most common cause of dementia, which is a degenerative disease of the cerebral cortex and subcortical structures. The relative severity of the pathological changes in the associated cortex accounts for the clinical finding of diminished visual interpretation skills with normal visual acuity. Impairment of visuo‐cognitive skills often happens with this disease. This means that the patient may have difficulties with many complex visual tasks, such as tracing a target figure embedded in a more complex figure or identifying single letters that are presented briefly and followed by a pattern making stimulus. A specific indicator of dementia is the information obtained by using VEP. Several studies have confirmed that flash VEPs are abnormal while pattern VEPs are normal in patients with AD.

The most consistent abnormality in the flash VEP is the increase in the latency of the P100 component and an increase in its amplitude \[[6](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0006), [7](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0007)\]. Other ERP components such as N130, P165, N220, also have longer latencies in patients with AD \[[8](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0008), [9](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0009)\]. [Figure 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0001) illustrates the shape of two normal and two abnormal P100 components. It is seen that the peak of the normal P100s (normally shown in reversed polarity) has a latency of approximately 106 ms whereas, the abnormal P100 peak has a latency of approximately 135 ms and has lower amplitude.

![Figure 9.1 Four P100 components: (a) two normal P100 and (b) two abnormal P100 components. In (a) the P100 peak latency is at approximately 106 ms, whereas in (b) the P100 peak latency is at approximately 135 ms (waves are shown in reverse polarity).](images/c09f001.gif)

[**Figure 9.1**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0001) Four P100 components: (a) two normal P100 and (b) two abnormal P100 components. In (a) the P100 peak latency is at approximately 106 ms, whereas in (b) the P100 peak latency is at approximately 135 ms (waves are shown in reverse polarity).

Although determination of the locations of ERP sources within the brain is a difficult task the scalp distribution of an ERP component can often provide very useful and complementary information to that derived from amplitude and latency. Generally, two types of topographic maps can be generated: raw voltage (or surface potentials) and current source density (CSD), both derived from the electrode potentials.

The scalp‐recorded ERP voltage activity reflects the summation of both cortical and subcortical neural activity within each time window. Conversely, CSD maps reflect primary cortical surface activity \[[10](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0010), [11](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0011)\]. CSD is obtained by spatially filtering the subcortical areas as well as cortical areas distal to the recording electrodes to remove the volume‐conducted activity. CSD maps are useful for forming hypotheses about neural sources within the superficial cortex [\[12\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0012).

The functional MRI (fMRI) technique has become another alternative to investigate brain ERPs since it can detect the haemodynamics of the brain. However, there are at least three shortcomings with this brain imaging modality: firstly, the temporal resolution is low, secondly, the activated areas based on hemodynamic techniques do not necessarily correspond to the neural activity identified by ERP measures, and thirdly, the fMRI is not sensitive to the type of stimulus (e.g. target, standard, or novel). It is considered that the state of the subject changes due to differences in the density of different stimulus types across blocks of trials. By target P300, we refer to the P300 component elicited by events about which the subject has been instructed and to which the subject is required to generate some kinds of response. A novel stimulus indicates a sole or irregular stimulus.

The ERP parameters such as amplitude and latency are the indicators of the function of the brain neurochemical systems and can potentially be used as predictors of the response of an individual to psychopharmacotherapy [\[13\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0013). ERPs are also related to the circumscribed cognitive process. For example, there are interesting correlations between late evoked positivities and memory, N400 and semantic processes, or the latencies of ERPs and the timing of cognitive processes. Therefore, the ERP parameters can be used as indicators of cognitive processes and dysfunctions not accessible to behavioural testing. As an example, [Figure 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0002) shows how the average (over N = 100 subjects) P300 differs for normal and alcoholic subjects.

![Figure 9.2 The average ERP signals for normal and alcoholic subjects. The curves show reduced P300 amplitude in alcoholics \[14\].](images/c09f002.gif)

[**Figure 9.2**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0002) The average ERP signals for normal and alcoholic subjects. The curves show reduced P300 amplitude in alcoholics [\[14\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0014).

The fine‐grained temporal resolution of ERPs has been traditionally limited. In addition, overlapping components within ERPs, which represent specific stages of information processing, are difficult to distinguish \[[15](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0015), [16](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0016)\]. An example is the composite P300 wave, a positive ERP component, which occurs with a latency of about 300 ms after novel stimuli, or task relevant stimuli, which require an effortful response on the part of the individual under test \[[15](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0015)–[19](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0019)\].

The elicited ERPs are comprised of two main components: the mismatch negativity (MMN) and the novelty P300. By novelty P300, we refer to the P300 component elicited by events about which the subject has not been instructed prior to the experiment. The auditory MMN was discovered in 1978 by Näätänen, Gaillard, and Mäntysalo at the Institute for Perception, TNO in The Netherlands [\[20\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0020). The MMN is the earliest ERP activity (which occurs within the first 10 ms after the stimulus) indicating that the brain has detected a change in a background of brain homogeneous events. The MMN is thought to be generated in and around the primary auditory cortex [\[21\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0021). The amplitude of the MMN is directly proportional, and its latency inversely related, to the degree of difference between standard and deviant stimuli. It is most clearly seen by subtraction of the ERP elicited by the standard stimulus from that elicited by the deviant stimulus during a passive odd‐ball paradigm (OP) when both of those stimuli are unattended or ignored. Therefore, it is relatively automatic.

The applications of ERP abnormality analysis in clinical research are not limited to those above and have been shown in many other neurological conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) \[[22](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0022), [23](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0023)\], dementia [\[24\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0024), Parkinson's disease (PD) [\[25\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0025), multiple sclerosis [\[26\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0026), head injuries [\[27\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0027), stroke [\[28\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0028), and obsessive–compulsive disorder [\[29\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0029).

  

### 9.2.1 P300 and its Subcomponents

The P300 wave represents cognitive functions involved in orientation of attention, contextual updating, response modulation, and response resolution \[[15](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0015), [17](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0017)\] and consists mainly of two overlapping subcomponents P3a and P3b \[[16](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0016), [19](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0019), [30](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0030)\]. P3a reflects an automatic orientation of attention to novel or salient stimuli independent of task relevance. Prefrontal, frontal, and anterior temporal brain regions play the main role in generating P3a giving it a frontocentral distribution [\[19\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0019). In contrast, P3b has a greater centro‐parietal distribution due to its reliance on posterior temporal, parietal and posterior cingulate cortex mechanisms \[[15](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0015), [16](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0016)\]. P3a is also characterized by a shorter latency and more rapid habituation than P3b [\[30\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0030).

A neural event is the frontal aspect of the novelty P300, i.e. P3a. For example, if the event is sufficiently deviant, the MMN is followed by the P3a. The eliciting events in this case are highly deviant environmental sounds such as a dog barking. Non‐identifiable sounds elicit larger P3a than identifiable sounds. Accordingly, a bigger MMN results in a dominant P3a. [Figure 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0003) shows typical P3a and P3b subcomponents.

P3b is also elicited by infrequent events but unlike P3a, it is task relevant, or involves a decision to evoke this component.

The ERPs are the responses to different stimuli, i.e. novel or salient. It is important to distinguish between the ERPs when they are the response to novel or salient (i.e. what has already been experienced) stimuli, or when the degree of novelty changes.

The orienting response engendered by deviant or unexpected events consists of a characteristic ERP pattern, which is comprised sequentially of the MMN and the novelty P300 or P3a. Each of P3a and P3b has different cognitive or possibly neurological base.

The orienting response \[[32](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0032), [33](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0033)\] is an involuntary shift of attention that appears to be a fundamental biological mechanism for survival. It is a rapid response to a new, unexpected, or unpredictable stimulus, which essentially functions as a what‐is‐it detector [\[34\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0034). The plasticity of the orienting response has been demonstrated by showing that stimuli, which initially evoked the response no longer did so with repeated presentation [\[33\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0033). Habituation of the response is proposed to indicate that some type of memory for these prior events has been formed, which modifies the response to the repeated incidences.

![Figure 9.3 Typical P3a and P3b subcomponents of a P300 ERP signal viewed at Fz, Cz, and Pz electrodes \[31\].](images/c09f003.gif)

[**Figure 9.3**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0003) Typical P3a and P3b subcomponents of a P300 ERP signal viewed at Fz, Cz, and Pz electrodes [\[31\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0031).

Abnormalities in P300 are found in several psychiatric and neurological conditions [\[18\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0018). However, the impact of the diseases on P3a and P3b may be different. Both audio and visual P300 (i.e. a P300 signal produced earlier due to an audio or a visual stimulation) are used. Audio and visual P300 appear to be differently affected by illnesses and respond differently to their treatment. This suggests differences in the underlying structures and neurotransmitter systems [\[16\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0016). P300 has significant diagnostic and prognostic potential especially when combined with other clinical symptoms and evidences.

In many applications such as human‐computer interaction (HCI), muscular fatigue, visual fatigue, and mental fatigue are induced as a result of physical and mental activities. In order for the ERP signals and their subcomponents to be reliably used for clinical diagnosis, assessment of mental activities, fatigue during physical and mental activities, and for human‐computer interfacing, very effective and reliable methods for their detection and parameter estimation have to be developed. In the following section a number of established methods for detection of ERP signals, especially P300 and its subcomponents, P3a and P3b, are described in sufficient detail.

 

## 9.3 Detection, Separation, and Classification of P300 Signals

Although in many applications, such as assessment of memory, a number of ERPs are involved, detection and tracking of P300 and its subcomponents' variability have been under more intensive research. Traditionally, EPs are synchronously averaged to enhance the evoked signal and suppress the background brain activity [\[35\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0035).

Step‐wise discriminant analysis (SWDA) followed by peak picking and evaluation of the covariance, was first introduced by Farwell and Dounchin [\[36\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0036). Later, the discrete wavelet transform (DWT) was also added to the SWDA to better localize the ERP components in both time and frequency [\[37\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0037).

Principal component analysis (PCA) has been employed to assess temporally overlapping EP components [\[38\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0038). However, the resultant orthogonal representation does not necessarily coincide with the true component structure since the actual physiological components need not be orthogonal, i.e. the source signals may be correlated.

Independent component analysis (ICA) has been applied to ERP analysis by many researchers including Makeig et al. [\[39\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0039). Infomax ICA [\[40\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0040) was used by Xu et al. [\[41\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0041) to detect the ERPs for the P300‐based speller. In their approach those independent components (ICs) with relatively larger amplitudes in the latency range of P300 were kept, while the others were set to zero. Also, they exploited a priori knowledge about the spatial information of the ERPs and decided whether a component should be retained or wiped out. To manipulate the spatial information denote the *i*th row and *j*th column element in the inverse of the unmixing matrix, **W** ^(−1), by ![images](images/c9-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></math>, therefore, **x**(*n*) = **W** ^(−1)**u**(*n*). Then, denote the *j*th column of **W** ^(−1) by ![images](images/c9-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></math>, which reflects the intensity distribution at each electrode for the *j*th IC *u*[*j*] [\[39\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0039). Then, for convenience the spatial pattern **W** ^(−1) is transformed into an intensity order matrix **M** = {*m*[*ij*] } with the same dimension. The value of the element *m*[*ij*] in **M** is set to be the order number of the value ![images](images/c9-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></math> in the column vector ![images](images/c9-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></math>. For example *m*[*ij*] = 1 if ![images](images/c9-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ij</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msubsup></math> has the largest value, *m*[*ij*] = 2, if it has the second largest value, and so on. Based on the spatial distribution of the brain activities, an electrode set **Q** = {*q*[*k*] } of interest is selected in which *q*[*k*] is the electrode number and is equal to the row index of the multichannel EEG matrix **x**(*n*). For extraction of the P300 signals these electrodes are located around the vertex region (C[z], C[1], and C[2]) since they are considered to have prominent P300. The spatial filtering of the ICs is simply performed as:

(9.1)![equation](images/c9-disp-0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mspace width="0em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width=".2em"/><mo>&#8707;</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mspace width="1.9em"/><mtext>else</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

where *T*[*r*] is the threshold for the order numbers. *T*[*r*] is introduced to retain the most prominent spatial information about the P300 signal. Therefore, ![images](images/c9-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> holds most of the source information about P300 while other irrelevant parts are set to zero. Finally, after the temporal and spatial manipulation of the ICs, the ![images](images/c9-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>j</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> s, *j* = 1, 2, …, *M*, where *M* is the number of ICs, are back projected to the electrodes by using **W** ^(−1) to obtain the scalp distribution of the P300 potential, i.e.:

(9.2)![equation](images/c9-disp-0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where ![images](images/c9-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#732;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> is the P300 enhanced EEG. The ![images](images/c9-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#732;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced></math> features can then be measured for classification purposes [\[41\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0041).

 

### 9.3.1 Using ICA

Assuming ERP as an IC from other brain generated and artefact signals, ICA has been used by many researchers for detection and analysis of the ERP components from EEG, electromyogram (EMG) and fMRI (in the form of blood oxygen level dependence \[BOLD\]) data [\[42\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0042). Four main assumptions underlie ICA decomposition of EEG or MEG time series: (i) signal conduction times are equal and summation of currents at the scalp sensors is linear, both are reasonable assumptions for currents carried to the scalp electrodes by volume conduction for EEG or for superposition of magnetic fields at SQUID sensors; (ii) spatial projections of components are fixed across time and conditions; (iii) source activations are temporally independent of one another across the input data; and (iv) statistical distributions of the component activation values are not Gaussian [\[42\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0042).

After application of ICA to the signals, the brain activities of interest accounted for by single or by multiple components can be obtained by projecting the selected ICA component(s) back onto the scalp, ![images](images/c9-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></msup></math> where **W** is the estimated separating matrix using ICA and **Y** ^((*i*)) is the matrix of estimated/separated sources when all except source **y**[*i*] have been set to zero. As the main conclusions here, ICA can separate stimulus‐locked, response‐locked, and non‐event‐related background EEG activities into separate components, allowing: (i) removal of pervasive artefacts of all types from single‐trial EEG records, making possible analysis of highly contaminated EEG records from clinical populations; (ii) identification and segregation of stimulus‐ and response‐locked event‐related activity in single‐trail EEG epochs; (iii) separation of spatially overlapping EEG activities over the entire scalp and frequency band that may show a variety of distinct relationships to task events, rather than focusing on activity at single frequencies in single scalp channels or channel pairs; and (iv) investigation of the interaction between ERPs and ongoing EEG [\[42\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0042).

![Figure 9.4 Block diagram of the ICA‐based algorithm proposed in \[43\]. Three recorded data channels Cz, Pz, and Fz are the inputs to the ICA algorithm.](images/c09f004.gif)

[**Figure 9.4**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0004) Block diagram of the ICA‐based algorithm proposed in [\[43\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0043). Three recorded data channels C[z], P[z], and F[z] are the inputs to the ICA algorithm.

The work in [\[43\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0043) involved application of a matched filter together with averaging and applying a threshold for detecting the existence of the P300 signals. The block diagram in [Figure 9.4](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0004) shows the method.

The IC corresponding to the P300 source is selected and segmented to form overlapping segments from 100 to 600 ms. Each segment is passed through a matched filter to give one feature that represents the maximum correlation between the segment and the average P300 template. However, a very obvious problem with this method is that the ICA system is very likely to be underdetermined (i.e. the number of sources is more than the number of sensors or observations) since only three mixtures are used. In this case the independent source signals are not separable.

Although ICA appears to be generally useful for EEG and fMRI analysis, it has some inherent limitations. First, ICA, in its general form, decomposes at most *N* sources from data collected at *N* scalp electrodes. Usually, the effective number of statistically independent source signals contributing to the scalp EEG is unknown and it is likely that the observed brain activity arises from more physically separable effective sources than the available number of EEG electrodes [\[42\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0042).

Second, ICA fails to separate correlated sources of ERP signals. The assumption of temporal independence used by ICA may not be satisfied when the training data set is small, or when separate topographically distinguishable phenomena nearly always co‐occur in the data. In the latter case, simulations show that ICA may derive single components accounting for the co‐occurring phenomena, along with additional components accounting for their brief periods of separate activation [\[42\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0042).

Third, ICA assumes that physical sources of artefacts and cerebral activity are spatially fixed over time. In general, this is not always true. Applying ICA to brain data shows the effectiveness of the independence assumption. ERP is generally the largest components (after eye‐blink artefact,) within the scalp map emitted from one or two dipoles. This is unlikely to occur unless time courses of coherently synchronous neural activity in patches of cortical neurons generating the EEG are nearly independent of one another [\[44\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0044).

Fourth, application of ICA to fMRI does not necessarily provide the full information about the actual components of the fMRI sequences. However, by placing ICA in a regression framework, it is possible to combine some of the benefits of ICA with the hypothesis‐testing approach of the general linear model (GLM) [\[45\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0045).

Current research on ICA algorithms has been focused on incorporating domain‐specific constraints into the ICA framework. This would allow information maximization to be applied to the precise form and statistics of biomedical data [\[42\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0042).

 

### 9.3.2 Estimation of Single‐Trial Brain Responses by Modelling the ERP Waveforms

Detection or estimation of EPs from only a single‐trial EEG is favourable since (i) online processing of the signals can be performed and (ii) variability of ERP parameters across trials can be tracked. Unlike the averaging (multiple trial) [\[46\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0046) scheme, in this approach the shape of the ERPs is first approximated and then used to recover the actual signals. A few good examples, including mental fatigue, are investigated in [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml) in which trial‐to‐trial variability of ERPs is of clinical importance.

A decomposition technique, which relies on the statistical nature of neural activity, is the one that efficiently separates the EEGs into their constituent components including the ERPs. A neural activity may be delayed when passing through a number of synaptic nodes each introducing a delay. Thus, the firing instants of many synchronized neurons may be assumed to be governed by Gaussian probability distributions. In a work by Lange et al. [\[35\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0035) the EP source waveform is assumed to consist of superposition of *p* components *u*[*i*] delayed by *τ*[*i*] :

Assuming that the background EEG is statistically stationary, **W**(z) is identified from the pre‐stimulus data via auto‐regressive (AR) modelling of the pre‐stimulus interval and used for post‐stimulus analysis [\[35\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0035). Therefore, the only parameters to be identified are the matrices **B**[*i*] (z). This avoids any iterative identification of the model parameters. (9.11)![equation](images/c9-disp-0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#958;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#949;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

is minimized. Then, the optimal vector of parameters in the LS sense is obtained as:

(9.12)![equation](images/c9-disp-0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover></math> 

The model provides an easier way of analyzing the ERP components from single‐trial EEG signals and facilitates tracking of amplitude and latency shifts of such components. The experimental results show that the main ERP components can be extracted with a high accuracy. The template signals may look like those in [Figure 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0005).

A similar method has also been developed to detect and track the P300 subcomponents, P3a and P3b, of the ERP signals [\[47\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0047). This is described in the following section.

 

### 9.3.3 ERP Source Tracking in Time

The major drawback of blind source separation (BSS) and dipole methods is that the number of sources needs to be known a priori to achieve good results. In a recent work [\[47\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0047) P300 signals are modelled as spike‐shaped Gaussian signals. The latencies and variances of these signals are however subject to change. The spikes serve as reference signals onto which the EEG data are projected. The existing spatiotemporal information is then used to find the closest representation of the reference in the data. The locations of all the extracted components within the brain are later computed using the LS method. Consider the *n*[*e*] × *T* EEG signals **X**, where *n*[*e*] is the number of channels (electrodes) and *T* the number of time samples, then:

![Figure 9.5 Synthetic ERP templates including a number of delayed Gaussian and exponential waveforms.](images/c09f005.gif)

[**Figure 9.5**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0005) Synthetic ERP templates including a number of delayed Gaussian and exponential waveforms.

(9.13)![equation](images/c9-disp-0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Hs</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>m</mi></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where **H** is the *n*[*e*] × *m* forward mixing matrix and *s*[*i*] (*n*) are the source signals. Initially, the sources are all considered as the ERP components that are directly relevant and time locked to the stimulus and assumed to have transient spiky shape. *m* filters {**w**[*i*] } are then needed (although the number of sources are not known beforehand) to satisfy:

(9.14)![equation](images/c9-disp-0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

This can be achieved by the following minimization criterion:

(9.15)![equation](images/c9-disp-0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">opt</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">arg</mo><munder><mo>min</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></munder><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> 

where **X** = \[**x** [1], **x** [2], ⋯, **x**[*ne*] \] ^(*T*) , which however requires some knowledge about the shape of the sources. A Gaussian type spike defined as:

(9.16)![equation](images/c9-disp-0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#964;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mfrac></mrow></msup></math> 

where *τ*[*i*] , *i =* 1,2, … *T,* is the latency of the *i*th source and *σ*[*i*] is its width, can be used as the model. The width is chosen as an approximation to the average width of the P3a and P3b subcomponents. Then, for each of the *T* filters (*T* >> *m*) we have:

(9.17)![equation](images/c9-disp-0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mtext mathvariant="italic">lOpt</mtext><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">arg</mo><munder><mo>min</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></munder><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></math> ![Figure 9.6 The results of the ERP detection algorithm \[47\]. The scatter plot shows the peaks at different latencies. The concentration of samples around the peaks make the ERP classification straightforward.](images/c09f006.gif)

[**Figure 9.6**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0006) The results of the ERP detection algorithm [\[47\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0047). The scatter plot shows the peaks at different latencies. The concentration of samples around the peaks make the ERP classification straightforward.

Therefore, each **y**[*l*] has a similar latency to that of a source. [Figure 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0006) shows the results of the ERP detection algorithm. It can be seen that all possible peaks are detected first. However, because the number of ERP signals is limited the outputs may be grouped into *m* clusters. To perform such classification we examine the following criteria for the latencies of the *i*th and (*i* − 1)th estimated ERP components according to the following rule:

for *i* = 1 to *T*:

*   if *l*(*i*) – *l*(*i* − 1) < β, where β is a small empirical threshold, then **y**[*i*] and **y**[*i* − 1] are assumed to belong to the same cluster,
*   if *l*(*i*) – *l*(*i* − 1) > β then **y**[*i*] and **y**[*i* − 1] belong to different clusters.

Here *l*(*i*) denotes the latency of the *i*th component. The signals within each cluster are then averaged to obtain the related ERP signal, **y**[*c*] . *c* = 1, 2,…, *m*. [Figure 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0007) presents the results after applying the above method to detect the subcomponents of a P300 signal from a single‐trial EEG for a healthy individual (control) and a schizophrenic patient. From these results it can be seen that the mean latency of P3a for the patient is less than that of the control. The difference however is less for P3b. Conversely, the mean width of P3a is less for the control (healthy subject) than for the patient whereas the mean width of the P3b is more for the patient than for the control. This demonstrates the effectiveness of the technique in classification of the healthy and schizophrenic individuals.

 

### 9.3.4 Time–Frequency Domain Analysis

In places where some signal components are transient, i.e. a signal contains frequency components emerging and vanishing in time‐limited intervals, localization of the active signal components within the time–frequency (TF) domain is very useful [\[48\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0048). The traditional method proposed for such an analysis is application of the short time–frequency transform (STFT) [\[49\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0049). The STFT enables the time localization of a certain sinusoidal frequency but with an inherent limitation due to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle which states that resolution in time and frequency cannot be both arbitrary small, because their product is lower bounded by Δ*t*Δ*ω* ≥ 1/2. Therefore, the wavelet transform (WT) has become very popular instead. An advantage of the WT over the STFT is that for the STFT the phase space is uniformly sampled, whereas in the WT the sampling in frequency is logarithmic which enables one to analyze higher frequencies in shorter windows and lower frequencies in longer windows in time [\[50\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0050).

![Figure 9.7 The average P3a and P3b for a schizophrenic patient (a) and (b) respectively, and for a healthy individual (c) and (d) respectively.](images/c09f007.gif)

[**Figure 9.7**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0007) The average P3a and P3b for a schizophrenic patient (a) and (b) respectively, and for a healthy individual (c) and (d) respectively.

As explained in [Chapter 4](#c04.xhtml) of this book a multi‐resolution decomposition of signal *x*(*n*) over *I* octaves is given as:

(9.18)![equation](images/c9-disp-0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#8734;</mo></munderover><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></munder><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>Z</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ![images](images/c9-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#175;</mo></mover></math> refers to integer values. The DWT computes the wavelet coefficients *a*[*i,k*] for *i =* 1,…, *I* and the scaling coefficients *b*[*i*, *k*] given by:

(9.19)![equation](images/c9-disp-0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>DWT</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><msubsup><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

and

(9.20)![equation](images/c9-disp-0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mi>x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>i</mi></msup><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where (.)^(\*) denotes conjugate. The functions *g*(∙) and *h*(∙) perform respectively as highpass and lowpass filters. Among the wavelets, the discrete B‐Spline WTs have near‐optimal TF localization [\[51\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0051). Generally, they also have anti‐symmetric properties, which make them more suitable for analysis of ERPs. The filters for an *n*th‐order B‐Spline wavelet multi‐resolution decomposition, are computed as:

(9.21)![equation](images/c9-disp-0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>h</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><msub><mo>&#8593;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo>&#42;</mo><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced></math> 

and

(9.22)![equation](images/c9-disp-0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><msup><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><msub><mo>&#8593;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#42;</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced><mi>k</mi></msup><msup><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced></math> 

where ↑[2] indicates up‐sampling by 2 and *n* is an integer. For the quadratic spline wavelet (*n* = 2) employed by Ademoglu et al. to analyze pattern reversal VEPs [\[50\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0050) substituting *n* = 2 in the above equations, the parameters can be derived mathematically as:

(9.23)![equation](images/c9-disp-0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>5</mn></msup></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mfenced><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mfrac><mn>120</mn><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>26</mn><mi>z</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>66</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>26</mn><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></math> [(9.24)](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-disp-0024)![equation](images/c9-disp-0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><msup><mi>Z</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *Z* ^(−1) denotes inverse Z‐transform. To find \[(*b* ⁵)^(−1)\](*k*) the z‐domain term may be factorized into:

where α[1] = − 0.04309 and α[2] = − 0.43057. Therefore:

(9.26)![equation](images/c9-disp-0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>5</mn></msup></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mfenced><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>k</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mo>.</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><msubsup><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mi>k</mi></mfenced></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><msubsup><mi>&#945;</mi><mn>2</mn><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mi>k</mi></mfenced></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> 

Conversely, *p*(*k*) can also be computed easily by taking the inverse transform in [Eq. (9.24)](#c09.xhtml#c9-disp-0024). Therefore, the sample values of *h*(*n*) and *g*(*n*) can be obtained. Finally, to perform a WT only lowpass and highpass filtering followed by down‐sampling are needed. In such a multi‐resolution scheme the number of wavelet coefficients halves from one scale to the next. This requires and justifies longer time windows for lower frequencies and shorter time windows for higher frequencies.

In the above work the VEP waveform is recorded using a bipolar recording at electrode locations C[z] and O[z] of the conventional 10–20 EEG system. The sampling rate is 1 kHz. Therefore, each scale covers the following frequency bands: 250–500, 125–250, 62.5–125, 31.3–62.5, 15.5–31.5, 7.8–15.6 Hz (including N70, P100, and N130), and 0–7.8 Hz (residual scale). Although this method is not meant to discriminate between normal and pathological subjects, the ERPs can be highlighted and the differences between normal and abnormal cases are observed. By using the above spline wavelet analysis, it is observed that the main effect of a latency shift of the N70‐P100‐N130 complex is reflected in the sign and magnitude of the second, third, and fourth wavelet coefficients within the 7.8–15.6 Hz band. Many other versions of the WT approach have been introduced in the literature during the recent decade such as those in \[[52](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0052)–[54](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0054)\].

As an example, single‐trial ERPs have been analyzed using wavelet networks (WNs) and the developed algorithm applied to the study of ADHD [\[52\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0052). ADHD is a psychiatric and neurobehavioural disorder. It is characterized by significant occurrence of inattention or hyperactivity and impulsiveness. In this work it is assumed that the ERP and the background EEG are correlated, i.e. the parameters, which describe the signals before the stimulation, do not hold for the post‐stimulation period [\[55\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0055). In a WN topology they presented an ERP, ![images](images/c9-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>t</mi></mfenced></math> as a linear combination of *K* modified wavelet functions *h*(*n*):

(9.27)![equation](images/c9-disp-0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mi>h</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mfrac></mfenced></math> 

where *b*[*k*] , *a*[*k*] , and *w*[*k*] , are respectively, the shift, scale, and weight parameters and *s*(*n*) are called wavelet nodes. [Figure 9.8](#c09.xhtml#c9-fig-0008) shows the topology of a WN for signal representation. In this figure *ψ*[*k*] = *h*((*u* − *b*[*k*] )/*a*[*k*] ) in the case of a Morlet wavelet:

(9.28)![equation](images/c9-disp-0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo mathvariant="italic">cos</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo mathvariant="italic">sin</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo mathvariant="italic">exp</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mfrac></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced></math> 

In this equation each of the frequency parameters *ω*[*k*] and the corresponding scale parameter *a*[*k*] define a node frequency *f*[*k*] = *ω*[*k*] /2*πa*[*k*] , and are optimized during the learning process.

In the above approach a WN is considered as a single hidden layer perceptron whose neuron activation function [\[56\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0056) is defined by wavelet functions. Therefore, the well‐known back‐propagation neural network algorithm [\[57\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0057) is used to simultaneously update the WN parameters (i.e. w [*1*,*k*] , w [*2*,*k*] , *ω*[*k*] , *a*[*k*] , and *b*[*k*] of node *k*). The minimization is performed on the error between the node outputs and the bandpass filtered version of the residual error obtained using auto‐regressive moving average (ARMA) modelling. The bandpass filter and a tapering time window applied to ensure that the desired range is emphasized and the node sees its specific part of the TF plane [\[52\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0052). It has been reported that for the study of ADHD this method enables detection of the N100 ERP components in places where the traditional time averaging approach fails due to the position variation of this component.

![Figure 9.8 Construction of an ERP signal using a WN. The nodes in the hidden layer are represented by modified wavelet functions. The addition of the images value is to deal with functions whose means are non‐zero.](images/c09f008.gif)

[**Figure 9.8**](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-fig-0008) Construction of an ERP signal using a WN. The nodes in the hidden layer are represented by modified wavelet functions. The addition of the ![images](images/c9-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#38;c.macr;</mo></mover></math> value is to deal with functions whose means are non‐zero.

In a recent work there has been an attempt to create a wavelet‐like filter from simulation of the neural activities which is then used in place of a specific wavelet to improve the performance of wavelet‐based single‐trial ERP detection. The main application of such a filter has been found to be in BCI [\[58\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0058).

 

### 9.3.5 Application of Kalman Filter

The main problem in linear time invariant filtering of ERP signals is that the signal and noise frequency components highly overlap. Another problem is that the ERP signals are transient and their frequency components may not fall into a certain range. Wiener filtering which provides optimum solution in the mean square (MS) sense for the majority of noise removal cases is not suitable for nonstationary signals such as ERPs.

With the assumption that the ERP signals are dynamically slowly varying processes the future realizations are predictable from the past realizations. These changes can be studied using a state‐space model. Kalman filtering and generic observation models have been used to denoise the ERP signals [\[59\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0059). Considering a single‐channel EEG observation vector at stimulus time *n*, as **x**[*n*] = \[*x*[*n*] (1), *x*[*n*] (2), …, *x*[*n*] (*N*)\] ^(*T*) , the objective is to estimate a vector of parameters such as ***θ*** [*n*] of length *k* for which the map from **x**[*n*] to ***θ*** [*n*] is (preferably) a linear map. An optimum estimator, ![images](images/c9-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">opt</mi></mrow></msub></math>, which minimizes ![images](images/c9-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mfenced></math>, is ![images](images/c9-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">opt</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> and can be shown to be:

(9.29)![equation](images/c9-disp-0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">opt</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ![images](images/c9-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub></math> and ![images](images/c9-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub></math> are respectively, the means of ***θ*** [*n*] and **x**[*t*] , and ![images](images/c9-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> is the cross‐covariance matrix of the observations and the parameters to be estimated, and ![images](images/c9-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub></math> is the covariance matrix of the column vector **x**[*n*] . Such an estimator is independent of the relationship between ***θ*** [*n*] and **x**[*n*] . The covariance matrix of the estimated error ![images](images/c9-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub></math> can also be found as:

(9.30)![equation](images/c9-disp-0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#949;</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></msub><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> 

In order to evaluate ![images](images/c9-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> some prior knowledge about the model is required. In this case the observations may be assumed to be of the form ***x*** [*n*] = ***s*** [*n*]  +  ***v*** [*n*] , where ***s*** [*n*] and ***v*** [*n*] are considered respectively as the response to the stimulus and the background EEG (irrelevant of the stimulus and ERP). Also, the ERP is modelled as:

(9.31)![equation](images/c9-disp-0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> 

where **H**[*n*] is a deterministic *N* × *k* observation model matrix. The estimated ERP ![images](images/c9-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub></math> can then be obtained as:

(9.32)![equation](images/c9-disp-0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub></math> 

where the estimated parameters, ![images](images/c9-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub></math>, of the observation model **H**[*n*] , using a linear MS estimator and with the assumption of ***θ*** [*n*] and **v**[*n*] being uncorrelated, is achieved as [\[60\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0060):

[(9.33)](#c09.xhtml#R_c9-disp-0033)![equation](images/c9-disp-0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> 

This estimator is optimum if the joint distribution of ***θ*** [*n*] and **x**[*n*] is Gaussian and the parameters and noise are uncorrelated.

However, in order to take into account the dynamics of the ERPs from trial to trial the evolution of ***θ*** [*n*] has to be taken into account. Such evolution may be denoted as:

(9.34)![equation](images/c9-disp-0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">G</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> 

and some initial distribution for ***θ*** [0] assumed. Although the states are not observed directly, the parameters are related to the observations through [Eq. (9.33)](#c09.xhtml#c9-disp-0033). In this model it is assumed that **F**[*n*] , **H**[*n*] , and **G**[*n*] are known matrices, ( ***θ*** [0], ***w*** [*n*] , ***v*** [*n*] ) is a sequence of mutually uncorrelated random vectors with finite variance, E\[**w**[*n*] \] = E\[**v**[*n*] \] = 0 ∀*n*, and the covariance matrices ![images](images/c9-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> are known.

With the above assumptions the Kalman filtering algorithm can be employed to estimate ***θ*[*n*]** as [\[61\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0061):

(9.35)![equation](images/c9-disp-0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where ![images](images/c9-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> is the prediction of ***θ*** [*n*] subject to ![images](images/c9-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mfenced></math>, which is the optimum MS estimate at *n* − 1. Such an estimator is the best sequential estimator if the Gaussian assumption is valid and is the best linear estimator disregarding the distribution. in which the state vector models a random walk process [\[62\]](#c09.xhtml#c9-bib-0062).
