(10.6)![equation](images/c10-disp-0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ls</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mo>&#8869;</mo></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">&#8721;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> 

In this case orthogonal matrices preserve the Frobenius norm. The matrix **Z** = **U∑** is *m × m* unlike **X** which is *n*[*e*] × *T*, where *T* is the number of samples. Generally, the rank of **X** satisfies *rank*(**X**) ≤ m, and *T* >> *m*, and **∑** can have only *m* non‐zero singular values. This means that the overall computation cost has been reduced by a large amount. The SVD can also be used to reduce the computation cost for ![images](images/c10-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8869;</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup></mrow></mfenced></math>. The pseudo‐inverse ***H*** ^† can be decomposed as ![images](images/c10-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#8721;</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8224;</mo></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>H</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math>, where ![images](images/c10-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">U</mi><mi>H</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#8721;</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>&#8224;</mo></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi><mi>H</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math>.

The dipole model, however, requires a priori knowledge about the number of sources, which is usually unknown.

Many experimental studies and clinical experiments have examined the developed source localization algorithms. Yao and Dewald [\[16\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0016) have evaluated different cortical source localization methods such as the moving dipole (MDP) method [\[17\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0017), minimum *Lp* norm [\[18\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0018), and low‐resolution tomography (LRT) as for LORETA [\[19\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0019) using simulated and experimental EEG data. In their study, only the scalp potentials have been taken into consideration.

In this study some other source localization methods such as the cortical potential imaging method [\[20\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0020) and the three‐dimensional resultant vector method [\[21\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0021) have not been included. These methods, however, follow similar steps as minimum norm methods and dipole methods respectively.

 

## 10.3 Head Model

One of the requirements for brain source localization, particularly for the forward model, is the information about the head model. The head model is the model for which the EEG forward solution is calculated. The forward solution determines how much a given electrical source in the brain will impact each electrode on the scalp. It provides the lead field matrix from which the inverse problem will be solved. For a more accurate solution the individual's MRI is often used to construct the head model, particularly in clinical studies where the source localization is used to guide surgery as for example in epilepsy or in functional mapping of the eloquent cortex. In a less precise application where the MRI is not available, a template MRI can be used (for example the MRI brain) [\[22\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0022). The MRI needs several preprocessing steps in order to achieve a proper delineation of the grey matter in which the source activity is estimated, and to describe the different head tissue layers with different conductivity parameters. Since the electric field that spreads from the sources to the scalp surface is attenuated by these layers (particularly by the skull), a proper incorporation of the head shape and the conductivity parameters in the head model is essential during the localization/reconstruction process. Once the MRI is pre‐processed, the electrodes have to be positioned on the head corresponding to how they were positioned during the recordings. It is evident that the localization accuracy depends on how accurately the electrode positions correspond to the real position from which the signals are recorded during the experiment.

For an exact model where simultaneous MRI and EEG are recorded, the imposed magnetic field artefacts have to be removed. Since this is only for one still MRI, the rest of the EEG remains unaffected.

As soon as the MRI is captured the lead field has to be calculated. The lead field determines how the electric activity at a certain electrode is related to the activity of the different sources in the brain. The more precise and anatomically correct this lead field is determined, the more precise the source localization will be. In order to calculate the lead field, a head model has to be created that incorporates as realistically as possible the shape of the head and the conductivity parameters of the different tissues between the current sources in the brain and the potential on the scalp. There have been many attempts to construct realistic head models. Yet, even the most complicated approaches are simplified descriptions of the complex structure of head tissues. The often‐used realistic models are the boundary element model (BEM) and the finite element model (FEM). These models are much superior to the simple three‐shell spherical head models \[[23](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0023)–[25](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0025)\] when applied to real data \[[26](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0026), [27](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0027)\]. The downside of these sophisticated head models is an increased computational load to achieve numerical solutions. They are also more sensitive to any mishap happening during the brain and grey matter extraction, as there would be more brain tissues and more parameters involved. Given the low temporal resolution of MRI, [Figure 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0003) shows the steps in building up the head model [\[22\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0022).

Nevertheless, there are other parameters which affect the usable human head model. One more important one is age. The conductivity of skull decreases nonlinearly with age. In recent studies for a 10 year old subject the conductivity ratio between the brain and skull is approximately 10 to 1, whereas for a 55 year old subject this ratio is approximately 25 to 1. For elderlies this ratio can be 50–80 to 1 \[[28](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0028), [29](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0029)\].

![Figure 10.3 The steps in using MRI data to build up a head model. (a) Original anisotropic MRI. (b) Result of up‐sampling and rotation with red, green, and blue axis pointing, respectively to x,y,z. (c) Adjustment of the cutting planes and setting the correct geometrical coordinate origin. (d) The result of skull‐stripping to isolate the brain.](images/c10f003.jpg)

[**Figure 10.3**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0003) The steps in using MRI data to build up a head model. (a) Original anisotropic MRI. (b) Result of up‐sampling and rotation with red, green, and blue axis pointing, respectively to x,y,z. (c) Adjustment of the cutting planes and setting the correct geometrical coordinate origin. (d) The result of skull‐stripping to isolate the brain.

  

## 10.4 Most Popular Brain Source Localization Approaches

Although most of the methods described here have been used from both EEG and MEG signals, those specifically used for dipole source localization perform much more accurately for MEG signals since the brain is more linear and homogenous with respect to its magnetic field compared with its electric fields used for EEG registration.

The traditional approaches for brain source localization use linear or recursive signal processing techniques. These techniques exploit the multichannel nature of EEG or MEG data, the spatial or in some cases temporal or spectral sparsity of the sources, and if available an approximate shape of the desired source. However, in recent years where powerful computers and graphic cards with large memory allow the use of very computationally intensive machine learning methods, application of deep neural networks (DNNs) in source localization seem inevitable. The use of DNNs in solving similar problems such as sound source separation \[[30](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0030), [31](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0031)\] and communication channel estimation [\[32\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0032) have become popular in recent years.

In such methods the DNN learns the best arrangement of the cortical source locations for having particular patterns of EEG recordings over the scalp. The inherent nonlinearity property of the activation functions and the kernel‐type nature of the multilayer system elegantly accommodates the nonlinearity imposed on the brain EEG sources by the head nonhomogeneous layers.

 

### 10.4.1 EEG Source Localization Using Independent Component Analysis

In a simple though not very accurate approach ICA is used to separate the EEG sources [\[33\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0033). The correlation values of the estimated sources and the mixtures are then used to build up the model of the mixing medium. The LS approach is then used to find the sources using the inverse of these correlations, i.e. *d*[*ij*] ≈ 1/(C [*ij*] )^(0.5), where *d*[*ij*] shows the distance between source *i* and electrode *j*, and C [*ij*] shows the correlation of their signals. The use of correlation values makes the scheme a simple approach to inverse problem based localization. The method has been applied to separate and localize the sources of P3a and P3b subcomponents for five healthy subjects and five schizophrenic patients. Study of ERP components such as P300 and its constituent subcomponents is very important in analysis, diagnosing, and monitoring of mental and psychiatric disorders. Source location, amplitude, and latency of these components have to be quantified and used in the classification process. [Figure 10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0004) illustrates the results overlayed on two MRI templates for the above two cases. It can be seen that for the healthy subjects the subcomponents are well apart whereas for the schizophrenic patients they are geometrically mixed.

 

### 10.4.2 MUSIC Algorithm

Multiple signal classification (MUSIC) [\[34\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0034) has been used for localization of the magnetic dipoles within the brain \[[35](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0035)–[38](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0038)\] using EEG signals. In an early development of this algorithm a single‐dipole model within a three‐dimensional head volume is scanned and projections onto an estimated signal subspace are computed [\[39\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0039). To locate the sources, the user must search the head volume for multiple local peaks in the projection metric. In an attempt to overcome the exhaustive search by the MUSIC algorithm a recursive MUSIC algorithm was developed [\[35\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0035). Following this approach, the locations of the fixed, rotating, or synchronous dipole sources are automatically extracted through a recursive use of subspace estimation. This approach tries to solve the problem of how to choose the locations, which give the best projection on to the signal (EEG) space. In the absence of noise and using a perfect head and sensors model, the forward model for the source at the correct location projects entirely into the signal subspace. In practise, however, there are estimation errors due to noise. In finding the solution to the above problem there are two assumptions which may not be always true: first, the data are corrupted by additive spatially white noise and second, the data are produced by a set of asynchronous dipolar sources. These assumptions are waved in the proposed recursive MUSIC algorithm [\[35\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0035).

![Figure 10.4 Localization results for (a) the schizophrenic patients and (b) the normal subjects. The circles represent P3a and the squares represent P3b.](images/c10f004.jpg)

[**Figure 10.4**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0004) Localization results for (a) the schizophrenic patients and (b) the normal subjects. The circles represent P3a and the squares represent P3b.

The original MUSIC algorithm for the estimation of brain sources may be described as follows. Consider the head model for transferring the dipole field to the electrodes to be **A**(**ρ,θ**), where **ρ** and **θ** are respectively the dipole location and direction parameters. The relationship between the observations (EEG), **X**, the model **A**, and the sources **S** is given as:

(10.7)![equation](images/c10-disp-0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo mathvariant="bold">=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">AS</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo mathvariant="bold">+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">E</mi></math> 

where **E** is the noise matrix. The goal is to estimate the parameters {**ρ, θ, S**}, given the data set **X**. The correlation matrix of **X**, i.e. **R** [x] can be decomposed as:

(10.8)![equation](images/c10-disp-0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>F</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mspace width="1em"/><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup></math> 

or

(10.9)![equation](images/c10-disp-0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math> 

where ![images](images/c10-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></math> is the *m* × *m* diagonal matrix combining both the model and noise eigenvalues, and ![images](images/c10-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>&#963;</mi><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></math> is the (*n*[*e*] *− m*) × (*n*[*e*] *− m*) diagonal matrix of noise‐only eigenvalues. Therefore, the signal subspace span (**Φ** [s]) and noise‐only subspace span (**Φ** [e]) are orthogonal. In practise, *T* samples of the data are used to estimate the above parameters, i.e.

(10.10)![equation](images/c10-disp-0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>x</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><msup><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><msup><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub><mi>T</mi></msup></math> 

where the first *m* left singular vectors of the decomposition are designated as ![images](images/c10-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></math> and the remaining eigenvectors as ![images](images/c10-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub></math>. Accordingly, the diagonal matrix ![images](images/c10-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#923;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></math> contains the first *m* eigenvalues and ![images](images/c10-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#923;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>e</mi></msub></math> contains the remainder. To estimate the above parameters the general rule using least‐squares (LS) fitting is:

(10.11)![equation](images/c10-disp-0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">arg</mo><munder><mo>min</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#961;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi></mrow></munder><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#961;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> 

where || . ||[F] denotes Frobenius norm. By optimal substitution [\[40\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0040) we achieve:

(10.12)![equation](images/c10-disp-0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#961;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">arg</mo><munder><mo mathvariant="italic">min</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#961;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi></mrow></munder><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> 

where **A** ^† is the Moore‐Penrose pseudo‐inverse of **A** [\[41\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0041). Given that the rank of **A**(**ρ, θ**) is *m* and the rank of ![images](images/c10-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></msub></math> is at least *m*, the smallest subspace correlation value, *C*[*m*] = subcorr{**A**(**ρ, θ**),![images](images/c10-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></math>} [*m*] , represents the minimum subspace correlation (maximum principal angle) between principal vectors in the column space of **A**(**ρ,θ**) and the signal subspace ![images](images/c10-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></math>. In MUSIC, the subspace correlation of any individual column of **A**(**ρ, θ**), i.e. **a**(**ρ**[*i*] **,θ**[*i*] ) with the signal subspace must therefore equal or exceed this minimum subspace correlation:

(10.13)![equation](images/c10-disp-0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>subcorr</mtext><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#961;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8805;</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math> 

![images](images/c10-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></math> approaches **Φ**[*s*] when the number of samples increases or the signal‐to‐noise ratio (SNR) becomes higher. Then the minimum correlation approaches unity when the correct parameter set is identified, such that the *m* distinct sets of parameters (**ρ**[*i*] **,θ**[*i*] ) have subspace correlations approaching unity. Therefore a search strategy is followed to find the *m* peaks of the metric [\[35\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0035):

(10.14)![equation](images/c10-disp-0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="italic">subcor</mtext><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#961;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#952;</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#961;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></mfenced><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#961;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#961;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mfrac></math> 

where ![images](images/c10-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mo>&#183;</mo></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> denotes squared Euclidean norm. For a perfect estimation of the signal subspace *m* global maxima equal to unity are found. This requires searching for both sets of parameters **ρ** and **θ**. In a quasilinear approach [\[35\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0035) it is assumed that **a**(**ρ**[*i*] **,θ**[*i*] ) = **G**(**ρ**[*i*] **)θ**[*i*] where **G**(.) is called the gain matrix. In the EEG source localization application therefore, we first find the dipole parameters **ρ**[*i*] which maximize the *subcorr*{**G**(**ρ**[*i*] **),** ![images](images/c10-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></math>} and then extract the corresponding quasilinear **θ**[*i*] which maximize this subspace correlation. This avoids explicitly searching for these quasilinear parameters, reducing the overall complexity of the nonlinear search. Therefore, the overall localization of the EEG sources using classic MUSIC can be summarized to the following steps: (i) Decompose **X** or **XX**^(*T*) and select the rank of the signal subspace to obtain ![images](images/c10-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></math>. Slightly overspecifying the rank has little effect on the performance whereas, underspecifying it can dramatically reduce the performance; (ii) form the gain matrix **G** at each point (node) of a dense grid of dipolar source locations and calculate the subspace correlations *subcorr*{**G**(**ρ**[*i*] **),** ![images](images/c10-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mi>s</mi></msub></math>}; and (iii) find the peaks of the plot ![images](images/c10-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></msqrt></math>, where *C* [1] is the maximum subspace correlation. Locate *m* or fewer peaks in the grid. At each peak, refine the search grid to improve the location accuracy and check the second subspace correlation. A large second subspace correlation is an indication of a rotating dipole [\[35\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0035). Unfortunately, often there are errors in estimating the signal subspace and the correlations are computed at only a finite set of grid points. A recursive MUSIC algorithm overcomes this problem by recursively building up the independent topography model. In this model the number of dipoles is initially considered as one and the search is carried out to locate a single dipole. A second dipole is then added and the dipole point that maximizes the second subspace correlation, *C* [2], is found. At this stage there is no need to recalculate *C* [1]. The number of dipoles is increased and the new subspace correlations are computed. If *m* topographies comprise *m* [1] single‐dipolar topographies and *m* [2] two‐dipolar topographies, then, the recursive MUSIC will first extract the *m* [1] single‐dipolar models. At the (*m* [1] + 1)th iteration, no single‐dipole location that correlates well with the subspace will be found. By increasing the number of dipole elements to two, the searches for both have to be carried out simultaneously such that the subspace correlation is maximized for ![images](images/c10-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math>. The procedure continues to build the remaining *m* [2] two‐dipolar topographies. After finding each pair of dipoles that maximizes the appropriate subspace correlation, the corresponding correlations are also calculated.

Another extension of MUSIC‐based source localization for diversely polarized sources, namely recursively applied and projected (RAP) MUSIC [\[37\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0037), uses each successively located source to form an intermediate array gain matrix (similar to the recursive MUSIC algorithm) and projects both the array manifold and the signal subspace estimate into its orthogonal complement. In this case the subspace is reduced. Then, the MUSIC projection to find the next source is performed. This method was initially applied to localization of MEG sources \[[37](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0037), [38](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0038)\].

In another study by Xu et al. [\[42\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0042), an approach to EEG three‐dimensional (3D) dipole source localization by using a non‐recursive subspace algorithm, called FINES, has been proposed. The approach employs projections onto a subspace spanned by a small set of particular vectors in the estimated noise‐only subspace, instead of the entire estimated noise‐only subspace in the case of classic MUSIC. The subspace spanned by this vector set is, in the sense of principal angle, closest to the subspace spanned by the array manifold associated with a particular brain region. By incorporating knowledge of the array manifold in identifying the FINES vector sets in the estimated noise‐only subspace for different brain regions, this approach is claimed to be able to estimate sources with enhanced accuracy and spatial resolution, thus enhancing the capability of resolving closely spaced sources and reducing estimation errors. The simulation results show that, compared to classic MUSIC, FINES has a better resolvability of two closely spaced dipolar sources and also a better estimation accuracy of source locations. In comparison with RAP‐MUSIC, the performance of the FINES is also better for the cases where the noise level is high and/or correlations among dipole sources exist [\[42\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0042).

A method for using a generic head model, in the form of an anatomical atlas, has also been proposed to produce EEG source localization [\[43\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0043). The atlas is fitted to the subject by a nonrigid warp using a set of surface landmarks. The warped atlas is used to compute a FEM of the forward mapping or lead‐fields between neural current generators and the EEG electrodes. These lead‐fields are used to localize current sources from the EEG data of the subject and the sources are then mapped back to the anatomical atlas. This approach provides a mechanism for comparing source localizations across subjects in an atlas‐based coordinate system.

 

### 10.4.3 LORETA Algorithm

The LORETA for localization of brain sources has already been commercialized. In this method, the electrode potentials and matrix **X**, are considered to be related as:

[(10.15)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0015)![equation](images/c10-disp-0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">LS</mi></math> 

where **S** is the actual (current) source amplitudes (densities) and **L** is an *n*[*e*]  × 3*m* matrix representing the forward transmission coefficients from each source to the array of sensors. **L** has also been referred to as the system response kernel or the lead field matrix [\[44\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0044). Each column of **L** contains the potentials observed at the electrodes when the source vector has unit amplitude at one location and orientation and is zero at all others. This requires the potentials to be measured linearly with respect to the source amplitudes based on the superposition principle. Generally, this is not true and therefore such an assumption inherently creates some error. The fitted source amplitudes, **S**, can be approximately estimated using an exhaustive search through the inverse LS solution, i.e.:

(10.16)![equation](images/c10-disp-0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi></mi></msub><mo mathvariant="bold">=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo mathvariant="bold" form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></math> 

**L** may be approximated by 3D simulations of current flow in the head, which requires a solution to the well‐known Poisson [equation \[45\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0045):

(10.17)![equation](images/c10-disp-0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext>&#8711;</mtext><mo>.</mo><mtext>&#963;&#8711;</mtext><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#961;</mi></math> 

where σ is the conductivity of the head volume (Ωm)^(−1) and **ρ** is the source volume current density (A/m³). An FEM or BEM may be used to solve this equation. In such models the geometrical information about the brain layers and their conductivities [\[46\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0046) have to be known. Unless some a priori knowledge can be used in the formulation, the analytic model is ill‐posed and a unique solution is hard to achieve.

Conversely, the number of sources, *m*, is typically much larger than the number of sensors, *n*[*e*] , and the system in [(10.15)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0015) is underdetermined. Also, in the applications where more concentrated focal sources are to be estimated such methods fail. As we see later, using a minimum norm approach, some researchers choose the solution which satisfies some constraints such as the smoothness of the inverse solution.

One approach is the minimum norm solution, which minimizes the norm of S under the constraint of the forward problem:

(10.18)![equation](images/c10-disp-0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>min</mo><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>subject&#8201;to</mtext><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">LS</mi></math> 

with a solution as:

[(10.19)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0019)![equation](images/c10-disp-0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">LL</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mfenced><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></math> 

The motivation of the minimum norm solution is to create a sparse solution with zero contribution from most of the sources. This method has the serious drawback of poor localization performance in three‐dimensional (3D) space. An extension to this method is the weighted minimum norm (WMN) solution, which compensates for deep sources and hence performs better in 3D space. In this case the norms of the columns of **L** are normalized. Hence the constrained WMN is formulated as:

(10.20)![equation](images/c10-disp-0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>min</mo><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mi mathvariant="bold">WS</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>subject&#8201;&#8201;to</mtext><mspace width="0.12em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">LS</mi></math> 

with a solution as:

(10.21)![equation](images/c10-disp-0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">LW</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></math> 

where **W** is a diagonal 3*m* × 3*m* weighting matrix, which compensates for deep sources in the following way:

(10.22)![equation](images/c10-disp-0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">diag</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mfenced></math> 

where ‖**L** [**i**] ‖[2] denotes the Euclidean norm of the *i*th column of **L**, i.e. **W** corresponds to the inverse of the distances between sources and electrodes.

In another similar approach a smoothing Laplacian operator is employed. This operator produces a spatially smooth solution agreeing with the physiological assumption mentioned earlier. The function of interest is then:

[(10.23)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0023)![equation](images/c10-disp-0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>min</mo><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mi>BWS</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>subject&#8201;to</mtext><mspace width="0.12em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">LS</mi></math> 

where **B** is the Laplacian operator. This minimum norm approach produces a smooth topography in which the peaks representing the source locations are accurately located.

An FEM has been used to achieve a more anatomically realistic volume conductor model of the head, in an approach called adaptive standardized LORETA/FOCUSS underdetermined system solver (FOCUSS) [\[47\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0047). It is claimed that when using this application‐specific method a number of different resolution solutions using different mesh intensities can be combined to achieve the localization of sources with less computational complexities. Initially, FEM is used to approximate the solutions to [(10.23)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0023) with a realistic representation of the conductor volume based on magnetic resonance (MR) images of the human head. The dipolar sources are presented using the approximate Laplace method [\[48\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0048).

 

### 10.4.4 FOCUSS Algorithm

The FOCUSS [\[47\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0047) algorithm is based on a high‐resolution iterative WMN method that uses the information from the previous iterations as:

(10.24)![equation](images/c10-disp-0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>min</mo><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mi mathvariant="bold">CS</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mtext>subject&#8201;to</mtext><mspace width="0.12em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">LS</mi></math> 

where ***C*** = ( ***Q*** ^(−1)) ^(*T*) ***Q*** ^(−1) and ***Q*** [*i*] = ***WQ*** [*i* − 1]\[*diag*( ***S*** [*i* − 1](1)⋯ ***S*** [*i* − 1](3*m*)\] the solution at iteration *i* becomes:

(10.25)![equation](images/c10-disp-0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></math> 

The iterations stop when there is no significant change in the estimation. The result of FOCUSS is highly dependent on the initialization of the algorithm. In practise, the algorithm converges close to the initialization point and may easily become stuck in some local minimum. A clever initialization of FOCUSS has been suggested to be the solution to LORETA [\[47\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0047).

  

### 10.4.5 Standardized LORETA

As another option referred to as sLORETA, a unique solution to the inverse problem is found. It uses a different cost function, which is:

(10.26)![equation](images/c10-disp-0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mo>min</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></mrow></munder><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">LS</mi></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">&#955;</mi><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> 

Hence, sLORETA uses a zero‐order Tikhonov‐Phillips regularization \[[49](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0049), [50](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0050)\], which provides a possible solution to the ill‐posed inverse problems:

(10.27)![equation](images/c10-disp-0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msubsup><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi></math> 

where **s** [i] indicates the candidate sources and **S** are the actual sources. **R**[*i*] is the resolution matrix defined as:

[(10.28)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0028)![equation](images/c10-disp-0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msubsup><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> 

The reconstruction of multiple sources performed by the final iteration of sLORETA is used as an initialization for the combined ALF and WMN (or FOCUSS) algorithms [\[48\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0048). The number of sources is reduced each time and [(10.19)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0019) is modified to:

(10.29)![equation](images/c10-disp-0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>f</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msubsup><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>f</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></math> 

**L**[*f*] indicates the final *n* × *m* lead field returned by the sLORETA. **W**[*i*] is a diagonal 3*m*[*f*]  × 3*m*[*f*] matrix, which is recursively refined based on the current density estimated by the previous step:

(10.30)![equation](images/c10-disp-0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">diag</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>1</mn></mfenced><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>2</mn></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

and the resolution matrix in [(10.28)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0028) after each iteration changes to:

(10.31)![equation](images/c10-disp-0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>f</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msubsup><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>f</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">L</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math> 

Iterations are continued until the solution does not significantly change. In another approach by Liu et al. [\[51\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0051) called shrinking standard LORETA–FOCUSS (SSLOFO), sLORETA is used for initialization. Then, it uses the re‐WMN of FOCUSS. During the process the localization results are further improved by involving the above standardization technique. However, FOCUSS normally creates an increasingly sparse solution during iteration. Therefore, it is better to eliminate the nodes with no source activities or recover those active nodes which might be discarded by mistake. The algorithm proposed in [\[52\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0052) shrinks the source space after each iteration of FOCUSS, hence reducing the computational load [\[51\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0051). For the algorithm not to be trapped in a local minimum a smoothing operation is performed. The overall SSLOFO is therefore summarized by the following steps \[[51](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0051), [52](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0052)\]:

1.  Estimate the current density ![images](images/c10-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></msub></math> using sLORETA.
2.  Initialize the weighting matrix as **Q** [0] = *diag*\[![images](images/c10-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></math>(1), ![images](images/c10-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></math>(2)… ![images](images/c10-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mn>0</mn></msub></math>(3*m*)\].
3.  Estimate the source power using standardized FOCUSS.
4.  Retain the prominent nodes and their neighbouring nodes. Adjust the values on these nodes through smoothing.
5.  Redefine the solution space to contain only the retained nodes, i.e. only the corresponding elements in **S** and the corresponding column in **L**.
6.  Update the weighting matrix.
7.  Repeat steps 3–6 until a stopping condition is satisfied.
8.  The final solution is the result of the last step before smoothing.

The stopping condition maybe by defining a threshold, or when there is no considerable change in the weights in further iterations.

 

### 10.4.6 Other Weighted Minimum Norm Solutions

In an LD approach by Phillips et al. [\[5\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0005) a WMN solution (or Tikhonov regularization) method [\[53\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0053) has been proposed. The solution has been regularized by imposing some anatomical and physiological information upon the overall cost function in the form of constraints. The squared error costs are weighted based on spatial and temporal properties. The information such as hemodynamic measures of brain activity from other imaging modalities such as fMRI, are used as constraints (or priors) together with the proposed cost function. In this approach it is assumed that the sources are sufficiently densely distributed and the sources are oriented orthogonal to the cortical sheet.

The instantaneous EEG source localization problem using a multivariate linear model and the observations, **X**, as electrode potentials, is generally formulated on the basis of the observation model:

(10.32)![equation](images/c10-disp-0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo mathvariant="fraktur">=</mo><mi mathvariant="fraktur">I</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">J</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi></math> 

where, **X** = \[**x** [1], **x** [2], …, **x**[*ne*] \] ^(*T*) has dimension *n*[*e*]  × *T*, where *T* represents the length of the data in samples and *n*[*e*] is the number of electrodes, **r** and **J** = \[**j** [1], **j** [2], …, **j**[*m*] \] are respectively source locations and moments of the sources, and **V** is the additive noise matrix. *ℑ* is the function linking the sources to the electrode potentials. In calculation of *ℑ* a suitable three‐layer head model is normally considered \[[54](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0054), [55](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0055)\]. A structural MR image of the head may be segmented into three isotropic regions namely, brain, skull, and scalp, of the same conductivity [\[56\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0056) and used as the model. Most of these models consider the head as a sphere for simplicity.

However, in [\[5\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0005) the EEG sources are modelled by a fixed and uniform three‐dimensional grid of current dipoles spread within the entire brain volume. Also, the problem is an underdetermined linear problem as:

(10.33)![equation](images/c10-disp-0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">LJ</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">V</mi></math> 

where, **L** is the head field matrix, which inter‐relates the dipoles to the electrode potentials. To achieve a unique solution for the above underdetermined equation some constraints have to be imposed. The proposed regularization method constrains the reconstructed source distribution by jointly minimizing a linear mixture of some weighted norm ‖**Hj**‖[2] of the current source **j** and the main cost function of the inverse solution. Assuming the noise is Gaussian with a covariance matrix **C** [v] then:

[(10.34)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0034)![equation](images/c10-disp-0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">j</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">arg</mo><munder><mo>min</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">j</mi></munder><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">v</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Lj</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#955;</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></msup><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mi mathvariant="bold">Hj</mi></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where the Lagrange multiplier **λ** has to be adjusted to make a balance between the main cost function and the constraint ‖**Hj**‖[2]. The covariance matrix is scaled in such a way to have trace(**C** [v]) = rank(**C** [v]) (recall that trace of a matrix is sum of its diagonal elements, and rank of a matrix refers to its number of independent columns \[rows\]). This can be stated as an overdetermined LS problem [\[20\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0020). The solution to the minimization of [(10.34)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0034) for a given **λ** is in the form of:

(10.35)![equation](images/c10-disp-0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">J</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">BX</mi></math> 

where

(10.36)![equation](images/c10-disp-0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">B</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo stretchy="true">\]</mo><msup><mrow/><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> 

These equations describe the WMN solution to the localization problem. However, this is not complete unless a suitable spatial or temporal constraint is imposed. Theoretically, any number of constraints can be added to the main cost function in the same way and the hyperparameters such as Lagrange multipliers, **λ,** can be calculated by expectation–maximization [\[57\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0057). However, more assumptions such as those about the covariance of the sources have to be implied in order to find effectively **L**, which includes the information about the locations and the moments. One assumption, in the form of constraint, can be based on the fact that (*diag*(**L** ^(***T***) **L**))^(−1), which is proportional to the covariance components, should be normalized. Another constraint is based on the spatial fMRI information which appears as BOLD when the sources are active. Evoked responses can also be used as temporal constraints.

Various inverse problem methods for localization of EEG sources can be seen in [Figure 10.5](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0005).

In reality, EEG and MEG recordings are the spatial integration of the activity from large and multiple remotely located populations of neurons. Functionally connected brain networks are those temporally correlated and spatially remote neurological sources. Such functional networks have been described in brains engaged in complex cognitive tasks that necessarily require the transient integration of numerous functional areas widely distributed over the brain and in continuous interaction.

One way of doing this integration can be by neural phase synchrony. This refers to neuronal groups, oscillating in specific frequency bands, that are engaged into precise phase‐locking over a limited period of time. In turn, this has motivated the search for robust methods to directly measure such phase synchrony from experimentally recorded biological signals. Some applications of phase synchrony can be found for monitoring mental fatigue as described in [Chapter 13](#c13.xhtml) of this book.

Generally, massive diffusive effects and poor SNR preclude accurate estimation of indices related to the cortical dynamics from non‐averaged scalp recordings.

In [\[58\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0058) a similar WMN approach used for dipole source localization has been utilized for estimation of neural dynamics of cortical sources. In their method surrogate data have been used to reduce the source space in order to reconstruct such data.

The activity is expected to be produced by a large number of brain regions interacting together in different dynamic networks. The distributed‐source model considers a great   number of current dipoles placed on the whole cortical surface. Similar to the single‐dipole source model, a WMN solution associated with the cortical distributed‐source model is proposed here [\[58\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0058).

![Figure 10.5 Flow diagram of inverse methods used for EEG source localization.](images/c10f005.gif)

[**Figure 10.5**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0005) Flow diagram of inverse methods used for EEG source localization.

 

### 10.4.7 Evaluation Indices

The accuracy of inverse solution using the simulated EEG data has been evaluated by three indices: (i) the error distance (ED), i.e. the distance between the actual and estimated locations of the sources, (ii) the undetected source number percentage (USP), and (iii) the falsely detected source number percentage (FSP). Obviously, these quantifications are based on the simulated models and data. For real EEG data it is hard to quantify and evaluate the results obtained by different inverse methods.

ED between the estimated source locations, ![images](images/c10-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover></math>, and the actual source locations, ***s*** , is defined as:

(10.37)![equation](images/c10-disp-0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>ED</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></munderover><munder><mo>min</mo><mi>j</mi></munder><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>N</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ud</mi></msub></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">ud</mi></msub></munderover><munder><mo>min</mo><mi>i</mi></munder><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mfenced></math> 

where *i* and *j* are the indices of locations of the estimated and actual sources, and *N*[*d*] and *N*[*ud*] are respectively the total numbers of estimated and undetected sources.

USP and FSP are respectively defined as USP = *N*[*un*] */Nreal* × 100% and FSP = *N*[*false*] */N*[*estimated*] × 100% where *N*[*un*] *,N*[*real*] , *N*[*false*] , and *N*[*estimated*] are respectively the numbers of undetected, real, falsely detected, and estimated sources.

In practise three types of head volume conductor models can be used: a homogeneous sphere head volume conductor model, a BEM or a FEM model. Since the FEM is computationally very intensive, the subject specific BEM model, albeit for an oversimplifying sphere head model, is currently used [\[59\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0059).

In terms of ED, USP, and FSP, LRT1 (i.e. p = 1) has been verified to give the best localization results.

Use of the temporal properties of brain signals to improve the localization performance has also been attempted. An additional temporal constraint can be added assuming that for each location the change in the source amplitude with time is minimal. The constraint to be added is ![images](images/c10-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>min</mo><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math>, where *n* denotes the time index.

 

### 10.4.8 Joint ICA–LORETA Approach

In another study [\[60\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0060) Infomax ICA‐based blind source separation (BSS) has been implemented as a preprocessing scheme before the application of LORETA to localize the sources underlying the mismatch negativity (MMN). MMN is an involuntary auditory ERP, which peaks at 100–200 ms when there is a violation of a regular pattern. This ERP appears to correspond to a primitive intelligence. MMN signals are mainly generated in the supramental cortex \[[61](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0061)–[65](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0065)\].

The LORETA analysis was performed with the scalp maps associated with selected ICA components to find the generators of these maps. Only values greater than 2.5 times the standard deviation of the standardized data (in the LORETA spatial resolution) were accepted as activations.

The inverse problem has also been tackled within a Bayesian framework [\[66\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0066). In such methods some information about the prior probabilities are normally essential. Again we may consider the EEG generation model as:

(10.38)![equation](images/c10-disp-0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Hs</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">v</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></math> 

where **x**(*n*) is an *n*[*e*]  × 1 vector containing the EEG sample values at time *n*, **H** is an *n*[*e*]  × *m* matrix representing the head medium model, **s**(*n*) includes the *m* × 1 vector sample values of the sources at time *n* and **v**(*n*) is the *n*[*e*]  × 1 vector of noise samples at time *n*. The a priori information about the sources imposes some constraints on their locations and their temporal properties. The estimation may be performed using a maximum a posteriori (MAP) criterion in which the estimator tries to find **s**(*n*) that maximizes the probability distribution of **s**(*n*) given the measurements **x**(*n*). The estimator is denoted as:

(10.39)![equation](images/c10-disp-0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">max</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></math> 

and following Bayes' rule where the posterior probability is:

(10.40)![equation](images/c10-disp-0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mi>p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>/</mo><mi>p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *p*( ***x*** (*n*) ∣  ***s*** (*n*)) is the likelihood,*p*( ***x*** (*n*)) is the marginal distribution of the measurements, and *p*( ***s*** (*n*)) is the prior probability. The posterior can be written in terms of energy functions, i.e.:

(10.41)![equation](images/c10-disp-0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>z</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>z</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfrac><mo mathvariant="italic">exp</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mi>U</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

and *U*( ***s*** (*n*)) = (1 − *λ*)*U* [1]( ***s*** (*n*)) + *λU* [2]( ***s*** (*n*)) where *U* [1] and *U* [2] correspond to the likelihood and the prior respectively, and 0 ≤ λ ≤1. The prior may be separated into two functions, spatial priors, *U*[*s*] , and temporal priors, *U*[*t*] . The spatial prior function can take into account the smoothness of the spatial variation of the sources. A cost function that determines the spatial smoothness is:

(10.42)![equation](images/c10-disp-0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#934;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>u</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> 

where *K* is the scaling factor which determines the required smoothness. Therefore, the prior function for the spatial constraints can be written as:

(10.43)![equation](images/c10-disp-0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></munderover><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#934;</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>x</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#934;</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>y</mi></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>y</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where the indices *x* and *y* correspond to horizontal and vertical gradients respectively.

The temporal constraints are imposed by assuming that the projection of **s**(*n*) to the space perpendicular to **s**(*n* − 1) is small. Thus, the temporal prior function, as the second constraint, can be written as:

(10.44)![equation](images/c10-disp-0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#8869;</mo></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

where ![images](images/c10-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#8869;</mo></msubsup></math> is the projection onto the perpendicular space to **s**(*n* − 1). Therefore, the overall minimization criterion for estimation of **s**(*n*) becomes:

(10.45)![equation](images/c10-disp-0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mo stretchy="true">&#38;c.circ;</mo></mover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mo mathvariant="italic">arg</mo><munder><mo>min</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi></munder><mfenced open="{" close="}"><mrow><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Hs</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>&#945;</mi><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></munderover><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#934;</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">x</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>&#934;</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>y</mi></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">y</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced><mo>&#8739;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mspace width="3.8em"/><mo>+</mo><mi>&#946;</mi><msup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#8869;</mo></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>n</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where *α* and *β* are the penalty terms (regularization parameters).

According to the results of this study the independent components can be generated by one or more spatially separated source. This confirms that each dipole is somehow associated with one dipole generator [\[67\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0067). In addition, it is claimed that a specific brain structure can participate in different components, working simultaneously in different observations. The combination of ICA and LORETA exploits spatiotemporal dynamics of the brain as well as localization of the sources.

In [\[51\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0051) four different inverse methods namely, WMN, sLORETA, FOCUSS, and SSLOFO have been compared (based on a spherical head assumption and in the absence of noise). It has been shown that in their original forms SSLOFO gives more accurate localization when WMN and sLORETA fail in achieving unique and accurate solutions.

Conversely, while sLORETA has the best performance when only one source is present, for two or more sources LORETA with *p* equal to 1.5 outperforms other methods. When the relative strength of one of the sources is decreased, all algorithms have more difficulty reconstructing that source. However, LORETA with *p* = 1.5 continues to outperform other algorithms. If only the strongest source is of interest sLORETA is recommended, while LORETA with *p* = 1.5 is recommended if two or more of the cortical sources are of interest. In [\[68\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0068) these results are used as a guidance for choosing a CSD algorithm to locate multiple cortical sources of EEG and for interpreting the results of these algorithms.

 

## 10.5 Forward Solutions to the Localization Problem

In these approaches often an approximation of the shape (morphology) of the desired source is available. Some examples are as follows.

 

### 10.5.1 Partially Constrained BSS Method

In a recent work [\[69\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0069) the locations of the known sources such as some normal brain rhythms have been used as a prior in order to find the locations of the abnormal or the other brain source signals using constrained BSS. The cost function of the BSS algorithm is constrained by this information and the known sources are iteratively calculated. Consider ![images](images/c10-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8942;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">uk</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> is the mixing matrix including the geometrical information about the known, **A**[*k*] , and unknown, **A**[*uk*] , sources. **A**[*k*] is an *n*[*e*]  × *k* matrix and **A**[*uk*] is an *n*[*e*]  × (*m* − *k*) matrix. Given **A**[*k*] , **A**[*uk*] may be estimated as follows:

(10.46)![equation](images/c10-disp-0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="italic">uk</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="italic">uk</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#958;</mi><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">uk</mi></msub></msub><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></math> 

where

(10.47)![equation](images/c10-disp-0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">uk</mi></msub></msub><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8942;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">uk</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> (10.48)![equation](images/c10-disp-0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfenced></math> 

and
