(10.49)![equation](images/c10-disp-0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> (10.50)![equation](images/c10-disp-0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>J</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> 

with

(10.51)![equation](images/c10-disp-0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></msub><mi>J</mi></math> 

where *J*(**W**) = *J*[*m*] (**W**) + *λJ*[*c*] (**W**); *J*[*m*] is the main BSS cost function. The parameters *μ*, *γ*, and *ζ* are either set empirically or changed iteratively; they decrease when the convergence error decreases and recall that **A**[*k*] is known and remains constant.

 

### 10.5.2 Constrained Least‐Squares Method for Localization of P3a and P3b

Often some information about the shape of the source helps in its localization. ERPs look like positive and negative humps in the EEG signals. Such humps may be approximated by Gaussian or Laplacian functions. A method based on LS can be followed [\[70\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0070). Using this method, the scalp maps (the column vectors of the forward matrix **H**) are estimated. Consider:

(10.52)![equation](images/c10-disp-0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mo mathvariant="bold">=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">XY</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">HSY</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></math> 

where **Y** is a matrix with rows equal to **y** [***c***] and **Y** = **DS**, where **D** is a diagonal scaling matrix:

(10.53)![equation](images/c10-disp-0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8230;</mo><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.5em"/><msub><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8230;</mo><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mo>&#8942;</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mspace width="1em"/><mo>&#8945;</mo><mo>&#8942;</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

Post‐multiplying **R** by ![images](images/c10-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>:

(10.54)![equation](images/c10-disp-0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mi>y</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">HS</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> 

The order of the sources is arbitrary. Therefore, the permutation does not affect the overall process. Hence, the *i*th scaled scalp map corresponds to the scaled *i*th source. An LS method may exploit the information about the scalp maps to localize the ERP sources within the brain.

Assuming an isotropic propagation model of the head, the sources are attenuated with the third power of the distance [\[71\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0071), i.e. ![images](images/c10-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, where *h*[*j*] is the *j*th element of a specific column of the **H** matrix. The source locations **q** are found as the solution to the following LS problem:

(10.55)![equation](images/c10-disp-0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mo>min</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></munder><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><munder><mo>min</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></munder><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></munderover><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi>M</mi><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></math> 

where **a**[*j*] are the positions of the electrodes, **d**[*j*] s are the scaled distances, and *M* (scalar) is the scale to be estimated together with **q**. *M* and **q** are iteratively estimated according to:

(10.56)![equation](images/c10-disp-0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mfenced open="" close="|"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></msub><mi>E</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> 

and

(10.57)![equation](images/c10-disp-0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mfenced open="" close="|"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>M</mi></msub><mi>E</mi></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>&#961;</mi></msub></mrow></msub></math> 

where *μ* [1] and *μ* [2] are the learning rates and ∇[**q**] and ∇ [*M*] are respectively the gradients with respect to **q** and *M* which are computed as [\[71\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0071)

(10.58)![equation](images/c10-disp-0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></msub><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></munderover><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>M</mi><mfrac><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math> (10.59)![equation](images/c10-disp-0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mo>&#8711;</mo><mi>M</mi></msub><mi>E</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="italic">ne</mi></munderover><mi>M</mi><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math> 

The solutions to **q** and *M* are unique given *n*[*e*]  ≥ 3 and *n*[*e*] > *m*. Using the above localization algorithm 10 sets of EEGs from five patients and five controls, each divided into 20 segments, are examined. [Figure 10.6](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0006) illustrates the locations of P3a and P3b sources for the patients. From this figure it is clear that the clusters representing the P3a and P3b locations are distinct. [Figure 10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0007) conversely, presents the sources for the control subjects. Unlike in [Figure 10.6](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0006), the P3a and P3b sources are randomly located within the brain.

### 10.5.3 Spatial Notch Filtering Approach

For the brain the propagation media is not homogenous. The current flow is strongly attenuated by the skull due to its high resistivity. This attenuation has to be properly modelled when solving the so‐called forward problem, i.e. determining the potential at each scalp electrode generated by a known source in the brain. In many cases, such as in localization of ERPs or epileptiform discharges, the morphology of the source of interest is vaguely known. The following approach is a solution to such a forward problem.

A spatial notch filter (SNF), also called a null beamformer (BF), has been designed to maximize the similarity between the extracted ERP source and a generic template which approximates an ERP shape, and at the same time enforce a null at the location of the source [\[72\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0072). This method is based on a head and source model, which describes the propagation of the brain sources. The sources are modelled as magnetic dipoles, potentially located at some vertices within the brain, and their propagation to the sensors is mathematically described by an appropriate forward model. The considered 3D grid can be fine or coarse depending on the required accuracy of the results. In this model the EEG signal is considered as an *n*[*e*] × *T* matrix, where *n*[*e*] is the number of electrodes and *T* is the number of time samples for an EEG channel signal block:

(10.60)![equation](images/c10-disp-0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">HMS</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">N</mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">m</mi></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">N</mi></math> 

where **H** is an *n*[*e*]  × 3*m* matrix describing the forward model of the *m* sources to the *n*[*e*] electrodes. **H** is further decomposed into *m* matrices **H**[*i*] *, i* = 1, …, *m* as:

(10.61)![equation](images/c10-disp-0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8943;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8943;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> 

where **H**[*i*] are *n*[*e*]  × 3 matrices whose each column describes the potential at the electrodes due to the *i*th dipole for each of the three orthogonal orientations. For example, the first column of **H**[*i*] describes the forward model of the *x* component of the *i*th dipole when *y* and *z* components are zero. Similarly, **M** is a 3*m* × *m* matrix describing the orientation of the *m* dipoles and is decomposed as:

(10.62)![equation](images/c10-disp-0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">M</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mo>&#8943;</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mo>&#8943;</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mn>0</mn><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

where **m**[*i*] is a 3 × 1 vector describing the orientation of the *i*th dipole; **s** [***i***] , a 1× *T* vector, is the time signal originated from the *i*th dipole, and **N** is the measurement noise and the modelling error. In addition, the ERP signal **r**[*i*] for the *i*th source has been modelled as a Gaussian shape template with variable width and latency.

A constrained optimization procedure is then followed in which the primary cost function is the Euclidean distance between the reference signal and the filtered EEG [\[72\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0072), i.e.:

(10.63)![equation](images/c10-disp-0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></math> 

The minimum point for this can be obtained by the classic LS minimization and is given by:

(10.64)![equation](images/c10-disp-0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi mathvariant="italic">opt</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></math> 

Following this method an *n*[*e*]  × 1 filter **w**[*opt*] is designed which gives an estimate of the reference signal when applied to EEGs. However, this procedure does not include any spatial information unless **w**[*i*] s for all the sources are taken into account. In this way, we can construct a matrix **W**, similar to the separating matrix in an ICA framework, which could be converted to the forward matrix **H**. To proceed with this idea a constraint function is defined as:

(10.65)![equation](images/c10-disp-0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>p</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> 

where **H**(*p*) is the forward matrix of a dipole at location *p* and perform a grid search over a number of locations. The constrained optimization problem is then stated as [\[72\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0072):

(10.66)![equation](images/c10-disp-0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mo>min</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math> 

without going through the details the SNF **w** for extraction of a source at location *j*, as the desired source (ERP component), when there is neither noise or correlation among the components, is described as:

[(10.67)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0067)![equation](images/c10-disp-0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><munder><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></munder><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> 

where **C** [x] = **XX** ^T. In the case of correlation among the sources, the BF, **w**[*c*] , for extraction of a source at location *j*, includes another term as [\[72\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0072):

(10.68)![equation](images/c10-disp-0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>p</mi></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>p</mi></mfenced><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>p</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>p</mi></mfenced><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi>x</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> 

where ![images](images/c10-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover></math> includes all the sources correlated with the desired source and **w** is given in [Eq. (10.67)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0067). A similar expression can also be given for when the noise is involved [\[72\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0072).

The SNF algorithm finds the location of the desired brain ERP components (by manifesting a sharp null at the position of the desired source) with a high accuracy even in the presence of interference and noise and where the correlation between the components is considerable.

The ability of the algorithm for correct localization of the sources in various scenarios has been investigated. A forward model has also been built up using the Brainstorm software [\[73\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0073). Brainstorm is a collaborative, open‐source application for MEG and EEG data analysis (visualization, processing, and advanced source modelling).

A three‐layer spherical head model with conductivities of 0.33, 0.0042, 0.33 *μ*S/cm, for the scalp, skull, and brain, respectively has been used. 32 Gaussian pulses in 32 different locations with random orientations were created, peaking at different latencies and using 30 electrodes. This represents an underdetermined system. Several different cases have been examined in order to evaluate the effect of noise and correlation between the sources. 2700 voxels have been considered. The source of interest is originally placed at location numbered 1000. For the simple case of no noise and uncorrelated sources, an accurate localization of the source has been achieved as depicted in [Figure 10.8](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0008). In this figure, the numbers on the horizontal axis show the location of the vertices within the grid inside the brain. Also, to apply the proposed spatial notch filtering method to real data a Gaussian shape (which could be Laplacian shape) template has been selected and used as **r**.

The method has been compared to the standard linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV) BF for various levels of noise and correlation between the ERP and the background EEG. The results of this comparison can be viewed in [Figures 10.9](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0009) and [10.10](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0010).

To examine the algorithm for real EEG data the reference electrodes were linked to the earlobes, the sampling frequency set to *Fs* = 2 kHz, and the data were subsequently bandpass filtered (0.1–70 Hz). The EEG data were recorded for control and schizophrenic patients. The stimuli were presented through ear plugs inserted in the ear. Forty rare tones (1 kHz) were randomly distributed amongst 160 frequent tones (2 kHz). Their intensity was 65 dB with 10 and 50 ms duration for rare and frequent tones, respectively. The subject was asked to press a button as soon as he heard a low tone (1 kHz). The ability to distinguish between low and high tones was confirmed before the start of the experiment. The task is designed to assess basic memory processes for both healthy subjects and schizophrenic patients. ERP components measured in this task included N100, P200, N200, and P3a and P3b. However, the results for the P3a and P3b have been demonstrated [\[72\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0072). [Figures 10.11](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0011) and [10.12](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0012) show the results of P3a and P3b source localization for the control  and schizophrenic patients. In these figures the numbers next to the circles and squares show the patient number.

## 10.6 The Methods Based on Source Tracking

 

### 10.6.1 Deflation Beamforming Approach for EEG/MEG Multiple Source Localization

Poor spatial resolution of EEG/MEG motivates research into methods that can more accurately localize the sources from the recordings using these modalities. A popular strategy in brain source localization is by using the dipole source assumption [\[74\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0074). Physiologically, this assumption may not be always true. Under this assumption, electric current dipoles are specified by their three‐dimensional locations and their three‐dimensional moments. The LCMV BF is a well established method in MEG dipole source localization [\[75\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0075). BF provides an adaptive method which places nulls, using some linear constraints, at positions corresponding to the noise sources. The transient and often correlated nature of the neural activation in different parts of the brain often, however, limits the BF performance. As an example, since MEG has variable sensitivity to source locations, the noise gain of the filter varies with the changes in location. One strategy to account for this effect is to normalize the output power of BF with respect to the estimated power in the presence of only noise [\[76\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0076). Beamspace transformations for dimension reduction which preserve source activity located within a given region of interest have also been presented in [\[77\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0077). For more details of different methods for MEG source localization, consider \[[78](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0078), [79](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0079)\].

In [\[74\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0074) the BF approach has been generalized to include more constraints. The first constraint additionally stops the noise power at the output of the BF. This method, the so‐called *deflation beamformer,* assumes the covariance matrix of the noise is known a priori. The second constraint places nulls at known locations where other dipoles have been detected previously to improve the detection of the unidentified dipoles. In this approach, a dipole is located by finding the grid node which has the maximum power, while deflating the power of any dipoles that have already been identified. Using a regularized optimization approach by means of penalty functions such as Lagrange multipliers, the multiple‐constraint problem is changed to an unconstrained problem and solved. During this process the power at each location is estimated and normalized with respect to the power in the presence of only noise. The deflation BF method helps to overcome two main problems of multiple dipole source localization using the BF, i.e. its shortcoming of dipole localization to the dominant sources, and its inaccurate performance in the presence of highly correlated sources. In addition, to improve the performance of the method further, an iterative approach for deflation and localization of dipoles has been developed [\[74\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0074). To formulate the problem let **y** be one of the measurements from *N* scalp electrodes. Each dipole is specified by its three‐dimensional location *ρ* and its three‐dimensional moment **m**. The medium between the sources and the electrodes is assumed to be homogeneous, and the MEG field **y** to be the superposition of the fields from *q* dipoles. Therefore, we may write:

(10.69)![equation](images/c10-disp-0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>q</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">n</mi></math> 

where **n** is the noise mutually uncorrelated with the signals. For a two‐source problem, assuming source *ρ* [1] is already localized, the deflation beamforming problem for locating source *ρ* [2] is stated as the following constrained optimization problem for **W** [\[74\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0074):

(10.70)![equation](images/c10-disp-0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><munder><mo>min</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></munder><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi></mrow></mfenced><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>subject to</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><munder><mo>min</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></munder><mfenced open="&#8214;" close="&#8214;"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">n</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#961;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mtext>and</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#961;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi> <ce:anchor id="pp:330 np:331" role="page-break"/> <ce:anchor id="pp:331 np:332" role="page-break"/></math> 

The term **W**^(*T*) **H**(*ρ* [1]) deflates the first source. For higher number of sources more sources should be deflated before the new source can be detected. The optimum solution for **W** can then be found as [\[74\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0074):

(10.71)![equation](images/c10-disp-0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>d</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msup><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi>y</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>&#955;</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math> 

where ![images](images/c10-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>d</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> and ![images](images/c10-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo stretchy="true">~</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfenced><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math>. **C**[*n*] and **C**[*y*] are the covariance matrices of noise and background EEG including the first source.

In many practical cases, we have no prior knowledge about the true source locations. Under these circumstances, if we locate the first source incorrectly, localization of other sources may also fail. To circumvent this problem, the sources are found via a number of iterations such that in each round the other sources are deflated while searching for the current source location; the sources then swap and source 1 is estimated while previously estimated source 2 is deflated.

To examine the method on real MEG, event‐related fields (ERFs) were recorded in an auditory paradigm. 1500 auditory stimuli were delivered every 0.5 second bilaterally to the subject. The stimulus was a broadband noise lasting 0.1 second. This data set was selected because the stimulus train generates activity in the left and right primary auditory cortices. The data were acquired from a 28 year old male subject. Whole head MEG recordings were made using a 275‐channel radial gradiometer system. The sampling rate was 1000 Hz and recordings were filtered off‐line with a bandpass of 0.03–40 Hz. After visual rejection of trials containing eye‐blink and movement artefacts, the remaining trials were averaged. The estimated noise covariance matrix **C** *n* used in both the BF and deflation BF approaches, was calculated from the 0.1 second pre‐stimulus segments. In this experiment, two dipoles were considered: one in the right and one in the left hemisphere of the brain).

[Figure 10.13](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0013)a and b show the power profiles of the BF and estimated locations in axial and coronal views. The estimated locations are shown with cross markers. The estimated power profile and estimated locations using the deflation BF method are shown in [Figure 10.13](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0013)c–f. [Figure 10.13](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0013)c and d show the location of the first dipole while deflating the second dipole, and [Figure 10.13](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0013)e and f show the location of the second dipole while deflating the first dipole. The deflation BF method converged after three iterations. It is seen from [Figure 10.13](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0013)a and b that for the BF the sources are bleeding towards the centre of the head due to the partial correlation between the sources. Conversely, the deflation BF places the sources at biologically plausible locations in the primary auditory cortices in the left and right hemisphere. The power obtained using the deflation BF is also more focal than the power obtained using the BF approach. Furthermore, unlike for the BF, no spurious activations near the centre of the sphere model were observed when deflation BF was implemented [\[74\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0074).

![Figure 10.13 Topographies or power profiles of real MEG data obtained using (a) BF method in axial view, (b) BF method in coronal view, (c) deflation BF while deflating the second source in axial view, (d) deflation BF while deflating the second source in coronal view, (e) deflation BF while deflating the first source in axial view, (f) deflation BF while deflating the first source in coronal view \[74\].](images/c10f013.gif)

[**Figure 10.13**](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0013) Topographies or power profiles of real MEG data obtained using (a) BF method in axial view, (b) BF method in coronal view, (c) deflation BF while deflating the second source in axial view, (d) deflation BF while deflating the second source in coronal view, (e) deflation BF while deflating the first source in axial view, (f) deflation BF while deflating the first source in coronal view [\[74\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0074).

 

### 10.6.2 Hybrid Beamforming – Particle Filtering

In EEG or MEG source localization often the number of unknown parameters is higher than the number of known measurements and therefore the system is underdetermined. *Dipole source localization* assumes that one or multiple current dipoles represent the electric sources [\[80\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0080). To express and formulate the problem, suppose the measured multichannel signals **y**[*k*] from *M* sensors at time *k* are produced by *q* dipoles, so we can model **y**[*k*] as:

[(10.72)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0072)![equation](images/c10-disp-0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>q</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> 

where *ρ*[*k*] (*i*) is a three‐dimensional location vector, **m**[*k*] (*i*) is a three‐dimensional moment vector of the *i*th dipole and **v**[*k*] is the observation noise. It is assumed here that the number of dipoles is known a priori and there locations are to be found. Hence, the states are defined as [\[80\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0080):

(10.73)![equation](images/c10-disp-0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>1</mn></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>q</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

By introducing an *M ×* 3*q* matrix of location **F**(**L**[*k*] ) and a 3*q* × 1 vector of moments ![images](images/c10-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mi>k</mi></msub></math> as [\[80\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0080):

(10.74)![equation](images/c10-disp-0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> (10.75)![equation](images/c10-disp-0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mn>1</mn></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>q</mi></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup></math> 

In that case a matrix form of [Eq. (10.72)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0072) is given as:

![equation](images/c10-disp-0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mfenced><msub><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> 

where **F** is a nonlinear function of *q* dipoles. The state‐space equations of the particle filter (PF) take the following form:

(10.76a)![equation](images/c10-disp-0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></math> (10.76b)![equation](images/c10-disp-0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mfenced><msub><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> 

In which **w**[*k*] is the state noise. In these equations to estimate **L**[*k*] however, ![images](images/c10-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mi>k</mi></msub></math> has to be known. The vector of moments linearly corresponds to the EEG (or MEG) measured data and under no noise assumption, ![images](images/c10-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mi>k</mi></msub></math>, can be recursively calculated as [\[80\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0080):

[(10.77)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0079)![equation](images/c10-disp-0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mfenced><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> 

where **F** ^† = (**F**^(*T*) **F**)^(−1)**F**^(*T*) which is the pseudo‐inverse of **F**. Note that in [Eq. (10.77)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0079), ![images](images/c10-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mi>k</mi></msub></math> is estimated from the location matrix **L**[*k−*1] at the previous step and measurements **y**[*k*] at the current step. This method is a grid‐based method meaning that the sources are considered to be in one of the predefined vertices of a 3D grid inside the head. Therefore, after the prediction stage, the locations might need to be adjusted to the nearest cells' locations.

To use a BF, assume that there are *G* grid points out of which *q* of them are the source locations and the EEG/MEG signals can be decomposed as [\[80\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0080):

(10.78)![equation](images/c10-disp-0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>G</mi></munderover><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>i</mi></mfenced></math> 

To select the source of interest coming from location ![images](images/c10-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover></math>, a linear spatial filter ![images](images/c10-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover></msub></math> is used to have the following ideal response:

(10.79)![equation](images/c10-disp-0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close=""><mtable><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfenced><mspace width="0.2em"/><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><maligngroup/><malignmark/><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext>else</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

where **O** is a 3 × *M* null matrix. Using two new matrices ![images](images/c10-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mfenced><mo>&#8230;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>G</mi></msub></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> and **F** [**O**] = \[**O**…**F**(*ρ*(1))…**F**(*ρ*(*q*))…**O**\] which has zero entries except at locations of the dipoles we can have:

(10.80)![equation](images/c10-disp-0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msubsup><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi></msub></math> 

From this an optimum solution can be found as [\[80\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0080):

[(10.81)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0083)![equation](images/c10-disp-0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msup><msup><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup><mi>T</mi></msup><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">O</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></math> 

To construct the beamforming PF the spatially filtered data are used instead of the original measurements to compute the moment vector ![images](images/c10-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mi>k</mi></msub></math>. The filter in [(10.81)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0083) now can be applied to the measurements to have

(10.82)![equation](images/c10-disp-0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><munder accentunder="false"><mi mathvariant="bold">m</mi><mo>\_</mo></munder><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mfenced><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></math> 

Matrix **F** [**O**] in [Eq. (10.81)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0083) is constructed for each particle using locations indicated by particles from the previous step. Moreover, since matrix **F** is the matrix of all gains and is independent of the desired locations, for computational efficiency, its pseudo‐inverse can be calculated only one time. This algorithm has been applied to synthetic and real sources and its good performance demonstrated [\[80\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0080).

 

## 10.7 Determination of the Number of Sources from the EEG/MEG Signals

For the majority of applications in source localization a priori information about the number of sources is required. The problem of detection of the number of independent (or uncorrelated) sources can be defined as analyzing the structure of the covariance matrix of the observation matrix. This matrix can be expressed as **C** = **C**[*sig*] + **C**[*noise*] , where **C**[*sig*] and **C**[*noise*] are respectively, the covariance of source signals and the covariance of noise. PCA and SVD may perform well if the noise level is low. In this case the number of dominant eigenvalues represents the number of sources. In the case of white noise, the covariance matrix **C**[*noise*] can be expressed as ![images](images/c10-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">noise</mtext></msub><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></math>, where ![images](images/c10-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></msubsup></math> is the noise variance and **I** is the identity matrix. In the case of coloured noise some similar methods can be implemented if the noise covariance is known apart from ![images](images/c10-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></msubsup></math>. The noise covariance matrix is a symmetric positive definite matrix ![images](images/c10-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mtext mathvariant="bold-italic">cnoise</mtext></msub><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">=</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#963;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">n</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">&#936;</mi></math>. Then, a non‐singular square matrix **ψ** (*m* × *m*) exists such that **Ψ** = **ψψ**^(*T*) [\[81\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0081).

For both white and coloured noises the eigenvalues can be calculated from the observation covariance matrices, and then analyzed by implementing the information theoretic criterion to estimate the number of independent sources [\[82\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0082).

However, it has been shown that this approach is suboptimal when the sources are temporally correlated [\[83\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0083). Selection of an appropriate model for EEG analysis and source localization has been investigated by many researchers, and several criteria have been established to solve this problem. In most of these methods the amplitudes of the sources are tested to establish whether they are significantly larger than zero, in which case the sources are included in the model. Alternatively, the locations of the sources can be tested to determine whether they differ from each other significantly, in which case these sources should also be included in the model.

PCA and ICA may separate the signals into their uncorrelated and independent components respectively. By backprojecting the individual components to the scalp electrodes both the above criteria may be tested. Practically, the number of distinct active regions within the backprojected information may denote the number of sources. The accuracy of the estimation also increases when the regions are clustered based on their frequency contents. However, due to the existence of noise with unknown distribution the accuracy of the results is still under question.

In [\[84\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0084) the methods based on residual variance (RV), Akaike information criterion (AIC), Bayesian information criterion (BIC), and Wald tests on amplitudes (WA) and locations (WL) have been discussed. These methods have been later examined on MEG data [\[85\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0085) for both pure white error and coloured error cases. The same methods can be implemented for the EEG data too. In this test the MEG data from *m* sensors and *T* samples are collected for each independent trial *j =* 1, …, *n*[*e*] in the *m × T* matrix **Y**[*j*] = (**y** [1*j*] *,…,***y**[*Tj*] ), with **y** [ij] = (*y* [1*ij*] *,…, y*[*mij*] ) ^(*T*) . Considering the average over number of trials *n* as ![images](images/c10-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>n</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>, the model for the averaged data can be given as:

(10.83)![equation](images/c10-disp-0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">GA</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">E</mi></math> 

where **G** includes the sensor gains of the sources of unit amplitudes. Matrix **G** depends on the location and orientation parameters of the dipolar sources. Based on this model the tests for model selection are as follows:

The RV test defined as [\[84\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0084):

(10.84)![equation](images/c10-disp-0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>RV</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn><mfrac><mrow><mi mathvariant="italic">tr</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">GA</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">GA</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="italic">tr</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfrac></math> 

compares the squared residuals to the squared data for all sensors and samples simultaneously. The RV decreases as a function of the number of parameters, and therefore over‐fits easily. The model is said to fit if the RV is below a certain threshold [\[86\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0086).

The AIC method penalizes the log‐likelihood function for additional parameters required to describe the data. These parameters may somehow describe the sources [\[86\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0086). The number of sources has been kept limited for this test since at some point any additional source hardly decreases the log‐likelihood function but increases the penalty. The AIC is defined as:

(10.85)![equation](images/c10-disp-0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>AIC</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">nmT</mi><mo>ln</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mi>tr</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">GA</mi></mrow></mfenced><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">GA</mi></mrow></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>p</mi></math> 

In this equation *s* ² is the average of diagonal elements of the spatial covariance matrix [\[84\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0084).

The BIC test resembles the AIC method with more emphasis on the additional parameters. Therefore, less over‐fitting is expected when using BIC. This criterion is defined as [\[87\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0087):

(10.86)![equation](images/c10-disp-0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>BIC</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="italic">mT</mi><mo>ln</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mfrac><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi></msub></mfrac></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><msup><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mi>tr</mi><mfenced open="\[" close=")"><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">GA</mi></mrow></mfenced><mfenced close="\]" open="("><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">GA</mi><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><msup><mrow/><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">pln</mi><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">mT</mi></mrow></mfenced></math> 

Similarly, the model with the minimum BIC is selected.

The Wald test is another important criterion, which gives the opportunity to test a hypothesis on a specific subset of the parameters [\[88\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0088). Both amplitudes and locations of the sources can be tested using this criterion. If **r** is a *q* vector function of the source parameters (i.e. the amplitude and location), **r**[*h*] the *q* vector of fixed hypothesized value of **r**, **R** the *q* × *k* Jacobian matrix of **r** with respect to *k* parameters, and **C** the *k* × *k* covariance matrix of source parameters, then the Wald test is defined as [\[89\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0089):

(10.87)![equation](images/c10-disp-0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>q</mi></mfrac><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mi>T</mi></msup><mo stretchy="true">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow></msup><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo><mo stretchy="true">)</mo><msup><mrow/><mrow><mo form="prefix">&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></msup><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></math> 

An advantage of using the WA technique in spatiotemporal analysis is the possibility of checking the univariate significance levels to determine at which samples the sources are active.

The tests carried out for two synthetic sources and different noise components [\[85\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0085) showed that the WL test has superior overall performance, and the AIC and WA perform well when the sources are close together.

These tests have been based on simulations of the sources and noise. It is also assumed that the locations and the orientations of the source dipoles are fixed and only the amplitudes change. For real EEG (or MEG) data, however, such information may be subject to change and generally unknown.

Probably the most robust approach for detection of the number of sources is that developed by Bai and He [\[81\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0081). In this approach an information criterion method in which the penalty functions are selected based on the spatiotemporal source model, has been developed to estimate the number of independent dipole sources from EEG or MEG In this approach the following steps are followed:

1.  Calculating the covariance matrix **C** [**X**] from the measured data matrix **X**.
2.  Applying the SVD to decompose **C** [**X**] to obtain the eigenvalues λ [*i*] , where λ[1] > … > λ[m.]
3.  Calculating the information criterion value using the eigenvalues. The information criterion (*IC*[*k*] ) can be calculated using either:
    
    [(10.88)](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-disp-0090)![equation](images/c10-disp-0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">IC</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>w</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo mathvariant="italic">log</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></mfrac><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></munderover><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>w</mi><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></munderover><mo mathvariant="italic">log</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>d</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mi>&#946;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")"><mi>w</mi></mfenced></math> 
    
    when the noise information is accurate. In [Eq. (10.88)](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0090) *d*(*k*, *m*) = *k*(2*m* − *k* + 1)/2. In places where the noise statistics is unknown or:
    
    (10.89)![equation](images/c10-disp-0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">IC</mi><mo>=</mo><mo open="(" close=")"><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">k</mi></mrow><mrow><mo     where in this equation *d*(*k*, *n*[*e*] ) = *k*(*n*[*e*]  − *k* + 2)(*n*[*e*]  − *k* − 1)/2, ![images](images/c10-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the average of the *n*[*e*]  − *k* smallest eigenvalues. In both equations *n*[*e*] is the number of electrode signals, *k* is the number of assumed dipole sources to be estimated, *w* is the number of time points to form a spatiotemporal data matrix, and *β*(*w*) is the penalty function which can have constant or logarithmic values [\[81\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0081).
    
4.   According to the rule of information criterion [\[81\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0081) the number of sources with minimum IC is selected as the estimated number of sources.

In various experiments it has been shown that in moderate noise environment, which is the case of EEG signals, the accuracy of the method is above 80%.

 

## 10.8 Other Hybrid Methods

In some other works the researchers have tried to better focus on the source of interest by applying some preprocessing of the data. As an example in [\[90\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0090), empirical mode decomposition followed by the wavelet transform have been used to filter the signals and focus on the sources within particular frequency bands active in certain time intervals. Then, multiple sparse priors (MSP) and iterative regularization algorithms have been used to solve the inverse localization problem.

In a recent review by Michel and Brunet [\[91\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0091) the different steps in brain source localization have been explained and a stand‐alone freely available academic software called Cartool has been used to illustrate the results of their analysis. In this article a brief table has been provided to illustrate various academic and commercial tools which can be used for source localization (see [Table 10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0001)). Most of these tools are used in many other EEG or MEG analyzes too.

 

## 10.9 Application of Machine Learning for EEG/MEG Source Localization

As stated in the previous sections of this chapter, the brain functional activity is associated with the generation of currents and resultant voltages which may be observed on the scalp as the EEG. The properties of the dipole sources may be studied by solving either the forward or inverse problems. The forward problem utilizes a volume conductor model for the head, in which the potentials on the conductor surface are computed based on an assumed current dipole at an arbitrary location, orientation, and strength. In the inverse problem, conversely, a current dipole, or a group of dipoles, is identified based on the observed EEG. Both the forward and inverse problems are typically solved by numerical procedures, such as a BEM and an optimization algorithm. The forward solutions require accurate head model and the inverse solutions are inaccurate, cannot handle multiple sources easily, and are computationally intensive.

In machine learning‐based methods, particularly by using DNNs, the learning system is trained to find the best arrangement of the cortical source locations for having a particular pattern of multichannel scalp EEG recordings \[[92](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0092)–[98](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0098)\].

An early work on using artificial neural networks (ANNs) for brain source localization has been carried out by Abeyratne et al. [\[99\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0099). In their design, they use the head, data, and sensor models as a priori information while a simple scenario of spherical head model and single source has been considered. The network is trained on the data files assuming the position of the dipole is known. During the training phase, a dipole‐parameter‐vector (*X*[*p*] , *Y*[*p*] , *Z*[*p*] , *M*[*xp*] , *M*[*yp*] , *M*[*zp*] ) from the training‐output file, and its corresponding scalp‐voltage‐vector (*V*1 [*p*] , *V*2 [*p*] , …, *Vm*[*p*] ) from the training‐input file, are applied to the ANN simultaneously. Scalp‐voltage‐vector is set as the input and the dipole‐parameter‐vector is set as the target output.

In [\[100\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0100) feed‐forward neural networks trained to solve the inverse single‐dipole localization problem have an input layer of 27 neurons, corresponding to the M = 27 potentials at the electrodes. The input layer is followed by one or two hidden layers having N neurons. The output layer finally contains the neurons that produce the desired dipole parameters. The neurons of the input layers have linear activation functions and the neurons of the hidden and output layers use hyperbolic tangent activation function. Each neuron of the hidden and output layers is connected at its input to a bias neuron with constant output equal to one, to permit a non‐zero threshold of the activation function. Every potential distribution presented to the network is first average referenced by subtracting the average of all potential values. Subsequently, the average referenced potentials are normalized by dividing them by the magnitude of the largest. The dipole location parameters are normalized to 1 with respect to the radius of the outer head boundary in the simple spherical head model (9.2 cm radius). In the case of a realistically shaped head model, the location parameters are normalized with respect to the radius of the best‐fitting sphere for the scalp–air interface. The optimal dipole orientation (in the LS sense) for a given location can be calculated in a straightforward manner. Therefore, here, the neural network is employed to estimate only the dipole location parameters.

To test the system, it is trained using a large number of inputs with the dipoles spread randomly over the cortex. The authors have achieved an average localization error of approximately 3.5 mm for a network of two hidden layers.

In [\[101\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0101) both forward and inverse problems have been attempted using ANNs which are trained off‐line using back‐propagation techniques to learn the complex source‐potential relationships of head volume conduction. Once trained, these networks are able to generalize their knowledge to localize functional activity within the brain with reasonable computational cost.

 

## 10.10 Summary

Source localization, from only EEG and MEG signals, is an ill‐posed optimization problem. This is mainly due to the fact that the number of sources is unknown. This number may change from time‐to‐time, especially when the objective is to investigate the EP or movement‐related sources. Most of the proposed algorithms fall under one of the two methods of ECD and LD approaches. Some of the above methods such as sLORETA have been commercialized and reported to have reasonable outcome for many applications. A hybrid system of different approaches seems to give better results. Localization may also be more accurate if the proposed cost functions can be constrained by some additional information stem from clinical findings or from certain geometrical boundaries. Non‐homogeneity of the head medium is another major problem for EEG source localization. This is less troublesome for MEG; comprehensive medical and physical experimental studies have to be carried out to find an accurate model of the head. Using or fusion of other modalities such as fMRI will indeed enhance the accuracy of the localization results. There are many potential applications for brain source localization such as for localization of the ERP signals [\[33\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0033) and MRPs useful for BCI [\[102\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0102), and seizure source localization [\[103\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0103). Recent advances in EEG and MEG source localization including application of computationally intensive machine learning systems such as DNNs, allow for more accurate localization of multiple sources. Head model parameters, electrode positions, and the number of sources still remain as the main requirements for machine learning‐based source localization techniques.
